He introduces it with these simple words: “Among the extraordinary treatises of Mîr Dâmâd, this epistle is evidence of the godlikeness (*ta'alloh*) of his inmost consciousness. It shows how holy his life was, and what form that life took[^EII4-9].”

Thus the same theologian who was a resolute opponent of the Sufis pays tribute to Mîr Dâmâd the ecstatic mystic.

One might be tempted to find an unintended comedy in this tribute, were the subject not so serious. Had Mîr Dâmâd really succeeded, as he told Mollâ Sadrâ in the dream, in enclosing his actual thought within a web so impenetrable to an outwardly minded theologian that the latter noticed nothing? Had his obscurity deceived Majlisî? That reading would be rather simplistic.

Majlisî’s attitude, despite his opposition to Sufism, is more complex than it first appears. Otherwise, how could he have reproduced, without acknowledgment and as though it were his own, an entire page of Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî in his commentary on Kolaynî’s *Kâfî*[^EII4-10]? Besides, the ecstatic confession that Majlisî copied and expressly attributed to Mîr Dâmâd says what it means. Its style is difficult, but it is not written in a deliberately closed or cryptic language.

We also find that, in praising Mîr Dâmâd and discussing this account, Majlisî uses the word *ta'alloh*. As we know (see Book II, Chapter II), this is a key term among our mystical theosophers, particularly in the vocabulary of the *Ishrâqîyûn*. It denotes the sacred, reverential devotion through which the Illuminationists aspire to the *apotheosis*—the becoming godlike—contemplated by the Neoplatonic commentators on the *Chaldean Oracles*. If Majlisî praises Mîr Dâmâd in these terms, then the horizon open to him in practice was higher and wider than that of a merely literal, outward religion.

The study of religious experience must proceed with the utmost delicacy here, uncovering what lies hidden (*bâtin*) beneath what is apparent (*zâhir*). At that deeper level, some oppositions that seem insurmountable on the outward level resolve themselves. It is especially important here to keep in mind a distinction reflected in ordinary Iranian theological usage: that between *tasawwof* and *'irfân*, between Sufism in the strict sense and mystical gnosis, or inward spiritual knowledge.

Majlisî’s reservations about the first are shared by some of the greatest Shiite spiritual masters and mystics. Their criticism is essentially directed at a particular kind of Sufism—the very kind against which Mollâ Sadrâ, who could himself so easily be mistaken for a Sufi, wrote an entire treatise. We have already suggested the reasons: the organization of the Sufi orders (*tarîqat*), the authority of the *shaykh*, certain interpretations of monistic metaphysics that did little to encourage moral reform, and certain practices, among other things. These spiritual masters would therefore not accept without qualification Haydar Âmolî’s paradoxical statement that Sufism is true Shiism.

But replace the word *Sufism* with *'irfân*, and one finds broad agreement among all the *'orafâ*, those devoted to mystical knowledge. A significant difference is thus concealed beneath a question of vocabulary. In the West, it has become customary simply to equate Islamic mysticism with Sufism. No doubt that is true of Sunnism, where a spiritual seeker who wishes to go beyond the literal forms of religion must “enter Sufism.” It is not true in quite the same way of Shiism, where a believer need only follow the teaching of the holy Imams to its fullest extent to “enter *'irfân*.” This is the kind of Shiite spiritual thinker exemplified so perfectly by Mîr Dâmâd and those who came after him. A few details of his life and spiritual descendants will help us see it more clearly.

Both Mîr Dâmâd’s family origins and his spiritual lineage, together with the education he received from an early age, place him within the circle of the great families representing Shiism. Mîr Mohammad Bâqir ibn Shamsoddîn Mohammad Dâmâd Fendereskî Astarâbâdî was born in Astarâbâd in the second half of the tenth Islamic century; his biographers do not allow us to establish the exact year. The name *Dâmâd*, by which he is usually known, means “son-in-law” in Persian.

Strictly speaking, it had been his father’s nickname, and a pious story explains its origin. His father, Shamsoddîn Mohammad, had been a pupil of Shaykh Nûroddîn 'Alî ibn 'Abd al-'Alî Karakî (d. 945/1538–1539), one of the greatest Imamite scholars[^EII4-11]. His exceptional learning had earned this *mojtahid*, a scholar qualified to exercise independent legal judgment, the title *Mohaqqiq Thânî*, “the Second Investigator”[^EII4-12].

Khwânsârî judged that, since Nasîroddîn Tûsî, no scholar had done more than this *shaykh* to advance Imamite learning. He had studied in Syria, Egypt, and Iraq, and came to Persia under Shah Tahmasp (d. 984/1576), acquiring enormous influence in Isfahan as *Shaykh al-Islâm*. One night, our Second Investigator dreamed that the First Imam appeared to him and instructed him to give his daughter in marriage to his pupil Shamsoddîn. From their marriage, the Imam said, would be born a child who would inherit the knowledge of the prophets and the holy Imams[^EII4-13].

Thus Shamsoddîn became the *Dâmâd*, the son-in-law of his *shaykh*. Known by that name, he passed it on to his son, whose life may indeed be said to have fulfilled the lofty destiny announced before his birth.

Mîr Dâmâd studied at Tûs (Mashhad)[^EII4-14]. He came to Isfahan during the reign of Shah 'Abbâs I (996–1038/1588–1629), and from the death of Shah Mohammad (1004/1595–1596)[^EII4-15] onward, he lived there, wholly devoted to his scholarship and teaching. He belonged to the circle of Shah 'Abbâs, who regarded him with great respect and even a measure of fear, such was his influence. Later he was also among the intimates of Shah Safî (1038–1052 AH).

All his biographers mention his close and lasting friendship with his great contemporary, the celebrated Shaykh Bahâ'oddîn 'Âmilî (*Shaykh-e Bahâ'î*), another pillar of Shiite scholarship. He died and was buried in the Holy Land, at Najaf, in 1041/1631–1632. Majlisî tells us that the last words Mîr Dâmâd murmured before dying were those of the Quranic verse: “O soul at peace, return to your Lord, well pleased and pleasing to Him” (89:27–28).

It would be premature to give a complete list of his works here[^EII4-16]. The *Kitâb al-Ofq al-Mobîn* (“Book of the Supreme Horizon,” on being, time, and eternity), the *Kitâb Taqwîm al-Imân* (“Book of the Rectification of Faith”), the *Kitâb al-Sîrat al-Mostaqîm* (“Book of the Straight Path”), and the *Kitâb al-Qabasât* (“Book of Burning Embers,” to which we shall return) were commented upon by his immediate pupils and by later scholars[^EII4-17].

Like almost all Iranian scholars of his time, he wrote not only in Arabic, the “liturgical language,” but also in Persian[^EII4-18]. And he would hardly have been a true Iranian scholar had he not also been a poet. Rezâ Qolî Hedâyat mentions a *mathnawî*, a poem in rhyming couplets, of his composition called *Mashriq al-Anwâr* (“The Orient of Lights”)[^EII4-19]. It is fair to say that no branch of Islamic learning was foreign to him.

In short, he emerges as a profound thinker with an extraordinary capacity for work, driven by an energy and a demand for self-discipline that approached austerity. His pupils were devoted enough to spend years commenting on his work, and his humanity shines through the lifelong friendship that united him with Bahâ'oddîn 'Âmilî. These two facts speak most eloquently for the man himself.

We should add that he possessed a sense of humor, as certain anecdotes show[^EII4-20]. His biographers agree in emphasizing his fervent devotion, his intense spiritual practice, and the mystical disposition that could carry him into ecstasy—as the brief confessions translated later in this chapter convincingly attest. Such was the man who deserved to be called *Mo'allim-e thâlîth*, *Magister tertius*, the Third Teacher. Unfortunately, apart from two or three books, the publication of his works has so far been neglected. It is almost as though the writings of his most famous disciple, Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî—read, reread, and commented upon by generation after generation of Iranian philosophers—had partly eclipsed those of the master.

To place Mîr Dâmâd within his spiritual family, we should now recall his teachers and pupils, the connections leading to and from each of them—in short, recover and follow further the web woven by their thoughts and souls. As we have said, there is no prior research on which we can draw to make even the beginning of this work easier. The man who, through his pupils and their pupils in turn, would dominate the religious philosophy of Iran over the next four centuries had first studied under his maternal uncle, Shaykh 'Abd al-'Âlî (926/1520–993/1585), and Shaykh 'Izzoddîn Hosayn ibn 'Abd al-Samad (912/1506–1507 to 984/1576–1577), the father of Shaykh-e Bahâ'î, who was to become his lifelong friend and brother in spirit.

Two other teachers united in themselves the twin Illuminationist and Shiite traditions. One was Mîr Fakhroddîn Mohammad Samâkî Astarâbâdî[^EII4-21], who had himself studied under Mîr Giyâthoddîn Mansûr Shîrâzî (d. 949/1548), a renowned philosopher and commentator on Sohrawardî’s *Temples of Light*. The other was Sayyed Nûroddîn 'Alî ibn Abî'l-Hasan al-'Âmilî, a pupil of Shaykh Zaynoddîn al-'Âmilî (911/1505–1506 to 966/1558–1559), known among the Imamites as the “Second Martyr” (*Shahîd-e thânî*)[^EII4-22].

Thus, both by spiritual inheritance and by family descent, Mîr Dâmâd received the most authentic Shiite heritage. At the same time, he inherited Sohrawardî’s *ishrâq*—if not every particular philosophical thesis advanced by the Master of Illumination, then at least the spiritual “orientation” he had given to philosophical inquiry. We have already emphasized how this joining of traditions characterizes Iranian philosophy under the Safavids and also under the Qajars, whose most distinguished representatives include Mollâ Hâdî Sabzavârî (d. 1878).

This union, embodied in Mîr Dâmâd, continued through his pupils. We shall mention only a few. There are secondary figures, such as Hosayn ibn Haydar Karakî, the *moftî* of Isfahan (d. 1029 AH), and 'Âdil Morâd Ârdastânî.

But towering above them, with a fame beyond comparison, is Sadroddîn Shîrâzî (Mollâ Sadrâ), who would die barely ten years after his teacher (1050/1640–1641). What Mîr Dâmâd had been to Isfahan, Mollâ Sadrâ became to Shiraz, where it is still possible to sit in quiet reflection in the small room in which he once gave his lessons[^EII4-23]. We have referred to him repeatedly in the preceding pages. As we shall recall in the chapter devoted to him, his work dominates the entire Iranian philosophical tradition of the past four centuries, and a revival of traditional philosophy in Iran is now taking shape around it[^EII4-24].

Another figure, less famous but no less engaging, is Sayyed Ahmad ibn Zayn al-'Âbidîn 'Alawî (d. around 1054–1060/1644–1650). He was Mîr Dâmâd’s own cousin, the son of his maternal aunt. He became his pupil and then his son-in-law, but above all he was, and remained, his “spiritual child” (*walad rûhânî*), as Mîr Dâmâd calls him in one of the formal authorizations (*Ijâzât*) he granted him[^EII4-25].

As I have gradually reconstructed his writings, I have come to recognize their importance for the structure of Iranian Shiite Avicennianism[^EII4-26], and his major role in interpreting his master’s thought[^EII4-27]. He deserves a monograph of his own and would naturally occupy a prominent place in any comprehensive account of our School of Isfahan. The title of his great commentary on Avicenna, *The Key to the Shifâ*, is especially revealing, for it presents “Oriental philosophy” itself as that key.

Beside Mollâ Sadrâ and our Sayyed stands a whole procession of pupils and followers.

Let us name a few more. Mollâ Khalîl Qazwînî (1001/1592–1089/1681) wrote a substantial and very useful Persian commentary on Kolaynî’s *Osûl min al-Kâfî*[^EII4-28], one of the four foundational books of Shiism, to which we have already referred. All the commentaries on this work ought to be studied side by side.

Yet Mollâ Sadrâ’s philosophical commentary, though unfinished, surpasses them all in breadth of thought. The poet Mohammad Hasan Zalâlî (d. around 1031/1622) composed, in imitation of Nizâmî and Jâmî, a collection of seven *mathnawî* poems[^EII4-29]. Special mention must be made of Qotboddîn Mohammad Ashkevarî, who composed an immense kind of rhapsody in Arabic and Persian.

In three parts, it assembles traditions, quotations, and commentaries concerning the ancient sages; the philosophers and spiritual masters of Sunni Islam; and finally the Imams and great spiritual figures of Shiism[^EII4-30]. It is a kind of *speculum historiale*, a historical mirror of “divine philosophy,” the *Divinalia*, beginning with Adam and ending with the author’s own master, Mîr Dâmâd. In the chapter devoted to him, Ashkevarî reproduces in full the two ecstatic confessions translated later in this work.

Of course, this immediate circle around Mîr Dâmâd by no means exhausts the history of the School of Isfahan. We would also have to name the great pupils of Mollâ Sadrâ, such as Mohsen-e Fayz and 'Abdorrazzâq Lâhîjî; and Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, who comments on Ibn Bâbûyeh’s *Kitâb al-Tawhîd* as a true master of gnosis and stands beside Mollâ Sadrâ as one of the indispensable authorities for any study of Shiite mystical knowledge. A later chapter is devoted to him.

The school of Mollâ Rajab 'Alî Tabrîzî, whose pupil Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî was, remains almost entirely unknown: Mohammad Rafî'â, Shamsâ Gîlânî, and others. Nor have all these names yet brought us to the crucial fact of the age, already mentioned in discussing the Illuminationist tradition (Book II, Chapter VII): the extraordinary movement back and forth between Iran and India prompted by Shah Akbar’s generous religious reform. One great traveler, Mîr Abû'l-Qâsim Fendereskî, is named in the translations then being made from Sanskrit into Persian.

As an instance of spiritual traditions entering into one another, this undertaking can be compared to the translation of Greek works into Syriac and Arabic, or Arabic works into Latin, yet it has scarcely been studied[^EII4-31]. It was during this same period, as we have said—at the turn of our sixteenth and seventeenth centuries—that a whole group of Zoroastrians from Shiraz migrated to India with their high priest, Azar Kayvân.

Among them, Sohrawardî’s work found understanding and even devotion, as in the case of Farzanah Bahrâm, answering the very intention with which it had been written: to “revive the wisdom of ancient Persia.” These Zoroastrians recognized their own inheritance in the wisdom of *Ishrâq*. It was also at this time, in 1008/1599–1600, that Mohammad Sharîf ibn Harawî, an Iranian deeply familiar with Indian Sufism, translated the *Book of Oriental Theosophy* from Arabic into Persian[^EII4-32]. Through all this devotion and inquiry, and through the wounds and anxieties of the age, we come at last to the close of our eighteenth century and the emergence of the Shaykhi school with Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î—a living witness to the metaphysical and spiritual possibilities contained in Shiism (see Book VI below).

Mîr Dâmâd’s name has thus led us to evoke a long procession of sages, philosophers, theologians, and mystics. It may be said that what we have offered is a program for future research. Certainly.

But setting it out at least justifies the complaint we echoed earlier. We are dealing with an entire spiritual culture whose great works await the philosopher and researcher. They call for the long, demanding labor of examining and thinking them through anew, until a whole region, a whole spiritual “style,” finally becomes present on the horizon of our consciousness. Its absence is a paradox and an impoverishment that harms us all[^EII4-33]. Several signs allow us to believe that this other *jâhilîya*, this “age of ignorance,” is drawing to a close.

To conclude our account of Mîr Dâmâd’s work, his pupils, and his successors, I shall mention a work of extraordinary size, exceeding even Mollâ Sadrâ’s great philosophical *Summa*, the *Asfâr arba'a*. It is a commentary on Mîr Dâmâd’s *Qabasât*, written by Mohammad ibn 'Alî Rezâ ibn Âqâjânî Mazandarânî, a figure I have so far been unable to trace anywhere else.

Here we can only say that he completed it in 1071/1661 and that he was a pupil of Mollâ Sadrâ and probably of Mîr Dâmâd as well. A marginal note found in a related manuscript specifies that although he had studied under Mollâ Sadrâ, he did not follow him in his doctrine of the transcendent unity of being (*wahdat al-wojûd*). How many years of his life must this pupil have devoted to erecting so vast a *Summa* upon one of his master’s principal works—a work that was itself a monument of Shiite Avicennianism[^EII4-34]!

##### 2. Vision in the Mosque of Qom

Once again, we have used the expression “Shiite Avicennianism,” for it seems immediately appropriate not only to the thought and writings of Mîr Dâmâd but also to the entire body of inquiry that grew up around them. Certainly, as we have noted, this tradition contains many shades of opinion and many different philosophical positions. More often than not, its Avicennianism bears an Illuminationist coloring, even when our thinkers reject one or another doctrine associated with Sohrawardî’s line of thought.

Consider, for example, the crucial question of the *imaginal world* (*'âlam mithâlî*), the intermediate realm of spiritual images. Mollâ Sadrâ took a firm position on this question, affirming the “separate,” immaterial nature (*tajarrod*) both of the imaginal world and of Imagination as the faculty through which that intermediate world is perceived. Mîr Dâmâd does not accept the thesis of the imaginal world’s immateriality in this form; yet his argument includes the idea of an “imaginal matter,” which ultimately leads back to the perception of the very reality under discussion.

The delicate task is therefore to weigh exactly what each side means when it accepts or rejects the transcendence or immateriality of the imaginal, of the intermediate world called *barzakh*[^EII4-35]. Mîr Dâmâd the philosopher knew perfectly well what the reality of the world of visions implies. An Avicennian whose personal philosophy culminates in a visionary perception of the kind attested by the second ecstatic confession translated below is an Avicennian who has learned from Sohrawardî.

An Avicennian whose mystical experience flowers into a vision of the presence of the Prophet and the Imams is a *Shiite* Avicennian, as the account of Mîr Dâmâd’s vision in the mosque of Qom shows us. And that such visionary perception presupposes the spiritual teaching of *Ishrâq* is something Mîr Dâmâd himself confirms, by quoting at just the right moment a few lines from one of Sohrawardî’s most characteristic pages.

In short, this type of Shiite spiritual thinker deserves to be called *ishrâqî*, Illuminationist, because it decisively refutes an opposition too commonly assumed, and one we have already had reason to deplore: the supposed incompatibility between the most abstract philosophical speculation and the intimate devotion of the heart, between rigorous thought and an inner life so intense that it reaches genuine mystical experience. To maintain this opposition, one must hold a conception of philosophy fundamentally opposed to that of Sohrawardî and all those who share it, whether or not they call themselves *Ishrâqîyûn*. Some, for example, dispute the legitimacy of interpreting philosophically a mystical rhapsody such as the *Mathnawî* of Mawlânâ Jalâloddîn Rûmî.

But anyone who does so certainly understands philosophy very differently from these spiritual masters. What they regard as the very purpose and culmination of philosophical meditation flatly contradicts the claim that philosophy and mystical capacity cannot coexist. Since philosophical meditation stands at the threshold of the Way, it always remains possible, in the light of the Way’s successive stages, to recognize earlier moments and states as so many illuminations that first guided the traveler onto it.

Let us recall once again that Sohrawardî’s *Oriental Theosophy* begins with a reform of logic and ends with a reminder of ecstasy. In exactly the same way, Mîr Dâmâd’s extraordinarily difficult philosophical writings reach their summit in the lived states whose traces are preserved forever in the two accounts presented below. Of the second account we may say that it employs the technical vocabulary of Avicenna’s metaphysics of being, but that Avicennianism bursts beyond its own limits and ends far above itself. Even so, its Avicennian vocabulary attests full awareness of what preceded and made possible the emergence of the mystical vision. These echoes help us place both “ecstatic confessions” within the larger setting of Mîr Dâmâd’s teaching.

We owe the idea of collecting these two accounts together to Qotboddîn Ashkevarî. With a remarkable gift for arranging and weaving texts together, he brought into one sequence some of his master’s most revealing writings. What emerges is not a summary of theoretical teaching, but a spiritual personality appearing in flashes of light through these few texts[^EII4-36]. One of them comes from the conclusion of a book dealing with a precise point of religious law (*Kitâb zawâbit al-rizâ'*)[^EII4-37]—hardly the kind of work in which one would think to look for a mystical narrative.

But this is Mîr Dâmâd. The seal he places upon his treatise reveals his distinctive style and his mastery of *ta'wîl*, spiritual interpretation: his capacity to transform everything into symbols. A human being, he explains, is a recapitulation (*fadhlakat*) of the hierarchy of worlds, belonging to two orders of existence at once.

Through the “temple” (*haykal*) of the material, organic body, the human being belongs to the world of physical nature; through the thinking essence, the independent and immaterial soul (*mojarrada*), the human being belongs to the spiritual or angelic world. This is no harmless proposition of theoretical philosophy. It carries with it the necessity of a double birth and a double “nursing” (*rizâ'*), one in the sensible world and the other in the spiritual world. To be born into the spiritual world—one’s birth “in the true sense” (*wilâdat haqîqîya*)—the human being, as a spiritual child, must be nourished by the light of knowledge and the beauty of wisdom.

Now just as physical nursing (*rizâ' jasadânî*) legally establishes a kinship comparable to that arising from birth and has consequences and fruits in the order of life to which that birth belongs, so spiritual nursing (*rizâ' rûhânî*) creates a kinship belonging to the lineage of the spirit: an ancestry leading back to the communities of the angelic world. In that realm, too, it bears consequences and fruits. These are union with the holy, intelligible Lights, with the surpassing beauty of the archangels of the highest rank (*moqarrabûn*), and with the innumerable angelic communities.

Above all, it is union with the Holy Spirit (*Rûh al-Qods*), the *Giver of Forms* (*Wâhib al-sowar*): the Angel who, with the permission of his Lord, the Absolute Giver (*Wahhâb*), imparts to the soul the Forms or Ideas of knowledge. So it is written in that verse of the all-wise Book, the Quran, where the Angel addresses Maryam: “I am the messenger of your Lord, sent to give you a holy son” (19:19).

Mîr Dâmâd draws a further symbolic lesson from the legal status of *rizâ'*. The new kinship, with all its consequences, between a child and a woman who nurses the child without being its mother is legally established only when the child has been fed by her at least ten times. Likewise, the first stage of “intellectual or spiritual nursing” (*rizâ' 'aqlânî*) cannot be regarded as complete until the soul has assimilated the knowledge of the Ten Degrees distributed across the two hierarchies of Origin and Return—the two hemispheres, as it were, of the order of being (*nizâm al-wojûd*).

The whole Avicennian doctrine of the Intelligences is thus embraced by this double allusion. There are the Ten angelic Intelligences, marking the stages through which being proceeds, each giving rise to a world. The last of these is our own “Active Intelligence,” the Intelligence of humanity, the Holy Spirit: Angel of Knowledge, of the Annunciation, and of Revelation. In reality, however, all Ten are active Intelligences, and the Way of Return passes through successive elevations and teachings (*tarbiyat*), each presided over by one of them. This is also the spiritual initiation imparted in the long prologue to the *Mi'râj-Nâmeh* (*Book of the Heavenly Ascent*) attributed to Avicenna[^EII4-38].

These few pages, which bring such remarkable *ta'wîl* to the provisions of religious law, already reveal what Avicennianism means as Mîr Dâmâd lives it. By showing how a “kinship” is formed between the human soul, the “spiritual child,” and the angelic Intelligences, they confirm a feeling Avicenna himself expressed in his marginal notes on the so-called *Theology of Aristotle*: “The Active Intelligences,” he writes, “adorn and perfect the soul, which is like their child; for the soul’s intellectual nature is not given together with its substance, but is acquired[^EII4-39].”

Elsewhere, we have had occasion to emphasize the warmth of feeling implicit in the relationship between the soul and the angelic Intelligences. This “angelic education,” flowing from Avicenna’s cosmology, is itself enough to guard us against interpreting Avicennianism in a one-sided rationalist manner. The bond between a child and its parent is precisely the relationship now expressed in Mîr Dâmâd’s own terms.

The setting becomes richer still through the part played by the central figure of Avicenna’s theory of knowledge: the Active Intelligence, the Giver of Forms. It confirms our conviction that when our philosophers, through *ta'wîl*, “lead back” the Active Intelligence (*'Aql fa''âl*) to the Holy Spirit (*Rûh al-Qods*), they are very far from reducing spirit to intellect. Quite the reverse is true. Already in Avicenna, this movement back to the Holy Spirit shapes the mystical traveler’s personal relationship with his guide in the spiritual world, Hayy ibn Yaqzân.

The identification of the Active Intelligence with the Holy Spirit—that is, in the language of Quranic theology, with Gabriel, the Archangel of the Annunciation—is anything but artificial. As we have just seen, it governs Mîr Dâmâd’s entire vision of the “spiritual birth” to which the philosopher’s very vocation calls him. This vocation can be fulfilled only because the Angel of the Annunciation and the “Giver of Forms” (*wâhib al-sowar*, *Dator Formarum*) are one and the same.

Here this identity makes possible a mystical experience so genuine at its core that it immediately meets an archetypal theme: the divine birth within the soul, the human soul called to become the “mother of God,” as Meister Eckhart puts it. The same theme is expressed in the celebrated couplet of Angelus Silesius: “What good is it to me, Gabriel, that you greet Mary, if you have no such message for me?” The experience Mîr Dâmâd lived and expressed so briefly belongs to this same type of mystical experience.

The spiritual fact of decisive importance is that his soul’s union with the Active Intelligence places the philosopher-mystic in Maryam’s own position before the Angel who is the Holy Spirit. In both cases, the Angel’s message is received in the same way, as expressed in the Quranic verse of the Annunciation (19:19). Here, it seems, we have an unanswerable personal testimony to the meaning of Avicennianism: it is more than a philosophical doctrine; it is a form of spiritual life. And it is moving that this testimony should come to us, six centuries after Avicenna, from the master of the School of Isfahan, *Magister tertius*.

Mîr Dâmâd’s statements about the sage’s “theosophic” goal—the full realization of divine wisdom—are entirely consistent with this understanding. Ashkevarî also records the conclusion of the *Zawâbit*, which agrees word for word with statements found in the *Book of Celestial Dewdrops*; these, in turn, come almost literally from Sohrawardî.

“The soul,” Mîr Dâmâd writes, “must become capable of combining contemplation of the world of Mysteries with the vision of the sensible world: capable of shedding its body, of loosening the knots in the ropes of physical nature, so that it may ascend to the spiritual world and unite with the archangelic Intelligences, whose Orient shines upon it (*moshriqa*) with the radiance of their illuminations (*ishrâqât*). No one truly takes a place among the sages until he has acquired the practiced ability to cast off his body, until it has become for him like a tunic that he puts on at one moment and removes at another.” Word for word, this is what we read in Sohrawardî[^EII4-40].

These reflections form the spiritual setting in which Ashkevarî invites us to understand the two “confessions of ecstasy” that we shall now read. The broad outlines of this setting already reveal what we have called Illuminationist Avicennism.

The two accounts bring the nature of the spiritual experience into sharper focus, showing the specifically Shiite character of each. They demonstrate that when Mîr Dâmâd embraced Sohrawardî’s idea of a “metaphysics of ecstasy,” he was speaking from his own experience. He took care to record the dates of both spiritual events, which occurred roughly twelve years apart. The first took place in 1011 AH (1602–1603 CE): his vision in the mosque at Qom, whose imagery has since become established in Shiite devotion.

The second occurred in 1023 AH (1614 CE), and its character is quite different. Although the two experiences are inwardly connected, their visionary imagery is distinct. The first reveals the whole inner world of a devout Shiite: the sudden appearance, upon the illuminated mirror of his soul, of figures he loves and reveres in the secrecy of his heart.

The second gives us Mîr Dâmâd’s personal, experiential confirmation of the Avicennian vision of the cosmos, brought to incandescence in a visionary state. Whereas the second account survives in several transcriptions, the vision in the mosque at Qom is known to us, so far, only through Ashkevarî’s complete quotation of it, unfortunately without any indication of his source.

During the “month of God”—that is, Ramadan—in the year 1011 AH (1601 CE), Mîr Dâmâd, then presumably in the fullness of his youth and already settled for some years in Isfahan, was staying in Qom. This was the protected holy city of the members of the Prophet’s Household (Ahl al-Bayt), Qom the Well-Guarded (Qomm al-mahrûsa). He had taken refuge there, he tells us, from the troubles of the time.[^EII4-41]

One day, after the afternoon prayer, he lingered in the mosque.[^EII4-42] He remained kneeling where he had prayed, seated back upon his heels, still facing the direction of prayer, the qibla. Drowsiness gradually overcame him, and suddenly he felt himself swept away:

“Then,” he says, “I saw before me a radiant, translucent light (nûr sha'sha'ânî),[^EII4-43] shining with extraordinary splendor. It appeared in the form of a human figure lying on its right side.

“I also saw another figure, sublime in appearance, majestic beyond measure in the beauty of its shimmering radiance and the brightness of the light spreading all around it. This second figure was seated behind the one lying down. It was as though I knew instinctively—or as though someone had told me—that the reclining figure was our Master, the Commander of the Faithful, while the figure seated behind him was our Lord the Prophet.

“I was kneeling, seated upon my heels, directly opposite the reclining figure, facing him at the level of his chest. And then I saw him—the Imam, may God’s prayers and peace be upon him—honor me with a smile. He passed his blessed hand over my forehead, my cheek, and my chin, as though bringing me good news, dispelling my sadness, overcoming my disbelief, and shaking grief and desolation from my soul.”

The mystic then gathers the full attention of his inner faculties, but hears the Imam instructing him:

“Recite these words: Mohammad, the Prophet of God, is before me. Fâtima, the Daughter of the Prophet of God, is above me, over my head. The Commander of the Faithful, 'Alî ibn Abî-Tâlib, is at my right.

“Hasan and Hosayn; 'Alî (Zayn al-'Âbidîn); Mohammad (Bâqir); Ja'far (Sâdiq); Mûsâ (Kâzim); 'Alî (Rezâ); Mohammad (Taqî); 'Alî (Naqî); Hasan ('Askarî); and the Guarantor, the Awaited One—all my Imams—are at my left. Abu Dharr, Salmân, Miqdâd, Hodhayfa, and 'Ammâr, the Companions of the Prophet, are behind me. The angels are all around me. And God, my Lord, encompasses me and is my guardian.”[^EII4-44]

Having introduced the visionary to this recitation, which establishes a complete spiritual world—the Twelve Imams and the Five Companions arranged as though for the celebration of a solemn inward liturgy—the Imam makes his disciple repeat the formula that gives shape to this inner vision. He repeats it once, then a second time, and again and again, until he knows it perfectly by heart. Only when this newly formed structure has taken firm root in his consciousness does Mîr Dâmâd awaken.

“I shall long for that vision,” he concludes, “until the Day of Resurrection.” At the heart of this ecstatic experience was a supernatural initiation into a form of prayer whose deepest meaning lies in the integration of the soul and spirit into a complete whole. Such an experience calls for a fuller analysis than we can offer here, but we may at least indicate what seem to us its essential features. It should be compared with Haydar Âmolî’s vision beneath the night sky of Baghdad (above, Book IV, Chapter I, §4).

The complete image of Mîr Dâmâd’s vision in the mosque at Qom is arranged like a mandala, a symbolic pattern organized around a center, its outer boundary formed by the encircling angels. At the center stands the visionary himself. Around him are four groups: the Prophet; the First Imam; the eleven remaining Imams, ending with the Hidden Imam, the Awaited One; and finally the Prophet’s Companions.

Rising above the entire arrangement, directly over the mystic’s head—and thus above the field of his consciousness—is the person of Fâtima. Every condition of the symbolism of the center[^EII4-45] seems to be present, allowing us to grasp the significance of this ecstatic experience. It marks the resolution of a long process of inward maturation, one that must have involved severe spiritual trials.

The mystic has now truly reached the Center—his own center. In doing so, he has gained access to his own wholeness, the experience of integration: he recognizes the Self that encompasses him (mohît), yet remains beyond ordinary consciousness, on the far side of the boundary—the angelic crown—that both defines and surrounds him.

Similarly, in Haydar Âmolî’s vision, the mystic’s Self is represented by the empty center of a rectangular figure. This encounter with the Self must not be confused with a dissolution into something impersonal, as though it were the opposite of an encounter with the supreme personal God. No one has ever seen God, or the Self.

Yet their revelation takes shape through deeply personal symbols, within an encounter that is, above all, a dialogue. Mîr Dâmâd is surrounded by those who belong to him, and to whom he himself belongs. Fâtima’s commanding position is significant. Here she appears as Anima-Sophia, the soul as Wisdom, the symbol of personal wholeness.

We shall see again that she stands at the heart of a distinctively Shiite understanding of divine Wisdom, while the supreme God remains invisible, beyond them all (min warâ'ihim), in an untouched transcendence that will give rise to the entire Ismaili doctrine of angels.

In its structure, Mîr Dâmâd’s vision in the mosque at Qom might be compared with the ecstasy of Hermes, which culminates in the hymn: “Powers within me, sing the One and the All; sing in harmony with my will” (Corpus Hermeticum, XIII, 18). We might also compare it with the vision of Hermas (Similitude, X), who, accompanied by twelve young women representing twelve Holy Spirits, spends the night keeping watch near the Tower, awaiting the appearance at dawn of the “magnificent Angel.”

In each case, the vision brings together all the “powers of the soul”: presences dwelling within the soul, which an “angelic education” gradually makes familiar to the mystic’s consciousness. They bear the imprint of his origin and spiritual lineage. They are the very being of his being. These comparisons can only be suggested in passing.

What matters here is that, in Mîr Dâmâd’s first confession of ecstasy, we encounter a specifically Imami—that is, Twelver Shiite—form of the experience of integration. In it, the fullness of being begins to reveal itself through the manifestation of the pleroma, the complete spiritual world experienced as an all-embracing Presence. Its distinctive features disclose the images and hopes that remain silently alive and active within the fervor of Shiite devotion.[^EII4-46]

##### 3. Exaltation in Solitude

The second “confession of ecstasy” concerns a spiritual experience that came to Mîr Dâmâd some twelve years later (1023 AH / 1614 CE). The circumstances had changed. He was now in Isfahan; he had become a master, and his inner experience had deepened. This vision would come to him not in a mosque, but in solitude, during a private retreat.

Hence our choice of a phrase borrowed from Barrès, which we earlier applied to Isfahan itself: “exaltation in solitude.” Building upon what we have learned about the spiritual setting of these visions, we shall show—and this will be the conclusion of the chapter—how this ecstasy puts its final stamp upon Mîr Dâmâd’s Avicennism, transforming it into a visionary experience.

But first, the very date of the event offers a precious clue to its specifically Shiite character, confirming what the first account has already taught us. There can be little doubt that this narrative of ecstasy made a profound impression not only upon Mîr Dâmâd’s immediate disciples, as Ashkevarî’s careful transcription shows, but also upon later admirers whose intellectual outlook sometimes differed sharply from his own.

The great theologian Majlisî, for example, included a transcription in his monumental encyclopedia. All these readers, from different perspectives, must have been struck by the living example of a master whose personal experience demonstrated the primacy of spiritual realization over purely theoretical knowledge.

We must therefore begin with the date: Friday, 14 Sha'bân, in the year 1023 of the Hegira (1614 CE), eighteen years before Mîr Dâmâd’s death, when he must have been in the full strength of maturity. As in the earlier account, his care in recording the exact date—as someone today might do in a private diary—confirms the psychological significance of what he had undergone. He wished to preserve, in a brief account, the memory of an experience that had shaken his entire being.

It was brought about by the recitation of a dhikr, a meditative invocation of God, centered upon two divine names: al-Ghanî, the One who is sufficient unto Himself, and al-Moghnî, the One who grants sufficiency and makes up for all that is lacking. The meaning contained in these names would suddenly transform Avicennian cosmology into an intensely dramatic vision.

Yet if we consider the particular day on which Mîr Dâmâd chose to perform this dhikr, we discover that the elevation of Avicennian philosophy into visionary experience bears an unmistakably Shiite imprint.

Indeed, the date itself announces the meaning and significance of the ecstasy, once we recognize the wealth of associations it would have carried for anyone formed within Shiite religious life, whatever branch of Shiism they belonged to. The special excellence of the month of Sha'bân, and of the spiritual exercises chosen for its observance, are familiar themes of practical theology.[^EII4-47]

But the sacred power of this month reaches its height during the night between the fourteenth and fifteenth days, the night that divides the month into two halves. Religious traditions and liturgical prescriptions recommend particular prayers and spiritual exercises for its observance.[^EII4-48]

Above all, its special significance lies in the belief that it marks the birth, in 255 AH (869 CE), of the Imam of our time: the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam, knowledge of whom is a saving spiritual knowledge, and whose eventual reappearance is to bring about the transfiguration of the world.[^EII4-49] Long before this, however, a traditional report (khabar) attributed to the Fifth Imam, Mohammad Bâqir (d. 115 AH / 733 CE), had expressed the sacred meaning of this mystical night in the following terms:

“When someone asked Imam Bâqir—peace be upon him—about the excellence of the night of mid-Sha'bân, he replied: ‘It is the most exalted of nights after the Night of Destiny (Laylat al-Qadr). On this night, God bestows His grace upon His worshippers and forgives them in His mercy. Make every effort, then, to draw near to God in intimacy on this night.

“For this is the night concerning which God has sworn to Himself that He will not send away empty-handed anyone who calls upon Him, provided that person does not ask Him to sanction a transgression. ‘It is a Night that God established on our account and for our sake, we who are the members of the Prophet’s Household (Ahl al-Bayt), as a counterpart to the Night of Destiny established for our Prophet.

“‘Devote yourselves, therefore, to invocation and the praise of God. Whoever glorifies God a hundred times on this Night will receive forgiveness for all their faults, and God will provide for their needs both in this world and in the world to come.’”[^EII4-50]

The Ismaili traditions place particular emphasis on the inward meaning of this Night. A disciple asks why one sometimes hears of the excellence of the day (yawm) of mid-Sha'bân, when the saying attributed to the Prophet speaks of the night, not the day.[^EII4-51] The answer is that day and night here symbolize the respective positions of the Prophet and the Imam. The Prophet declared, “Sha'bân is my month,”[^EII4-52] referring to his prophetic mission, the Risâlat.

But his emphasis on the night of mid-Sha'bân points to the exalted rank of our Master, the Commander of the Faithful. The Imam is the Night, for he possesses the ta'wîl: the spiritual interpretation that discloses the hidden meaning (bâtin) of revelation. The Prophet, by contrast, occupies the rank of the Day, for he proclaims its outward wording and apparent meaning (zâhir) through the revelation itself (tanzîl).

Religion contains both an outward and an inward dimension. The Prophet’s task was to reveal the outward dimension, while the other half—the inward meaning—was entrusted to his spiritual heir (wasî), the Imam. The Prophet therefore designated the Imam’s position symbolically as the “Night of the Half”: he is the guardian of the ta'wîl, the secret and hidden half of religion understood in its fullness. This is the meaning of the special excellence of the night of mid-Sha'bân.[^EII4-53]

Among the Nusayri Shiites, moreover, the ritual and appointed readings for this same night are particularly elaborate.[^EII4-54] Here another feature comes into focus: the capacity to perceive each day, each month, as a “person.” This is not an allegorical device, but a way of understanding being itself, grounded in the visionary perception of archetypal persons.[^EII4-55]

Thus, for example, the thirty days and thirty nights of Ramadan each have their own archetypal person: thirty male figures for the days, thirty female figures for the nights. The archetypal person of the Night of Destiny (Laylat al-Qadr) is Fâtima the Creator (Fâtir, in its masculine form). This conception belongs to a whole Shiite tradition concerning divine Wisdom, a sophiology, of which Louis Massignon first brought to light a text of extraordinary significance: Fâtima understood as Initiation itself.[^EII4-56]

Fâtima is likewise perceived as the archetypal person of the night of mid-Sha'bân.[^EII4-57] Only a few pages ago, we saw her as the Figure presiding over the entire field of Mîr Dâmâd’s vision in the mosque at Qom, just as she presided over Haydar Âmolî’s vision beneath the night sky of Baghdad.

Taken together, these indications allow us to glimpse the background of consciousness and of the deeper consciousness beyond it against which the precise date of Mîr Dâmâd’s second confession of ecstasy stands out. Which of his retreats was he staying in? Perhaps somewhere near Isfahan, on the banks of the Zendeh-Rûd? One would like to picture the setting.

But what matters is the date: 14 Sha'bân. Although he does not tell us the hour, this was the day immediately preceding the most sacred night, that of the fourteenth to the fifteenth. Shiite ta'wîl has now shown us the profound meaning of this Day and this Night.

The fourteenth day announces the imminent arrival of the night containing the Imam’s secret: the night that marks the dividing line between tanzîl, the outward revelation, and ta'wîl, the passage beyond its letter into its inward meaning. This passage beyond the letter is an exegesis—in the word’s original sense, a leading out, an exodus. For Mîr Dâmâd, this exegesis had become ekstasis, a standing outside oneself: the great Exodus spoken of by Sohrawardî, which Mîr Dâmâd, taking up the very words of the master of Ishrâq, had proposed as the goal of the mystical sage.

Thus the date is far more than a chronological indication placing the event within historical time. The night of mid-Sha'bân is itself sacred, liturgical time: a revelation of the holy within time. It is the time of this ecstasy, an irruption of what lies beyond history. The spiritual and psychological event takes its distinctive form from the sacred date on which it occurred.

Some years ago we published a critical edition of the short Arabic text containing this confession of ecstasy.[^EII4-58] We reproduce our translation here. It will give us the opportunity to recall, in conclusion, the central lesson we have sought to draw from Mîr Dâmâd’s two confessions. Both may now take their rightful place within the study of spiritual experience to which they belong.

Epistle of Mohammad Bâqir (Mîr Dâmâd), recounting his ecstasy in the world of the Malakût.[^EII4-59] May God perpetuate the glory of its author! In the name of God, the Merciful, the All-Merciful. All glory belongs to the Lord of the worlds. May His blessings rest upon our lord Mohammad and the members of his Household, the Immaculate Ones.

> One day in the course of this present month—Friday, the fourteenth of the exalted Sha'bân, the month of the Prophet of God, in the year 1023 of his most holy Hegira—I was in one of my places of retreat, absorbed in meditation upon my Lord, multiplying my inward invocations and repetitions of His Name: “The One Who Is Sufficient unto Himself.”
>
> I went on repeating without ceasing: “O You who are sufficient unto Yourself! O You who make all things sufficient!” I became oblivious to every concern except the desire to penetrate more deeply into the sanctuary of His Mystery and to feel myself dissolve within the radiance of His Light.
>
> Suddenly it was as though the lightning flash of a divine ecstasy[^EII4-60] came rushing upon me and tore me from the dwelling of my body. I broke the rings that held fast the nets of sensory perception;[^EII4-61] I untied the knots of the net of physical nature. I began to take flight on the wing of awestruck wonder, into the heaven of the angelic world—the Malakût—of True Reality.
>
> It was as though I had been stripped of my body and had left my familiar dwelling behind; as though I had polished the blade of my thought and been drawn from the sheath of my body; as though I had folded the expanse of time back upon itself and reached the world of eternity.
>
> And suddenly I found myself in the City of Being, among the archetypes[^EII4-62] of all the peoples who make up the harmony of the cosmos: beings that are primordial and beings that undergo change; divine and natural beings; heavenly and material beings; beings that endure and beings that exist in time.
>
> There were the peoples of Unbelief and those of Faith, the nations of Ignorance and those of Islam; those who advance and those who fall behind; those who came before and those who follow after, throughout all the ages of the past and all the ages yet to come.
>
> In short, there were all the countless individual unities arising from the joining of possibilities, all the atoms of every universe of existing things. All were present in their entirety and in every aspect: the great and the lowly, the enduring and the perishable, those already gone and those yet to come. They stood there company after company, multitude after multitude, assembled without a single one missing.
>
> And all of them turned the face of their very essence toward His Threshold, and fixed the gaze of their existence upon the place of His Presence—yet they did not even know it.
>
> All of them spoke through the poverty of their own essence, an essence that possessed no being of its own. All gave voice to the distress of their fleeting selfhood. And all together, in one immense cry of distress and appeal for help, they named Him and invoked Him, implored Him and called upon Him:
>
> “O You who are sufficient unto Yourself! O You who make all things sufficient!”
>
> Yet of this too they were utterly unaware.
>
> Then, amid this appeal that vibrated for the spirit alone, amid this immense hidden clamor, I began to faint.[^EII4-63] Such was the force of the sadness and bewilderment that overcame me that I almost lost all awareness of my own thinking self. I all but disappeared from the sight of my immaterial soul.
>
> I was on the verge of departing forever from the desert of the Earth of Becoming, of leaving once and for all the shore on which the realm of existence stretches out.
>
> But already that fleeting ecstasy was taking its leave of me, leaving nothing behind except longing and tender desire. That lightning-swift rapture abandoned me there, sighing and wounded by sorrow.
>
> And so I returned, once again, to the Earth of ruins and the land of desolation, to the field of falsehood, to the country of illusion...

##### 4. “That Immense Hidden Clamor…”

This extraordinarily beautiful passage from Mîr Dâmâd is remarkable both for the growing intensity of its emotion and for the richness of the language through which he seeks to convey it. The experience was at once visual and auditory. One would need a mystical painter to give form to its symbols, assisted by a musician capable of making them resound.

Yet through the inexhaustible resources of his own language, Mîr Dâmâd manages to communicate something of the image—at once seen and heard—that overwhelmed him to the point of fainting. The successive stages of his ecstatic account closely parallel those in Sohrawardî’s visionary narratives, which themselves express experiences actually undergone. From the very beginning, when the dhikr and the concentration of the mind induce a state of suspension, certain familiar echoes make themselves felt. One is the Avicennian Tale of the Bird, already mentioned in a note.

Another, no less striking, is the ecstasy described by Plotinus, which seems to have served as both model and goal for so many of the spiritual figures we have been studying:

“Often I awaken to myself by escaping from my body. A stranger to everything else, alone in the intimacy of my own being, I behold a beauty beyond all imagining.”[^EII4-64]

This account of ecstasy reached Arabic- and Persian-speaking spiritual thinkers through the Plotinian text known as the Theology of Aristotle. Many, as we know, accepted its attribution to Aristotle without question. Sohrawardî, however, already suspicious of so strange an attribution, openly ascribed the account to Plato.[^EII4-65] In any case, the Arabic version supplied much of the technical vocabulary that later writers would adopt.

To take just one detail: in the account preserved by the Theology,[^EII4-66] we read wa-khala'to badanî jâniban; in Mîr Dâmâd’s account, we read fa-ka'annî qad khala'to badanî—“as though I had been stripped of my body.” It is precisely this word, khal', with its suggestion of being unclothed, released, or stripped of the body, that Mîr Dâmâd used in the title of his epistle: Risâlat khal'îya, an Epistle on Being Divested of the Senses, or on being stripped of the bodily condition.

But the comparison cannot be carried through to the end, for the differences soon become apparent. Ashkevarî, the perceptive disciple, had already recognized them. He could hardly avoid mentioning the ecstatic account in the Theology of Aristotle, which he knew so well. He had no wish to diminish its significance.

Yet he suggests quite clearly that the experience of his own master deserves even greater confidence, belief, and acceptance (tasdîq, taslîm, qabûl).

Indeed, he seems anxious to forestall the objections of those who are always ready to doubt for reasons they prefer not to acknowledge—people for whom the spiritual gifts of a contemporary could never possess the authority of events reported to have occurred centuries ago.

But to deny that such experiences can happen again, says Ashkevarî, is to know nothing of the spiritual stages (maqâmât) traversed by those who experience ecstasy. It is to imagine that the One from whom this fullness continually flows is somehow unwilling to give. And our author quotes two lines by Hâfez which, like so many of his verses, have become proverbial in Iran:

“If the outpouring of the Holy Spirit once again lends its help, others in their turn will do what Christ himself once did.”[^EII4-67]

We must carry the analysis of these differences further. The Plotinian vision, experienced anew by Sohrawardî, is an ecstasy of triumphant joy and exultation. It is an entrance into the Spheres or Heavens of light (aflâk nûrânîya), an admission into a world among beings whose radiance is untouched by anything that might tarnish it in the lower world.[^EII4-68]

Mîr Dâmâd’s ecstasy, by contrast, reaches its climax in an overwhelming sorrow, brought about by seeing and hearing a distress that embraces the whole of existence. This is precisely what his meditation and his deliberately chosen dhikr had prepared him to encounter. It is as though the invocation becomes contagious throughout the cosmos.

No longer is Mîr Dâmâd alone in reciting it: every universe, and every being within every universe, joins in an immense symphony. Or rather, the visionary himself becomes their organ, their instrument, vibrating with their cry until he can bear no more and loses consciousness. What perceives this sound is not the physical senses, which are adapted to objects outside us, but the Active Imagination alone.

Only this faculty can make such an immaterial resonance present to itself and perceive it: the “immense hidden clamor” that carries its distress from the deepest abyss to the highest reaches of the mystery of being. What this heartrending appeal lays bare is the very secret of the origin of beings, as described by Avicennian cosmology.

But what had been a theoretical description has now burst open into an infinite drama. Its sudden revelation engulfs the mystic and tears him away from the familiar dwelling of his ordinary self. The cosmological pattern in question is well known. It is not a system that establishes the contingency of the world, any more than it establishes the world’s intrinsic necessity, still less anything resembling a supposed “historical necessity.”

Rather, it keeps every existing thing suspended between two conditions. On the one hand, each thing necessarily exists through another. Its existence is necessary, certainly, but the source of that necessity lies outside itself.

On the other hand, each thing is incapable of existing through itself. If we imagine its possibility of existing in isolation, that possibility cannot bring itself into being or maintain itself there.

Considered in themselves, beings are merely possible. If they actually exist, then their existence is necessary—but only because they stand in relation to the Being that necessarily gives them existence. This is the Being whose overflowing fullness is sufficient unto itself (al-Ghanî), the Being that makes up for the deficiency of every creature, overcomes its neediness, and grants it what it needs in order to exist through Him (al-Moghnî).

Now try to grasp, not merely as an idea but as something real, the immense distance between these theoretical considerations and the experience out of which the invocation arises:

“O You who are sufficient unto Yourself! You who make up for all that is lacking! You who make all things sufficient!”

Then we can begin to measure the distance between a purely theoretical Avicennism and an Avicennism experienced in the depths of the soul, all the way to ecstasy. The two are not simply stages along the same continuous path. There is a break between them, a passage to another level of experience.

A being capable of existing but unable, through itself, to realize that possibility; a being whose necessity comes from Another; in short, an incapacity to create the necessity of one’s own existence, to make up for one’s own nothingness, to possess in oneself what is needed in order to be—this condition is felt from the very summit of existence to its lowest depths, from the angelic world to the realm of inanimate creatures. Mîr Dâmâd’s vision embraced every world, including all the peoples of human history.

From the beginning, each of the cherubic Intelligences of the spiritual pleroma produces the Intelligence that follows it, together with that Intelligence’s own heaven and the Soul that moves that heaven. It does so through a threefold ecstasy. Each of these ecstasies corresponds to one of the three dimensions of its being. The highest dimension is precisely its knowledge that it exists necessarily through the Being that eternally brings it forth.

Yet from the very beginning, in the first of all the Intelligences, there also appears the beginning of a shadow. This belongs to the Intelligence’s lowest dimension: its existence considered as pure possibility. The shadow will grow as the procession descends, until it reaches our earthly world, the “farthest West,” as Avicenna calls it in his Tale of Hayy ibn Yaqzân.

There is a tragedy of being that deepens with every descent from heaven to heaven through the Avicennian cosmos. How could this be reduced to a harmless theoretical diagram, when it gives rise to a spiritual situation whose resolution Avicenna himself had already begun to sketch in his Tale of the Bird?[^EII4-69] Here, where Mîr Dâmâd has led us to speak specifically of Shiite Avicennism, that resolution begins to appear with distinctive features of its own.

We can discern them not merely as an abstract structure revealed by our analysis, but in the light of what two of Mîr Dâmâd’s closest disciples themselves teach us: Sayyed Ahmad 'Alawî and Qotboddîn Ashkevarî. It is deeply significant that Sayyed Ahmad, when commenting on Avicennian angelology—the doctrine explaining how the Intelligences proceed from one another—explicitly referred to ancient Iranian Zurvanism.

He did so to illuminate the seemingly inevitable appearance of the dimension of Shadow, which arises together with the appearance of the very first Archangel of the pleroma.[^EII4-70] That Shadow spreads down into our earthly world, accompanied by a growing and boundless distress. This is the distress expressed in the “immense hidden clamor” perceived by Mîr Dâmâd during the hours preceding the night of mid-Sha'bân.

As we have recalled, this is the Night on which the Twelfth Imam was born: the Imam who, since the Greater Occultation (ghaybat), has remained the hidden Imam of this age, the invisible Guide and the Awaited One. The date thus gives its full significance to an explicit connection made by Ashkevarî in a text that deserves to be remembered. For his comparison supplies the necessary complement—the Shiite answer—to the connection that Sayyed Ahmad had established from another direction.

In his lengthy chapter on Zoroaster, or Zarathustra, Ashkevarî mentions the Zoroastrian belief in the Saoshyant, the final Savior who will bring about the “transfiguration” of the world. He does not hesitate to draw a correspondence between the Zoroastrian Saoshyant and the Shiite Twelfth Imam, going so far as to make Zoroaster a prophet who foretells the Imam’s future appearance.[^EII4-71]

Sayyed Ahmad, for his part, was following the tradition of Sohrawardî’s Eastern or Illuminationist wisdom, Ishrâq, when he turned to the philosophy of ancient Iran. The parallels he discovered between the figures of Zurvanite cosmology and those of Avicennian cosmology were enough to reveal the hidden drama within the latter.

But this drama of the Avicennian cosmos also called for a resolution. The sense that such a resolution must exist is what connects Sayyed Ahmad’s Avicennism, with its Zurvanite coloring, to Ashkevarî’s identification of the ancient Iranian vision of the end of time with the Shiite vision of the same final fulfillment.

And all this occurred long before Western Orientalists began to notice the correspondences between the two. Our Avicennian thinkers made the transition from the concluding pages of Avicenna’s Shifâ' to the opening of Sohrawardî’s Hikmat al-Ishrâq through the idea of the Imam as the “Perfect Human Being.”

In the same way, they found the passage from the deliberately Iranian orientation of Ishrâq to Shiite teaching about the Imam by identifying the Saoshyant with the Twelfth Imam. Certainly, the Avicennian cosmology as they understood it equipped them to grasp the meaning of the eternal Ahriman, still undefeated. What we have sketched here is necessarily no more than a brief outline.

Yet it shows one way in which the remarkable and original synthesis of Shiite, Sohrawardian Avicennism took shape: the worldview shared by certain members of the School of Isfahan who were among Mîr Dâmâd’s most distinguished pupils.

Let us now bring this vision together with the personal demand that ta'wîl, spiritual interpretation, makes upon the philosopher-mystic—a demand of which we have already seen an example. Once we do so, it becomes impossible to confine our interpretation of Avicennism within limits that the Iranian Avicennians of Isfahan themselves would certainly never have recognized.

Mîr Dâmâd has given us a personal, experiential confirmation of the ta'wîl he embraces, by recognizing the “Agent Intellect”—the active Intelligence—as the Holy Spirit, the Angel of the Annunciation. In doing so, he reached one of the summits of mystical experience. For here lies the mystery of the soul’s rebirth, the condition of its eternity—a truth of which no theoretical demonstration could ever fully convince the soul.

“But the beings do not know it. The beings are not conscious of it.”

Hence their “immense hidden clamor.” This was the great lament at the heart of the ecstatic account, the cause of the overwhelming sorrow that brought the visionary almost to unconsciousness. And yet, when he comes back to himself, he is left longing for the very vision that caused such pain.

Are we to say that he longs for that sorrow, that he regrets its passing? Or should we rather say that, within the sorrow and through it, he discovered a sweetness so powerful that it overcame the very cause of his grief? We believe the answer lies in Mîr Dâmâd’s deeply tested Shiite devotion itself. It preserves a paradox that I have already been inclined to describe by placing it alongside one of the paradoxes of Lutheran spirituality: desperatio fiducialis, a despair that nevertheless trusts. Perhaps this is one of the enduring characteristics of Iranian spirituality, reaching back into the distant past: the simultaneous presence of opposites.

We can still experience it in the symphonic poems through which this spirituality expresses itself today, adopting the forms and laws of our own musical language. There is sadness within joy, and joy within sadness.[^EII4-72] Perhaps this, too, is part of the secret of the Night that marks the birth of the Twelfth Imam.

At the beginning of this chapter, we expressed the hope that, with Mîr Dâmâd as our guide, we might penetrate to the heart of the spiritual city of Isfahan. Perhaps we are now better able to sense the approach to that heart. And, as we suspected from the outset, to sense what this approach means is also to begin to grasp the very secret of a spiritual tradition that remained unknown to us for far too long.

We can now see how Avicennism and Shiism come together. Avicennism has undergone an inner transformation: from a philosophical system explaining the world, it has become a teaching about spiritual life, a form of experience actually lived. It is precisely this dimension of Avicennism that, in the West, people have sometimes found so difficult to understand.

Yet the process itself is not difficult to analyze. One figure dominates Avicenna’s entire account of how knowledge is possible: the Active Intelligence, the Nous poïetikos of the Aristotelians. Unlike the Active Intellect of classical Greek Aristotelianism, however, the Active Intelligence in al-Fârâbî and Avicenna is a separate Intelligence, an angelic Spirit.

Within the hierarchy of angels, it is the Intelligence closest to us, the “Angel of our humanity,” as Sohrawardî calls it (above, Book II, Chapter III). As we have recalled, our philosophers identified this Intelligence with the Holy Spirit, which Quranic revelation in turn identifies with the Archangel of Revelation and the Annunciation. We have repeatedly emphasized the profound implications of this identification.

When the Active Intelligence, which is the Holy Spirit, impresses the forms of knowledge upon the human soul, it is the Holy Spirit thinking itself within that soul and bringing forth there a form of itself. In this way it raises the human intellect from potentiality into actuality—from the capacity to know to the living exercise of knowledge.

Here we begin to discern the idea of the spiritual child (walad ma'nawî): the new being, the true being, gradually brought to birth through our efforts toward an ever-rising horizon of knowledge and love. We have already seen Mîr Dâmâd express this idea in an admirable text, where he presents the mystical experience through the figure of Maryam at the Annunciation.

Perhaps we can now understand more clearly the place occupied by Fâtima in the mandala that took shape in the mind of our master of theology during his vision in the mosque at Qom. We have also glimpsed certain unsuspected correspondences with the spiritual traditions of the West. What Mîr Dâmâd is seeking to express here, Meister Eckhart and Angelus Silesius, each in his own way, have articulated with an unsurpassed depth.

And since we are speaking of the transformation of Avicenna’s doctrine of knowledge into a teaching about spiritual life, we should recall an important fact. In the West, despite the failure of what has been called “Latin Avicennism,” meditation upon this same figure, the Active Intelligence, led Dante’s companions to recognize in it the features of heavenly Wisdom, or Sophia. It was to this figure that they eventually gave the name Madonna Intelligenza—Lady Intelligence.

The admirable text of Mîr Dâmâd does not contain a secret belonging to him alone. That secret gives shape to the entire spiritual tradition whose traces we have been following. The way Mîr Dâmâd meditates upon the Annunciation is exactly the way Mawlânâ Jalâloddîn Rûmî develops it in one of the most beautiful passages of his Mathnawî. It is quite possible that the master of Isfahan remembered Rumi’s account.

Maryam becomes the archetype of mystical experience. After a long period of preparation, the mystic suddenly encounters a person who is at once their own Self and a Self who stands before them as Another. The first impulse is fear and flight.

Only afterward does the mystic recognize that the very presence from which they wish to flee is their Refuge. It is the birth of a new being within the human being. The divine dimension of the person comes into flower: the transcendent heavenly Self, the person’s own true being, but encountered in the “second person,” as a Thou.

This brings us back, finally, to the Mazdean idea of the Fravarti, and to the many variations upon the same theme: the “Perfect Nature” of the Illuminationists (Ishrâqiyûn) (above, Book II, Chapters III and VI); the “invisible guide”; and the “Gabriel of your being” in Semnânî (Book IV, Chapter IV), among others. It is therefore fitting to quote here this magnificent passage from Mawlânâ Rumi’s Mathnawî: At the appearance of a beauty beyond all human measure, Before that Form rising from the earth, blooming like a rose before her, Like an Image lifting its head from the hidden depths of the heart, Maryam, beside herself, seeks refuge in God's protection.

But the Angel says to her: You flee from my visible Form into the invisible... Yet it is in that invisible world that I make my home and dwelling. O Maryam, look carefully, for I am a Form not easily seen.

I am the new Moon, and I am the Image within the heart. When an Image enters your heart and makes its home there, You may flee as far as you wish: that Image will remain within you, Unless it is an empty Image, without substance, Sinking away and disappearing like a false dawn.

But I am like the true dawn. I am the light of your Lord. For no night wanders about my Day... You seek refuge in God against me, Yet from all eternity I am the Image of the one Refuge. I am the refuge that has so often been your deliverance. You seek refuge against me, And I am the Refuge.[^EII4-73] One hesitates to weaken the suggestive power of this beautiful passage by adding commentary. In any case, a few words could never explain it. It would take an entire book.

Yet in the end, that book could only be the book of our own life—the book each of us is responsible for writing, and which is nothing other than our life itself. For the teaching of Mîr Dâmâd, like that of Sohrawardî, is that the personal search for philosophical understanding and the growth of our spiritual individuality depend upon one another. Neither can reach its fulfillment without the other.

### CHAPTER II

#### Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî

*(1050 AH / 1640 CE)*

##### 1. The Life and Work of Mollâ Sadrâ

Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî, the most famous student of Mîr Dâmâd, has appeared so often in the course of this book that it seems almost unnecessary to introduce him here as one of the great figures of Islamic thought—of Shiite thought in particular, and, more particularly still, of the thought and spiritual life of Iranian Islam.[^EII4-74] *Sadroddîn Mohammad ibn Ibrâhim Shîrâzî*, more commonly known by his honorific name Mollâ Sadrâ, or as *Sadr al-Mota'allihîn* (“the foremost of the mystical theosophers”), was born in Shîrâz around 979–980 AH, or 1571–1572 CE, during the reign of Shah Tahmasp (1524–1576).

We owe this more precise dating to the distinguished Shaykh Mohammad Hosayn Tabâtabâ'î, a professor at the theological university of Qomm. While preparing a new edition of Mollâ Sadrâ's principal work, he discovered a manuscript copied in 1197/1703 from the author's autograph, now lost. It reproduced a number of marginal notes that Mollâ Sadrâ had added to his own text.

Beside the chapter affirming the union (*ittihâd*) of the knowing subject (*'âqil*) with the form it knows (*ma'qûl*), Mollâ Sadrâ had written: “This inspiration came to me at sunrise on Friday, 7 Jomâdâ I, in the year 1037 of the Hijra [14 January 1628], when fifty-eight years of my life had already passed.” The calculation is straightforward: counting back in lunar years places his birth in 979 or 980 AH, corresponding to 1571 or 1572 CE.[^EII4-75] This date and that of his departure from this world (1050/1640) are the only two dates in his biography of which we can be entirely certain.

But the richness of his life lay elsewhere than in its outward circumstances. Those circumstances chiefly mattered for the difficulties they imposed on him, not because they eased his way toward worldly honors. The true biography of Mollâ Sadrâ is the unfolding of his inner life: the progress of his meditations, the books he wrote, his teaching, and his relationships with students who went on to produce works of which their master could have been proud.

These dates mean that the lunar year 1380 AH (spanning 1960–1961 in our calendar, and corresponding to 1338–1339 in the solar Hijri calendar used in Iran) marked the fourth centenary of our philosopher's birth in Shîrâz. In Iran, the anniversary prompted a number of publications and raised hopes that Mollâ Sadrâ's immense body of work would soon inspire and guide a revival of traditional metaphysics. Those hopes have since found confirmation.[^EII4-76]

I am thinking particularly of the monumental studies published by our friend Professor Sayyed Jalâloddîn Ashtiyânî, who seems, in some respects, like a Mollâ Sadrâ reborn in our own time. His vast learning, joined to a keen philosophical intelligence, is opening the way to renewed study of traditional philosophy.

There is, on the other hand, a tendency among some writers to interpret Mollâ Sadrâ by making rough comparisons with modern Western philosophies whose basic assumptions are entirely foreign to his thought. Such comparisons disregard the conditions that any serious attempt at comparative philosophy must meet.[^EII4-77]

For my part, I have tried to contribute as much as I could to this renewal of Islamic philosophical studies, especially in a field that had been almost entirely neglected until our own day.[^EII4-78] Comparisons, however, must rest not on the likeness of isolated terms but on analogous relationships.

Since such analogies can be found within the respective worlds of thought, I have sometimes suggested that Mollâ Sadrâ's genius combines, in a sense, the constructive, synthesizing power of a Saint Thomas Aquinas with the intuitive vision of a mystical theosopher like Jacob Boehme.

Perhaps so surprising a pairing is possible only within the horizon of *ishrâq*, the philosophy of illumination. And it is precisely within that horizon that we may hope for the renewal of a kind of thinking which, unlike our passing enthusiasms for this or that philosophy as a mere “moment of history,” seeks access to the eternal reality toward which the *fitrat*—the human being's original, fundamental nature—is always directed.

We can distinguish three periods in Sadroddîn's life. His father, a man of standing and comfortable means, spared no effort in his son's education; the boy, for his part, showed remarkable early promise, both intellectual and moral. At that time Ispahan was not only the political capital of the Safavid monarchy but also the center of Iran's intellectual life.

The numerous colleges mentioned earlier in connection with Mîr Dâmâd were flourishing there, and some can still be visited today. The greatest teachers were gathered in the city, offering instruction across the whole range of knowledge. It was therefore natural that young Sadroddîn should leave his native Shîrâz to complete his studies in Ispahan.

We must not imagine this course of study on the model of our modern universities, where one earns degrees in a handful of years. It occupied an entire period of life—or rather, it assumed that a person would devote a lifetime to the disciplines he hoped to master. It took at least twenty years to become a *mojtahed*, a scholar qualified to exercise independent judgment in religious law.

In Ispahan, Sadroddîn studied chiefly with three men whose names are celebrated in the history of Iranian thought and spirituality. The first was Shaykh Bahâ'oddîn 'Amilî, commonly called Shaykh-e Bahâ'î (d. 1030/1621).[^EII4-79]

From him Sadroddîn learned the traditional Islamic sciences: *tafsîr*, or Qur'anic interpretation; Shiite *hadîth*, the transmitted sayings and teachings; religious law; and related disciplines. He continued until he received his *ijâzat*, the personal authorization by which a teacher licenses a student to teach in turn. Throughout his life, Shaykh Bahâ'î maintained an exceptionally faithful friendship with the master whose life and work we examined in the previous chapter: *Magister tertius*, Mîr Dâmâd.

As we have seen, Mîr Dâmâd believed, like Sohrawardî, that philosophy is a vain undertaking unless it leads to spiritual realization and mystical experience. It was to Mîr Dâmâd that Mollâ Sadrâ turned as his master and guide in speculative philosophy, and in this respect he proved a worthy disciple. His reverence for his teacher is illustrated by the little story told earlier (p. 25, n. 20): in an impromptu conversation with a stranger, the young Sadrâ did not hesitate to rank his master among the very greatest. That reverence comes through even more clearly in two letters to Mîr Dâmâd concerning philosophical questions, which have fortunately survived.

One opens with a moving expression of gratitude and ends by placing Mîr Dâmâd among the highest company: if the supreme *pleroma*, the fullness of the intelligible world, contains ten archangelic Intelligences, Mîr Dâmâd deserves to be counted as the eleventh.[^EII4-80]

Finally, Sadroddîn is said to have been a student of a quite extraordinary figure, Mîr Abû'l-Qâsim Fendereskî.[^EII4-81] The evidence is less secure here. Biographical collections agree on the connection, but it is strange that Sadrâ himself never mentions it. In any case, we should recall the intense movement of people and ideas between Iran and India at the time, encouraged by Shah Akbar's generous religious reforms. Many Iranian philosophers, especially followers of Sohrawardî's *ishrâqî* tradition, gathered at the Mughal sovereign's court.

Mîr Abû'l-Qâsim Fendereskî seems to have been closely involved in the translation of Sanskrit texts into Persian. This was a cultural event of the first importance: through these translations, Hindu thought began to speak Persian in the language of Sufism. (Let us remember that Anquetil-Duperron came to know the Upanishads through their Persian version.) The names of these three masters give us, in broad outline, an idea of the education Mollâ Sadrâ received during the first period of his life: his years of apprenticeship.

Now the second period begins. Learning to think for oneself is never simple, anywhere, for anyone. It requires an uncompromising effort, and the farther an independent thinker advances, the more certain he is to provoke the hostility of every kind of conformism—of all those who fail to understand that there can be no “tradition” without continual “rebirth.”

Mollâ Sadrâ learned this harsh lesson firsthand.
