Since the power and sovereignty of the Imams belong to the western side of the higher world—the “place” of walāyat—we can now understand the full meaning of the Imam's gesture at the beginning of the tale, when he stretches the hand of his subtle body toward the west.

As for the two clouds brought into appearance by that gesture, Qāzī Saʿīd suggests their meaning by referring to a hadith of the Sixth Imam, Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq.[^EII4-194] This tradition states:

“The Imam ʿAlī is sovereign over what is upon the Earth and over what is beneath the Earth. It happened that two clouds appeared before him: a heavy cloud and a light cloud. The Imam chose the heavy cloud. Now, the heavy cloud contained dominion over what is beneath the Earth, while the light cloud contained dominion over what is upon the Earth. But the Imam gave his preference to the heavy cloud.”

Our commentator explains that “what is upon the Earth” means what is apparent, external, and outward—the exoteric. “What is beneath the Earth” means what is hidden, internal, and inward—the esoteric. It does not mean the underworld or hell (infernum) at all, but the Malakūt.

In the hadith we are examining, the light cloud follows the heavy cloud. This is because the Imam commands both. Although he has expressed a preference for the heavy cloud, he remains sovereign over everything upon the Earth and everything beneath it, as the tradition explicitly declares.

Having established this general principle, Qāzī Saʿīd sets out to explain the metaphysical reality (ḥaqīqat) represented by the two clouds. He begins with two premises, from which the truth of what is symbolized will emerge—that is, the truth of the reality perceived imaginally in the form of a “cloud.”

A) The premises. The first is this: the heavy cloud—the first cloud that the Imam's hand “spreads out” in our tale—represents dominion over what lies beneath the Earth, in other words, over inward reality. As such, it gathers time into itself, causing it to fold inward. For the journey through metaphysical realities (ḥaqāʾiq), those belonging to the inward level of existence, takes place outside the laws of chronological time, the dark and dense time called kathīf.

The light cloud, on the other hand—the second cloud in our tale—represents dominion over what is upon the Earth, in other words, over outward reality. It gathers into itself the visible aspect of the Earth: place, and the spatial character of place.

It follows naturally that within the hierarchy of being, this second cloud, representing outward reality, appears only in second position. For the folding inward of time brings about the folding inward of space, and not the other way around.

The second premise is this. The philosophers of divine wisdom hold that every species in the visible world has a corresponding being in the Malakūt. With God's permission, this being governs and protects the species, preserving its unity and holding its multiplicity together.

The Ishrāqiyyūn—the philosophers of illumination belonging to Suhrawardī's Eastern school—call this being the rabb al-nawʿ, the “Lord” or “Angel of the Species.” The work known as the Theology of Aristotle calls it the Kalima, the Logos, or the Word. The philosopher-theologians sometimes speak of a particular divine Name and sometimes of the Angel acting under the authority of that Name.

This malakūtī lord, or Angel of the earthly species, has two faces. Through one face it receives the influence flowing down from what is above it; through the other, it transmits that influence to what is below it.

When the spiritual knower fixes his gaze upon this celestial or malakūtī sovereign, holding his inner vision steadily upon it, he may himself come to be invested with the same quality: that of an intermediary and mediator between two worlds.

*B)* Having established these premises, Qâzî Sa'îd considers the following. The first cloud, which the Imam stretches out above his dwelling with his hand (the heavy cloud), represents the power of the celestial Angel or lord (*malakûtî*) over the inner reality of the species he governs—that is, over its *malakût*, its spiritual or heavenly state. He can therefore enfold time.

The second cloud (the light cloud) represents his power over the outward reality, the *molk*, or perceptible manifestation, of that species: the power to enfold space. The Imam, however, by virtue of his imamate and his all-embracing *walâyat*, has authority over both powers, that of the *malakût* and that of the *molk*. His case differs, then, from that of Alexander.

For Alexander, only space was enfolded (represented here by the second cloud) when he reached the land of darkness, where Khezr gave him to drink from the Spring of Life. For and through the Imam, both space and time can be enfolded. That double transformation is precisely what drives the action of the “Tale of the White Cloud.”

Qâzî Sa'îd now defines his terms. (a) One being of the *Malakût* is lord of the Earth's outward reality. He calls this being the Angel or Word of the earthly aspect of Earth (*Kalimat arzîya*). (b) Another being of the *Malakût* is lord of the Earth's inner reality. He calls this being the Angel or Word of the Earth's *malakût* (*Kalimat malakûtîya*). (c) Above both stands the lord of the Earth's *jabarût* and *lâhût*—the Earth at the level of the cherubic Intelligences and at the level of the divine Names. He calls this being the Logos or divine Word (*Kalimat ilâhîya*).

The metaphysical reality of time lies under the authority of the Angel of the Earth's *malakût*, its inner reality; it is through this Angel that the time of our chronology is enfolded. That is the meaning of the Imam's gesture when he extends the hand of his “*malakûtî* body” toward the west of the *Malakût*, where his *walâyat* holds sway.

By stretching the “heavy cloud” over his dwelling, he places that earthly dwelling under the authority of the Angel of the Earth's inner reality, who has the power to enfold time. This power acts upon time's original metaphysical reality (*haqîqat aslîya*), which embraces every past and every future.

When, in a secondary gesture, the Imam extends the second, lighter cloud over his earthly home, he places it under the authority of the Angel of the Earth's outward reality, the Angel who governs earthly space. At the Imam's invitation, the companions then take their places on the first cloud, the White Cloud (*ghamâma*)[^EII4-195]. This tells us that the Imam has already granted their wish to “enter the *Malakût*”: he has brought about the enfolding of time and space.

Consequently, measured by the dense time (*kathîf*) of our ordinary experience, only a very brief interval will be needed for the Imam and his companions to travel to the many worlds mentioned later in the tale. They will see prophets of the past: Sâlih, for example, who was sent to the people of Thamûd. They will see the Imam fight the people of 'Âd, whom the Quran (7:63; 11:52) describes as rejecting the prophet Hôd sent to them. This is possible only because the companions are present (*hozûr*) in the time inhabited by the people of 'Âd—or, more precisely, present to the time that exists within the people of 'Âd.

“Observe carefully for yourself what you are about to see,” Qâzî Sa'îd tells his reader, “so that your foot does not stumble after it has been made firm”[^EII4-196].

Next, the Imam commands a particular breath of wind. Our commentator explains that this breath is the *malakût* of movement, its Angel: the Logos or divine Word who has authority over the other two Angels, representing respectively the *malakût* of time and that of space.

The Prophet said of this “celestial” (*malakûtî*) breeze—the inner reality of the wind our senses perceive in this world—that “it proceeds from the Breath of the Merciful” (*Nafas al-Rahmân*). Through the faithful service of these three Angels or divine Words, governing movement, time and space, the Imam and his companions will undertake their strange journey over immense distances.

Yet by the “dark and dense” time measured on our clocks, they will have been “absent” from this world for only a few hours.

Salmân the Pure continues his account in the following words. We should now be able to understand the allusions: “Then the Imam made a sign to a certain breath of wind, saying: ‘Come down to us, O wind!’ And I swear by the exalted God: we saw the wind and the cloud descend, saying: ‘We bear witness that there is no god but the One, who has no partner. We bear witness that Mohammad is His servant and Messenger, and that you [the Imam] are the Friend [or One Close to] God.

“Whoever doubts you is already lost. Whoever holds fast to you is already on the path of salvation.’ (We shall encounter this threefold profession of faith, constitutive of Shiite belief, in one episode after another.) Then the two clouds came down until they resembled two carpets, fragrant as musk. The Imam said to us: ‘Take your places on the White Cloud.’ We sat down upon it. Then the Imam said: ‘O wind, carry us away!’ And we were lifted into the heights” (§§ 6–7).

The companions are now present in the *Malakût*, and their journey is a visionary experience. They perceive the beings and things of its subtle world through the faculties of their own subtle, *malakûtî* bodies. Naturally, the Imam no longer appears to them clothed in the perishable flesh he assumed during his fleeting earthly manifestation: the form of his earthly humanity (*nâsût*). They see him as he is in his celestial, divine reality, his “person of theophanic Light,” the light belonging to the fullness, or *pleroma*, of the eternal Prophetic Reality (*Haqîqat mohammadîya*).

As they take their places on the White Cloud, the Imam is transfigured before them (*metamorphosis*). He appears in all the splendour of what Gnostic or Docetist Christology had already called *caro spiritualis*, spiritual flesh. Qâzî Sa'îd will examine in depth every symbolic detail of this transfiguration.

“Then,” Salmân the Pure's account continues, “upon that cloud we suddenly saw the Imam seated on a Throne of light. He wore two yellow robes. On his head was a diadem of yellow hyacinth; the straps of his sandals sparkled at his feet; and on his finger was a seal of white hyacinth. The light of his Face almost blinded us” (§ 8).

Qâzî Sa'îd explains: the Imam has now cast aside the garment of his earthly humanity (*nâsût*). He appears to his companions clothed instead in the robe of his sovereignty over the spiritual world of the *Malakût*. This is the sovereignty of his universal *walâyat*: his investiture as God's Friend, or One Close to God, in relation to all humanity.

The Imam's Throne represents that sovereignty over the *Malakût* (over the cloud that is the *malakût* of time). The Throne therefore belongs to a world higher than the *Malakût*: the *Jabarût*, world of the Intelligences, and the *Lâhût*, world of the divine Names. It is pure, unmixed Light. We still have to explain the symbolism of the transfigured Imam's clothing and adornments in his “celestial” state. That explanation will follow from a theory of colours and their distribution across the three worlds.

The Light flowing from the supreme Principle—the sun in the heaven of the spiritual universes—takes on different colours according to its nearness to or distance from that Source, and therefore according to how pure it remains or how far it is mixed with “material matter” (*mâddat jismânîya*). Closest to the Orient of lights (*mashriq al-Anwâr*), the light is white. At the opposite extreme is the blackness of dark bodies, the farthest west, the “last of all wests” (*montahâ al-maghârib*) to which this light can descend: the point farthest from the Source.

Halfway between white and black is red. (We meet this same theory of colours in Sohrawardî, especially in the “Tale of the Crimson Archangel.”) Between white and red, nearer to the Light of lights, is yellow. Between red and black, nearer the material world, is green. This theory invites comparison both with the ordering of colours derived from the symbolism of the four pillars of the Throne (*'arsh*) and with the subtle centres (*latîfa*) of Semnânî's mystical physiology, discussed above (Book IV, chapter iv)[^EII4-197].

Applying his theory of colours to the three worlds—the highest, comprising the *Lâhût* and *Jabarût*; the intermediate world of the *Malakût*; and the lower world of *nâsût*, earthly human reality—our philosopher explains that white is the colour of the *Lâhût* and *Jabarût*, while black is the colour of *nâsût*. Between them lies the immense *Malakût*, containing every intermediate colour between white and black. Whatever lies near the outer boundary of the *Malakût*, where it adjoins the higher world, is yellow. Red lies midway between the two extremes; as one descends through the *Malakût* toward *nâsût*, the colours gradually approach black.

The meaning of the Imam's clothing upon his Throne of light now becomes clear. It follows a single principle: the hierarchy of levels of being. Everything that exists in our world has its source or archetype (*asl*)—its imaginal metaphysical reality—in the *Malakût*. Everything in the *Malakût*, in turn, has its source or archetype in worlds higher still, the *Jabarût* and *Lâhût*. Qâzî Sa'îd is, in effect, setting out the rules of an imamological iconography, a way of representing the “Imam in majesty.” The colours correspond to the different levels of the Imam's *malakûtî* form.

1) **The diadem** upon the Imam's head is made of yellow hyacinth. Among the three kingdoms of our world, the mineral kingdom is named first; so it is with the mineral world of the *Malakût*. The diadem is yellow because it lies close to the higher world, resting as it does upon the Imam's head.

2) **The two robes** of the Imam are yellow. Our commentator suggests that they should probably be imagined as a deep yellow, tending toward orange and therefore closer to red, since the torso covered by the robe is nearer than the head to the middle region symbolized by red. The Imam wears two robes, an outer and an inner, perhaps because, having removed the robe of *nâsût* (the appearance of his earthly humanity), he reveals himself clothed in the double light of the *Lâhût* and the *Malakût*.

3) **The sandals.** In the Imam's figure, his two feet are the part closest to the material world. They “rest upon this world,” in the sense that his authority extends over it. The *hadith* does not specify the colour of the sandals or their straps. Qâzî Sa'îd, perhaps remembering the iconographic details of the Prophet's celebrated vision—“I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms”[^EII4-198]—imagines the sandals as emerald-green and their straps as red hyacinth. The very idea of hyacinth undoubtedly evokes red. But there is more to it. The straps hold the sandals in place, just as the *Malakût* (spiritual reality) sustains *nâsût* (human reality). They are made of red rather than yellow hyacinth because, although they belong to the world of Light, their function operates at the lower level of the human figure. Its colour, green, lies between red and black. All this, of course, is an interpretation of the symbolism of colours, not a theory of optics. The entire iconographic symbolism contemplated and meditated upon in the Imam's “celestial” person culminates in the symbolism of the ring.

4) **The ring.** The seal worn by the Imam on his finger is made of white hyacinth. In the Imam's case, the seal is the trace of the *Lâhût*'s authority over the *Malakût*: it is what authenticates his power. Since the light of the *Lâhût* is white, the Imam's seal is made of white hyacinth.

Finally, the tale tells us that the light of the Imam's Face almost blinded his companions. Qâzî Sa'îd's commentary closes here with a doxology, flowing without any break in tone into the next paragraph (§ 9), which repeats verbatim certain expressions from the celebrated “Sermon of the Theophany” (*Khotbat al-bayân*).

To understand what is at stake—the Imam as theophany, a manifestation of God—we must return to Qâzî Sa'îd's commentary on the theme of the Face, as it appears in Ibn Bâbûyeh's “Book of *Tawhîd*.” There the Imam is simultaneously the Face God turns toward humanity (*Deus revelatus*, God as revealed) and the face humanity turns toward God, since that face is the very form of human religious feeling and faith[^EII4-199].

“As for the fact,” Qâzî Sa'îd writes, “that the light of the Imam's Face almost blinded the eyes of his companions, it is because the Imam is the Face of God (*Wajh Allah*, the theophany), because he is turned wholly toward God, and because he wears no covering made of the Elements that might prevent his being seen at the level of pure light. Blessed, then, are those companions, for they saw with their own eyes—their *malakûtî* eyes—the Imam in his state of pure light (*nûrânîya*).

“Even to know the Imams in their state of pure light would be enough to ennoble a soul; how much more so to see them truly. According to one *hadith*, whoever does not know the Imams in their state of pure light does not know them with the knowledge their true being deserves.” These words lead directly into Salmân the Pure's narrative: “At that moment al-Hasan [the Imam's young son] said to him: ‘Father! Solomon son of David was obeyed because he possessed the Seal.

“But by what means is the Commander of the Faithful [that is, you yourself] obeyed?’ The Imam answered: ‘My child! I am the Face of God, the Eye of God, the Tongue of God. I am the Friend of God. I am the Light of God. I am God's Treasure upon the Earth. I am power, and I am the manifestation of that power. I am paradise, and I am hell’” (§ 9).

The Imam's answer takes up themes found in the “Sermon of the Theophany” and certain *hadiths*. Historical criticism loses its authority over such sermons and traditions, because even if we dispute their attribution to the First Imam, 'Alî ibn Abî Tâlib, they nonetheless give voice to the eternal Imam as Shiite gnosis understands him: the primordial theophanic Reality without which the Hidden One (*Absconditum*) would remain forever the unknown and unknowable God.

We should particularly notice the change of clothing that precedes and announces this transfiguration, for it is a familiar symbol in the rituals of the mystery religions. To take off one garment and put on another is the quintessential act of passing from one world to another.

We shall encounter another striking example later. Its meaning here becomes clearer still when, at this point in the tale, we see the Imam slip his hand beneath his robe and draw out Solomon's very seal, adorned with a red hyacinth, to show his astonished companions.

From now on the Imam will appear as a figure of the Logos, a cosmic reality present to every form of being and sustaining its existence. Two episodes immediately following this scene, with a magnificent vision between them, help us understand this. They mark the visionary travellers' entry into the *malakût* of the plant kingdom and the *malakût* of organic life.

In the first episode (I am considerably shortening the account here, although no explanation can replace the power of its visionary imagination), the wind carries the White Cloud and its travellers “to a mountain rising to a dizzying height. At its summit stood a great tree, drying up, its leaves falling one by one. ‘What is this tree?’ the companions asked.” The Imam replied, “Ask it, and it will tell you itself.”

But the tree speaks only when the Imam himself commands it, telling the companions that he used to come beneath its shade to celebrate the divine praise. For forty nights now the Imam has stayed away, and the tree is wasting with grief at his absence: it lives by the Imam's fragrance and the sight of him. At that very moment the Imam lays his hand upon the tree. To the companions' amazement it becomes green again, covered in flowers and fruit (§§ 11–13).

What does this apparition reveal? What secret lies in the Imam's gesture? The essential points of Qâzî Sa'îd's commentary are these. The high mountain is how the Earth's *malakût* appears, because a mountain is what holds things firm, and the *Malakût* makes the visible world, the *molk*, firm and supports it. The mountain is therefore the Earth's imaginal metaphysical reality as it appears in the *Malakût*, the *mundus imaginalis*, or imaginal world.

The great tree is the manifestation of the Angel or Logos (*Kalima*) entrusted with the growth of everything that sprouts on the earth and from it: the whole world of plants. The governing idea is this: the *Malakût* is the realm of life that never dies, and what pours out and transmits this life is a cosmic liturgy.

A familiar saying sums it up: each time you offer a doxology (*tasbîh*), you plant a tree in paradise. The heavenly worship of the beings of the *Malakût* fertilizes the realities of the visible world entrusted to their care and makes them flourish. Each higher level of being performs a liturgy that transmits life to the level below it.

Thus the Angel of the Earth receives his life from the liturgy the Imam performs beneath his shade. Between these acts of worship the tree does not die—nothing dies in the *Malakût*—but it dries up as it waits to become green again when the cycle of cosmic worship returns the Imam to its shade.

Qâzî Sa'îd believes that philosophers express this same liturgical outpouring of life in their hierarchy of Intelligences, from the *Nous*, or Intelligence of the universe, down to what they call the “Active Intelligence,” the Angel of the human race (identified by theologians as the Holy Spirit or Angel Gabriel).

Our visionaries hear the great tree speak because every being in the *Malakût* speaks through the soul within it, and the speech of that soul is its prayer or praise of God. When the tree speaks of the Imam's fragrance and the sight of him, it expresses its longing to receive the life that the Imam, as light and source of life, pours upon it.

A magnificent vision unfolds between this episode and the next. The Imam takes his place again on the White Cloud and commands the wind to carry him away. “And the wind lifted us so high that the surface of the earth appeared no larger than a shield. In the Air [that is, in the space of the *Malakût*] we saw an Angel whose head touched the sun and whose feet rested on the floor of the sea. Of his two outspread wings, one reached the East and the other the West.

“As we passed, we heard him utter the threefold *shahâdat* [testimony to the One, the Prophet and the Imam]” (§ 14). This towering figure is the Angel of the *malakût* of the element Air, in other words, the Angel of the space of the *Malakût*. (Later we shall learn that he is the one known in the fourfold company of archangels as Seraphiel.) Qâzî Sa'îd has tried elsewhere, in his metaphysics of time and space, to explain the immense proportions of such an appearance. That metaphysics shows that, when we speak of enfolding, it is equally correct to speak of an expansion of time and space.

When both are enfolded within the presence of the contemplating witness, the witness, in turn, becomes present to all of time and all of space. The Imam explains to his companions: “It is I who, by God's permission, caused this Angel to stand forth. I entrusted to him the darkness of Night and the brightness of Day, and so it shall remain until the day of Resurrection” (§ 15).

What the Angel spanning every horizon reveals, then, is the totality of times and places. Every past and every future, every “east” and every “west,” is present at once, gathered into the Angel's Image as it appears to the Imam and his companions. This is possible because the dimensions of that total Image correspond to what their *malakûtî* bodies, through their subtle faculty of vision, can perceive.

In the second episode surrounding that great vision, our pilgrims reach another lofty mountain near the famous wall Alexander raised against Gog and Magog (*Yâjûj* and *Mâjûj*). “The mountain was entirely black, as though it were a piece of night, and vapour rose from it” (§ 16). In the outward, literal sense, Gog and Magog (Quran 18:93) refers to certain peoples of Central Asia at the edge of the known world, against whom Alexander was said to have built a wall or embankment.

Esoterically, something quite different is meant. We are at the boundary where the *malakût* of the plant world ends and that of the animal kingdom begins: the realm of everything possessing the vital breath, or *pneuma*, made up of a vapour of its own kind. We are still at the level of a lower *malakût*, where subhuman souls, satanic souls and the souls of demons with human faces remain captive at the level of animal life, unable to rise toward the higher heavens of the *Malakût*.

The ascent toward the *malakût* of genuinely human reality will be experienced as a journey all around the mountain of Qâf and up to its summit. Here again we shall see what follows when time and space are enfolded or expanded to match the subtle organ of visionary perception—that is, to match human reality at the level of the *Malakût*.



##### 5. Exploring the Mountain of Qâf

*I. The Three Thirds of the Night.* — “Then the Imam said to the wind: ‘Take us to the mountain of Qâf.’ The wind carried us to the mountain of emerald, or green hyacinth, which encircles the world. An Angel rules over it, having a perfect human form; he is charged with governing that mountain.” As soon as the Angel has greeted the Imam, the Imam grants his wish by asking him to visit the mysterious prophet Khezr (§ 17).

We shall understand the meaning of this last detail a little later. For now, let us note that we have reached the third great stage of the visionary journey. In reaching the mountain of Qâf, the pilgrims reach the *malakût* of the human being, which itself comprises three levels.

The mountain of Qâf is well known throughout the visionary geography of Islamic theosophy. It is at once a cosmic and a psycho-cosmic mountain, and in both respects its characteristic colour is green[^EII4-200]. As the mountain encircling our world like a dome and marking the boundary between our world of becoming and the world of the *Malakût*, it is sometimes said to be made of emerald, sometimes to bear an emerald rock at the crown of its vault.

In either case, the *visio smaragdina*, the emerald vision, tells us that this mountain is one of the realities of the *Malakût* close to our world, the *Molk*. As such, it is a bodily reality, but in a subtle state, governed by a holy Spirit.

Considered as a psycho-cosmic mountain, it recalls for Qâzî Sa'îd the agreement among the Gnostics that green symbolizes the Orient where the light of the Spirit rises over the body. And since the Angel who rules the mountain has a perfect human form and governs the *malakût* of humanity, Qâzî Sa'îd calls him the Angel of the human race, the Angel of humanity (*Rabb al-nû' al-insânî*). This is the very designation found in Sohrawardî's “Oriental Theosophy.”

Salmân the Pure continues his story. Our pilgrims first reach the lowest level of the human *malakût*: the *malakût* of the vegetative life within us. That is why, just as at the first stage, they find themselves before a great tree whose leaves are drying up. This tree, however—speaking, as we have already learned that everything with a soul speaks through its soul—tells them how serious its plight has become: “I used to take pride in raising myself above the other trees. Now the other trees take pride in raising themselves above me.

“For the Imam used to visit me every night, during the first third of the night. He would remain in my shade for an hour. Then a black horse would come to him. He would mount it and ride away. I shall not see him again until his appointed hour, though I used to live by his fragrance and take pride in his presence. For forty nights now he has abandoned me. His absence has plunged me into sadness and grief, and I have become what you see before you” (§ 18).

Without our commentator's help, the tree's words would probably remain an enigma. The essential point is this: everything in the celestial world of the *Malakût* corresponds to a reality in earthly humanity, in *nâsût*. Now the human being as we know it here has three states: the vegetative state that allows the body to grow; the state of an animate, living creature; and the state of a thinking being.

The hierarchy of these three states must recur in the Image of humanity as it appears from world to world, beginning with the *Malakût*. Necessarily, then, the first thing to appear there is the vegetative level: the *malakût* of the activity that sustains growth and nourishment. Our commentator tells us that the tree is the visible manifestation of the *malakûtî* Angel or Logos with a Michaelic function (*Kalima malakûtîya mîkâ'îlîya*).

No doubt this is because, within the supreme fourfold order of archangels, Michael is responsible for providing the sustenance by which beings continue to exist. As for the tree's withering, we must again recall the liturgical mystery linking the worlds. Its plight is more serious here because humanity is more acutely conscious of its own shortcomings and suffers more keenly from the Imam's absence.

But that is also why the tree—which represents the *malakût* of vegetative life inherent in the human essence—once took pride in being above the other trees.

What is called Night here signifies both the absence of light and the capacity to receive the influx of the Lights of the *Malakût*. The Imam's coming, therefore—the coming of the very source of those Lights, the treasury of the secrets of a cosmic *walâyat*—must take place in the night of Matter's capacity for receiving what it awaits: its Light. Why does it happen during the “first third of the night”? Because this Night, the receptive capacity of humanity's subtle organism (*isti'dâd al-latîfat al-insânîya*), is divided into three thirds corresponding to the three levels of the human *malakût*.

The first belongs to the vegetative element in humanity, the second to animate life, and the third to the thinking nature (*vis intellectiva*, *qowwat 'aqlîya*). “That is why,” Qâzî Sa'îd counsels, “you should conscientiously fulfil the requirements of the liturgy of the last third. For that final third of the night is close to the day when the sun of True Reality rises over the human horizon.”

The black horse that comes to the Imam at the beginning of the second third of the Night is the luminous metaphysical reality, or Idea (*haqîqat nûrîya*), of the species of living creatures (*nu' al-hayawân*, the “animal”). It appears black—a black light—because the Source of Life is found in darkness. Its arrival beside the tree shows that the tree is rooted in animate life and is governed by the lord of life. The human being is a celestial “animate plant,” a “plant-animal” (*nàbât samâwî hayawânî*).

The perfection the Imam pours into this plant therefore passes through the Idea, the metaphysical reality of animate life (*bi-tawassot al-haqîqat al-hayawânîya*). The three human natures—vegetative, animate and thinking—are thus brought together in a single image: a rider mounted on a black horse beneath a great green tree. Having cared for the *malakûtî* plant through his liturgy, the Imam mounts the horse to attend to the education of animate life. Our commentator sums it up: “The first stage is the physical human being (*insân tahî'î*), the plant of the *Malakût* (*nabât malakûtî*).

“The second is the psychic human being (*insân nafsî*), the living creature of the *Malakût* (*hayawân malakûtî*).

“The third is the intellective human being (*insân 'aqlî*), the divine human being (*insân ilâhî*). The words ‘I shall not see him again until his appointed hour’ mean: until the fixed time each night, namely the first third. The Imam's nightly visit to the human vegetative principle in its subtle state within the *Malakût* lasts until the end of the first third, until it is interrupted for forty nights.” Here, as before, the Imam lays his hand upon the tree, “and behold, the tree became green again and was covered with leaves. We sat beneath its shade. Its greenery shone resplendently” (§ 19).

We may now begin to understand the secret meeting between the Angel of the human race and the mysterious prophet Khezr (*Khadir*), counterpart or companion of the prophet Elijah. Khezr initiates those who have had no human teacher and is always encountered near the Spring of Life. The Imam's companions, too, wonder about this meeting and ask what it means (§ 20). I can retain here only one aspect of our commentator's explanation.

In Avicenna's system, the last Intelligence in the cherubic hierarchy receives the influx of the higher Intelligences and passes it on to human souls. Here, the Angel governing the mountain of Qâf—the *malakût* of humanity, the Angel of the human race, who is the human Form of the divine Logos for the human world—receives light and spiritual influx from the Imam-Logos of the worlds, God's vicegerent (*Khalîfat Allah*), sovereign over all the lords or Angels of the species (compare Philo's ἀρχὴ τῶν ἀγγέλων).

The influx received by this Angel overflows from him. He must transmit it to the source from which it will branch out through the entire territory of his kingdom. For this Angel, that is what it means to be established upon his Throne, and that is what his meeting with Khezr signifies.

A short analysis by Qâzî Sa'îd makes this clear. The *Malakût* surrounds the *molk*, because spiritual substance surrounds bodily substance, not the other way around.

Hence the exodus from the bodily world, following the traces of the soul, is always described as a journey or descent into the region of darkness: a passage through the density of the material world until one emerges into the *Malakût* and the emerald vision, the *visio smaragdina*. The first sign of the soul is like the dampness encountered by someone digging a well. A second sign comes when water is reached. The first degree is the sight of water.

Then comes “the contact of water with the limbs, until one plunges into it and is completely immersed, so that the fish which is one's body disappears into that water. It is as though one had become the water itself. Such a person has truly reached the Spring of Life.” This was the exemplary experience of the prophet Khezr. “He cast the fish of his body into the Spring of Life, that is, into the ocean of the world of Spirits, so that his fish disappeared [an allusion to Quran 18:60], his body was effaced, absorbed into the Spirit. His was a body made spiritual, whereas other individuals are Spirits made bodily.”

That is why Khezr is the Throne of the Angel of humanity (of the *Kalima*, or divine Logos, set over the human species): through Khezr the life of the *Malakût* is maintained and spread throughout the Angel's kingdom, through all who learn from Khezr's example how to reach the Spring of Life (commentary on § 17). This is one of the first secrets of the mountain of Qâf.

*II. Intermezzo.* — At this point comes an interlude: the Imam's companions ask a question that would naturally occur to a Shiite Gnostic. Their extraordinary journey allows them to behold the Imam in his metaphysical reality within the *Malakût*, transfigured into the pure theophanic light of a *caro spiritualis*, a spiritual body. They learn that he has always existed, and always exists, in the *Malakût*.

What is the relationship between this divine person of the Imam (his *lâhût*) at the level of the supersensible worlds—his inner reality—and the purely outward appearance they had seen until now in the Imam's earthly, historical humanity? This relationship between the Imam's *lâhût* and *nâsût* corresponds term for term to the relationship, in Christology, between the eternally pre-existent *Logos Christos* and the flesh-and-blood man Jesus of Nazareth, who appeared for a brief interval in history.

So the companions ask the Imam: “Were you not with us in your dwelling? Then when were you on the mountain of Qâf?” The Imam answers: “Close your eyes.” We closed them. Then he said: “Open them.” We opened them, and behold, we were in Medina[^EII4-201], and no one noticed us [that is, noticed our arrival from the *Malakût*].

“So here we are in Medina,” the Imam said, “without anyone being aware of us. Well, in the same way I am on the mountain of Qâf without any of you being aware of me [that is, being aware that I am there]. I swear by God! If you could see with your own eyes what I possess of the *Malakût*, you would cry: ‘*Anta anta*’ [‘You are you’: you are the absolute Subject, needing nothing beyond yourself to be yourself].

“Yet I am a servant of God, one creature among His creatures. I am someone who eats and drinks”[^EII4-202] (§ 21).

This already reminds us that, however exalted the Imam-Logos becomes in Shiite theosophy, it remains within the limits observed elsewhere by the Christology of Arius: the Logos is the first and highest of created beings. Before explaining the Imam's concluding declaration, however, our commentator turns to the companions' question: “We were with you in Medina. We knew everything concerning you. We saw you with us in the mosque and elsewhere.

“We cannot see when you could have gone to the mountain of Qâf.” In reply, the Imam tells them to close and then open their eyes. They find themselves in Medina, which they had never left bodily; yet they no longer see themselves there quite as they did before. For they grasp that, while they are in Medina, they are also on the mountain of Qâf, and no one around them notices.

The companions must understand: through the light of *walâyat* and their perfect receptivity, they have become people of the *Malakût*, “persons of light.” Qâzî Sa'îd here reminds the reader of his metaphysical premises. At their respective levels, movement, time and space correspond to one another, just as the boundaries of the worlds correspond. The subtler the space, the subtler its movement and time.

The *malakûtî* body is perfectly subtle and luminous; neither curtain nor barrier can conceal anything from it; neither earth nor heaven obstructs it. Such is the condition of Angels when they descend upon the prophets. The persons of the *Malakût* (*ashkhâs malakûtîya*) are not bound to one place in perceptible space rather than another: all places are equally open to them, all on the same footing.

So too with time and movement in the *Malakût*: they are so subtle that the times and movements of “our” world are enfolded within them, so that a mere fragment of *malakûtî* time and movement equals months and years of time in our world. By the time of the *Malakût*, the distance from the Ninth Heaven to the centre of the Earth is no more than the blink of an eye.

What, then, is the inner meaning of the command to close and then open their eyes? To close them, Qâzî Sa'îd explains, means here to close them to their presence upon the mountain of Qâf, whose wonders they are contemplating. When the soul turns toward one thing, contemplating it prevents the soul from contemplating something else, so long as its contemplation remains at the level of the heart.

Indeed, it belongs to the soul's very nature that, when it turns toward something, it becomes that very thing, provided its movement toward it answers an essential, ardent longing—a longing rooted in its own nature. Opening the eyes, on the other hand, alludes here to the companions' return to their selves of light (*ilâ dhawâtî-him al-nûrîya*), to seeing things through inward vision, through *malakûtî* eyes.

“Just as, for the *malakûtî* gaze, pre-eternity and post-eternity (*azal wa abad*) embrace one another in a perpetual *nunc* [now], so for those who possess this gaze the easts and the wests meet and join together.” For such people, therefore, circling the mountain of Qâf does not in the least exclude being in Medina at the same time. In an instant they grasp that they are in Medina, but in a way different from that of the people around them, who cannot perceive that the Imam's companions are on the mountain of Qâf.

“My friend!” Qâzî Sa'îd writes, “if you look with this gaze, then most of the things you at first judged impossible you will now see reflecting their realities upon one another in this perspective, as though they were at once something outside you and an inward state of your own. ... These are things we entrust to you for safekeeping; reveal them only to those who are able to understand.”

This entrusted secret includes the paradox of imamology expressed in the Imam's declaration: if you could see with your own eyes what I possess of the *Malakût*, you would make me God's equal, whereas I am only a creature. The formula in which the personal pronoun serves as its own predicate—in the second person, *anta anta*—expresses the condition of the absolute Subject. A subject wholly identical with its predicate needs nothing other than itself to be what it is: it contains no negation and no deficiency[^EII4-203].

Qâzî Sa'îd quotes one of the invocations composed by the Fourth Imam (one of the *ad'iyat al-sajjâdîya*): “My God! How can I call upon You, insofar as I am sufficient unto myself to be myself (*anâ anâ*)? And how can I keep myself from placing my hope in You, when You are sufficient unto Yourself to be Yourself (*anta anta*)?”

This means that my own egohood (*anâ'îyatî*), insofar as it feels itself able to be itself through itself alone, cannot coexist with seeking You, with an invocation addressed to You.

Hence we hear the Imam deny such egohood of himself. Here too we can resolve the dilemma in which literalist theologians have sometimes tried to imprison the imamology of the theosophers. The latter do not begin their metaphysics of being with being as something already there (see § 2 above). They understand its primordial, uncaused coming-into-being as an imperative addressed to being. The fundamental philosophical question is therefore posed not in terms of being (*esse*) or a being (*ens*), but as a command: *Esto!*—“Be!”

Thus there is no longer any question of whether the Imam acts as a demiurgic being to whom divine power has been “delegated” (*tafwîd*). For the primordial self-creating Will eternally commands being to be, and the Imam-Logos is himself that imperative, that *Esto*, at every level of his manifestation. The simultaneous presence of *lâhût* and *nâsût*, then, will not be understood here in terms of a hypostatic union.

The interlude is brief, but it lets us grasp in a flash how initiation into the *Malakût* is, by that very fact, initiation into the secret of imamology. Our pilgrims' visionary journey on the White Cloud will now continue. At its fourth great stage they will reach the *malakût* of the vital reality within humanity. That is why the next episode will again present details like those we have already seen.

*III. The Prophet Sâlih.* — “Then we came to a garden among the gardens of paradise. And behold, before us was a young man (*shâbb*) performing the Prayer between two graves. We asked the Imam: ‘Who is this young man?’

“‘He is my brother Sâlih the prophet,’ he told us, ‘and the two graves between which he performs his worship are those of his parents.’ When Sâlih saw us, he approached the Imam in tears. We said to him: ‘Why are you weeping?’ He replied: ‘The Imam used to pass by me each morning and sit with me. My worship grew more fervent as I gazed upon him.

“But he has not come for forty days now, and that has overwhelmed me with sorrow. I cannot hold back my tears of longing for him, because I have suffered the misfortune you see.’ Then we said to the Imam: ‘This is surely the most extraordinary thing we have seen! You were with us every day, and yet every day you came here to visit this knight of the soul (*fatâ*)?’” (§ 22).

My translation of *fatâ* as “knight of the soul” is especially significant here. It belongs to a way of thinking that sees the prophets' mission as one of “spiritual chivalry,” their struggle as the struggle of knights. Sâlih, mentioned repeatedly in the Quran, was a *nabi*, a prophet sent to the Arab people of Thamûd, who, of course, rejected his mission.

*Fotowwat* (in Persian, *javân-mardî*) signifies a youthfulness of the soul rather than of the physical person. Its chief virtue is generous, selfless devotion to a cause—here, God's cause. It played a considerable role in Islamic spirituality and, closely bound up with Shiite ideas, gave shape to a way of life governed by the principle of companionship. Others have already suggested “knight” as an equivalent, and it seems to me the best way of conveying what the word implies[^EII4-204].

Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî's explanation of this episode can be summarized as follows. The Imam now shows his companions the *malakût* of vital reality, of animate life (*hayât hayawânîya*, *virtus animalis*) as it exists in humanity. The “garden of paradise” is here the *malakût* of that vital reality, containing trees and flowers “planted in animate life,” living creatures carried along in the stream of life.

The young man, the “knight,” who appears as the prophet Sâlih, is the manifest form (*mazhar*) of the divine Logos or Angel who governs the world of life. As in the case of Khezr, Qâzî Sa'îd declares, in his own terminology, that Sâlih is the throne of the lord of the species of living creatures, the abiding dwelling of the spiritual gift that gives this Logos or divine Word (*Kalima rabbânîya*) its governing authority.

Among all the divine Names, some possess the privilege of being the Imams of those Names. Each prophet was the manifest form of one of these Imams of the divine Names, until the arrival of the last Prophet, who gathers them all into himself.

Sâlih was the manifest form of the divine Names and Words relating to life; the Angel charged with them is Seraphiel. That is why Sâlih here represents the form in which animate life reveals itself within the human being. It is also why the companions, seeing with their *malakûtî* gaze, find him alive—unlike Solomon in the next episode, where life is spiritual life in the strict sense, a resurrection brought about by the Imam-Logos.

What, then, are the two graves that Sâlih is digging and between which he performs his worship, his personal liturgy? They are called the “graves of his parents,” meaning the two levels of the plant world and the animal world. “At the level of human reality, these two worlds are indeed buried. For until a human being has died to these two levels of being, he has not yet reached the threshold of human reality, just as, until he has died to the level of human reality, he has not yet reached the level of the superhuman (*fawqânîya*).”

We might also think, Qâzî Sa'îd remarks, that the two graves represent the two deaths framing the human adventure in this world: death to the other world when we descend into this one, and death to this world at the *exitus*, our departure back to the other world. There remains the Imam's morning visit to Sâlih.

Sâlih's tears correspond to the falling leaves that, in the preceding episodes and for the same mystical reasons, fell from the withering tree. We need only recall the meaning of the three thirds of the Night explained earlier. Two thirds have already passed—and Sâlih is burying them—the vegetative third and that of the *virtus animalis*, animate life. The final third belongs to the human being.

And this last third of the Night of matter announces the imminent rising of a sun: not a sun rising in the East, as the physical sun of our world does, but a sun rising in the West, for it marks the appearance of the “day of Resurrection,” which is the “day of the Imam.” Resurrection means precisely this: the sun rising from the West. For whereas the fall into this world is a descent from the East, the spiritual world, resurrection is the return from West to East, to the origin.

That is what the fifth great stage of their visionary journey will mean for the companions, bringing them to the threshold where human reality reaches toward its spiritual, superhuman fulfilment. Their encounter with the prophet Sâlih already implies that chronological time has been enfolded for them. Now, within the *Malakût*, they will become contemporaries of Solomon's resurrection. Salmân the Pure continues his account.

*IV. The Seal of Solomon.* — “Then the Imam said to us: ‘Would you like me to show you Solomon, son of David?’ We answered: ‘Certainly!’ The Imam stood up and we rose with him. We walked until we entered an orchard (*bostân*) unlike anything we had ever seen. It contained every kind of fruit, streams of running water and singing birds. When the birds saw the Imam, they gathered to form a canopy over his head.

“Then we came upon a couch, and on it lay a young man [a ‘knight’], on his back. There was no seal [ring] on his finger. By his head was a serpent, and another lay by his feet. When the two serpents saw the Imam, they coiled themselves at his feet, their faces rolling in the dust of the ground. Then they became like the dust itself” (§ 23).

Here we have a description of the state in which the companions discover Solomon. The following paragraph will show the mystery of Solomon's Seal at work. Naturally, Solomon's condition and the figures around him in the *Malakût* are full of meaning. The orchard they enter is the human *malakût*. Because human nature gathers together the natures of plants and animals, its description includes many kinds of fruit and birds.

The fruits are all the theosophical knowledge mystics gather from the tree “which is neither of the East nor of the West” (Quran 24:35). The birds are the “hieratic” souls (in the Neoplatonic sense of the word), taking flight through the space of the spiritual world and the human *malakût*. “They sing in every variety of their knowledge and mystical perfection; they summon the homesick to the sweetness of the dwelling of intimacy; they kindle in pilgrims the ardent longing to reach the precincts of the supersensible worlds.”

At this mystical station, which the companions have reached through the Imam's spiritual influence and which Qâzî Sa'îd calls the “Lotus of the Boundary” (Quran 53:14), the Imam shows them the Throne of the human *malakût* in the person of the prophet Solomon. Because Solomon was given “a power belonging to no one after him,” he is the manifestation of humanity's caliphal function: the investiture of the human being as God's vicegerent upon His Earth. This is why spirits and humans, birds and beasts, winds and mountains were placed under Solomon's command.

No one since Gayomarth, the primordial human being of Iranian accounts of human origins, was invested with such a function. Even the Seal of the Prophets chose to be not a king-prophet but a servant-prophet, because the fullness of that caliphal function was to be granted only to his final successor, the last Imam, the Imam of the Resurrection (*Qâ'im al-Qiyâmat*). Why, then, do the companions find Solomon lying on a couch as a young man, apparently stripped of his sovereignty because the mysterious Seal from which that sovereignty comes is missing from his finger?

The companions had seen this Seal in the Imam’s possession at the very beginning of their journey on the White Cloud, when he appeared to them transfigured in his heavenly, theophanic reality. For the Imam is the Seal of absolute *walâyat*—the inner, spiritual reality of all the prophets and all their prophetic messages. It is therefore he who, by virtue of his cosmic sovereignty, bestows the mysterious power of the Seal upon whomever God wills. Just as the great tree on the mountaintop had appeared withered in his absence, and Sâlih had buried his parents in tears, so here Solomon, deprived of the Imam’s presence, appears deprived of life and power.

As for the two serpents lying at Solomon’s head and feet, their meaning is this. The first represents love of this world, for such love is the source of every error. The other is the serpent of worldly ambition. “There is certainly an indication here,” our commentator writes, “that earthly power is inseparable from these two serpents. This is why the love of power and political ambition bring about the ruin of so many people.”

Yet the arrangement of the figures shows that neither serpent, nor any trace of them, has penetrated Solomon, the prophet of God. And when the Imam appears—the one who is the source and center of all earthly life—the two serpents crumble into dust. At the sudden influx of spiritual power, the false appearances of this world vanish. Salmân the Pure then continues his account, revealing how the mystery of the Seal was disclosed to the companions.

“We said to the Imam: ‘Is that truly Solomon, son of David?’ ‘Yes,’ the Imam replied, ‘and here is his Seal.’ The Imam then removed the Seal from his own finger and placed it on Solomon’s finger. He said to him: ‘Rise, O Solomon, by the power of the One who raises the dead—the God besides whom there is no god, the Eternal, the Living, the Victorious, Lord of my earliest forefathers.’ Then Solomon stood up, and ‘we heard him pronounce the threefold testimony’: to the oneness of God, to the prophetic mission of Muhammad, and to the *walâyat* of the Imam.” Solomon concluded this threefold testimony by addressing the Imam: “I ask God, my Lord, to count me among your Shiites, for without this I possess nothing and have no power” (§ 24).

The mystery of the Seal therefore involves the folding back of time upon itself. Even before the Imam’s appearance in chronological history, the ancient prophets who preceded Muhammad received from him the Seal that invested them with their authority. Or rather, what appears to us, from the standpoint of chronological time, as a reversal of time is actually the way time unfolds in the “absolutely subtle time” belonging to the Imam’s heavenly reality. This is no longer the time of the Imam’s earthly history but the time of his theophanic person, existing in the suprasensible reality of the *Malakût*, the spiritual world beyond ordinary sense perception.

The Imam possesses the Seal in his *malakûtî* reality. When he places that Seal on Solomon’s finger, Solomon becomes alive in the human *Malakût*. In chronological time, Solomon has been dead for centuries. In the time of the *Malakût*, Solomon has already risen from the dead, and the Imam’s companions are witnesses and contemporaries of his resurrection. Qâzî Sa'îd insists on a point announced by numerous *hadiths*: the Imam is the Hand of God.

This means not that he issues commands by his own authority, but that he himself is the divine command that brings the dead to life—the command that is God’s Word. Likewise, as the center of faith, he is at once the Face that the hidden God turns toward humanity and the face that the believer turns toward God. He is therefore the imperishable Face of every being. That is also the meaning of Solomon’s final words: “May God count me among your Shiites; otherwise I have no power.”

Solomon’s power is thus a trace of the Imam’s cosmic sovereignty, and to possess even that trace is, by that very fact, to profess the Shiite faith (*tashayyo'*). When made sincerely, from the heart, this profession joins the believer to the Imam and to the *walâyat* of the Imams of the “Family of the Cloak” (*âl al-'abâ*). This is the complete spiritual assembly—the *pleroma*—of the twelve Imams of Twelver Shiism, whose lineage begins with those whom the Prophet gathered beneath his cloak on the celebrated occasion when he proposed a trial by divine judgment to the Christians of Najrân.

“This is why,” Qâzî Sa'îd concludes, “a Shiite in the true sense is someone who knows the Imam through the knowledge of light (*ma'rifat nûrânîya*). Anyone who knows him in another way may perhaps be an adherent, but is not a Shiite in the true sense (*shî'î haqîqî*).”

The story of the White Cloud thus reveals itself more and more clearly as an initiation into the secret of Shiite spiritual knowledge, whose very heart is the knowledge of the Imam: the Imam as the manifestation of the Complete Human Being (*Insân kâmil*). The companions’ gradual penetration into Mount Qâf will confirm this. From the multitude of worlds they are about to glimpse, a triumphant hymn of the Imam will arise, proclaiming that the Name revealed in every manifestation of being is itself a manifestation of the Imam as Logos, the divine Word.

##### V. The Multitude of Worlds

Salmân the Pure continues his account:

“We then prepared to make our way around Mount Qâf. I asked the Imam: ‘What lies beyond Mount Qâf?’ He replied: ‘Beyond it are forty worlds, each of them equal to forty times this world.’ We asked: ‘How do you know this?’ The Imam answered: ‘In the same way that I know this world and everything it contains, and that I know the pathways of the Heavens and the Earths’” (§ 25).

Naturally, such a declaration prompts our commentator to explore—or rather, briefly recall—some of the teachings about the creation and structure of the cosmos preserved in Shiite traditions. All concern universes that precede ours in the order of being: suprasensible worlds whose numerical descriptions always carry a symbolic meaning. Foremost among them is a tradition going back to the tenth Imam, 'Alî Naqî, which speaks of the belt of green emerald surrounding our world. This is the Veil beyond which extend the seventy thousand universes of the *Malakût*.[^EII4-205]

The choice of green is never arbitrary. It marks an intermediate state between the world of bodily things, represented by black or blue-black, and the world of the separate Intelligences, represented by yellow. Here Qâzî Sa'îd makes an extended reference to the universe whose mysterious cities are named in a long *hadith* of the sixth Imam, Ja'far al-Sâdiq, and in the systematic account of their place in the order of being developed by Suhrawardî: Jâbalqâ in the East, Jâbarsâ in the West, and Hûrqalyâ, their spiritual center.[^EII4-206]

The commentator also refers to a chapter by Ibn 'Arabî containing perhaps the most beautiful, and at the same time one of the most rigorous, descriptions of the *mundus imaginalis*, the imaginal world.[^EII4-207] These worlds are formed of matter in a subtle, luminous state (*mâdda latîfa nûrâniya*). In itself, such subtle, luminous matter has no fixed dimensions of its own. It is pure receptivity to whatever dimensions, large or small, may actually take form within it.

But as our commentator surveys these traditional accounts of the cosmos, he introduces a digression on the twelve worlds of light. This is another expression of the celebrated *hadith* of the Twelve Veils of Light, which signify the twelve Imams. We return here to the conversation between the fifth Imam, Muhammad Bâqir, and his disciple Jâbir ibn 'Abdallâh, to which we referred earlier (§ 2, p. 147). In this part of their conversation, the Imam reveals to his disciple the *Malakût* of the Earths, which was not shown to Abraham. I would like to dwell briefly on this passage.

First, it provides another example of a ritual change of clothing that announces the passage from one world to another, just as it does in the rites of certain mystery religions. Second, as in our story of the White Cloud, it illustrates the meaning of closing or opening the eyes.

Third, it contains a reference to the Spring of Life. And taken as a whole, its account of the twelve universes strikingly recalls the ancient theologies of *Aiôn*, or eternal cosmic time, with their twelve millennia. Here is the story as Jâbir tells it.[^EII4-208]

“I asked the Imam how to understand this verse of the Quran: ‘Thus We showed Abraham the *Malakût* of the heavens and the earth’ (6:75). I was sitting with my head lowered toward the ground. The Imam raised his hand and said to me: ‘Lift your head.’ I lifted my head and looked toward the ceiling. It had opened, and through the opening I could see a light so intense that it dazzled me. The Imam said: ‘That is how Abraham saw the *Malakût* of the heavens and the earth.’ Then he said: ‘Look toward the ground.’ I looked down. He said again: ‘Lift your head.’ I raised my head, and the ceiling was there once more.

“Then the Imam took me by the hand. We left the house where we had been sitting and entered another house. There the Imam took off the robe he was wearing and put on a different one. Then he said to me: ‘Lower your eyes.’ I lowered them. ‘Do not open your eyes,’ the Imam warned me. He let an hour pass, then asked: ‘Do you know where you are?’ ‘No, I do not.’ ‘You are in the Darkness through which Alexander traveled.’ I said to him: ‘May I be your ransom! Will you now allow me to open my eyes?’ ‘Open them. You will see nothing.’

“I opened my eyes, and indeed I found myself in a Darkness so complete that I could not even make out the ground beneath my feet. Then the Imam walked a few steps and stopped. He said: ‘Do you know where you are now?’ ‘No,’ I replied. ‘You are standing at the Spring of Life, from which Khezr drank. Drink this water.’ So I too drank. Then we left the world where we were and entered another world. We followed a road through it, and saw things whose forms resembled those of our own world: plants, dwellings, and inhabitants. Next we passed into a third world, which resembled the first and the second. Gradually we reached a fifth world.

“The Imam said to me: ‘All this is the *Malakût* of the Earth that Abraham did not see. He saw only the *Malakût* of the heavens. There are twelve universes like those you have seen. Whenever the time of one of us, the twelve Imams, is completed in the time of this earthly world, he dwells in one of these twelve worlds. This continues until the last of us, the Qâ'im—the twelfth Imam, the One Who Will Rise—comes into this universe in which we dwell with him.’ Then the Imam said to me: ‘Close your eyes.’

“I closed them. He took me by the hand, and suddenly we were back in the house from which we had set out. The Imam took off his robe and put on the one he had been wearing at the beginning. We returned to our original meeting place. I said to him: ‘May I be your ransom! How much time has passed?’ The Imam answered: ‘Three hours.’”

The exceptional interest of this account lies in its testimony to another actual entry into the *Malakût*, entirely comparable to the experience described in the story of the White Cloud. There would, of course, be much to say about the process and successive stages of this experience.

But the essential point is the organic connection, expressed through the number twelve, between our world and the *Malakût*, between the time of our world and the time of the *Malakût*. For these twelve universes are the very ones already described in the *hadith* of the Twelve Veils of Light (above, p. 148), with one difference: there they were presented in the order of their creation. That tradition told us that twelve Veils of Light were created either alongside the Muhammadan Light (*Nûr muhammadî*), first brought into being by the self-creating Will, or out of that Light itself. These twelve Veils of Light represent the respective universes of the twelve Imams, and they are also symbolized as twelve millennia.

During its descent toward its manifestation in the earthly world, in the person of the Seal of the Prophets, the Muhammadan Light dwells in each of these Veils.[^EII4-209] It spends twelve millennia in the first Veil, eleven in the second, and so on. From millennium to millennium it passes through the space of the *Malakût*, approaching the time of its earthly manifestation. Space has become time. Conversely, the twelve universes that the Imam shows Jâbir, now presented in the order of return, are the stages through which this Light rises again, from Imam to Imam, toward the “place” of its origin.

Time becomes space once more. Millennium after millennium, the time of its descent is folded back upon itself, returning the Light to the simultaneous fullness of the spiritual assembly of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. It is this conception of twelve millennia that appears, within Shiite theosophy, as a remembrance of the Iranian-Hellenistic theologies of *Aiôn*. With Qâzî Sa'îd, we immediately understand that the Spring of Life lies in the first world of the *Malakût*, the first of the twelve worlds they enter. For this Spring of Life is the *walâyat* of the first Imam—his spiritual authority and the inner reality of his mission—and it is through knowledge of this *walâyat* that eternal life is brought into actuality.

But we should notice that the fifth Imam, Muhammad Bâqir, takes Jâbir into only five of these worlds of the Imams. The reason is simple. An earthly human being can enter the *Malakût* only through the form in which that *Malakût* has manifested itself in our visible world. At the time of Jâbir’s conversation with the fifth Imam, only five of the twelve Imams had appeared in this world. Jâbir can therefore enter only the *Malakût* belonging to the worlds of those first five Imams.

Still less could Abraham have entered the *Malakût* of any of the Twelve. This is entirely consistent with Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî’s metaphysics of time, in which time first expands and then folds back upon itself. With the twelfth Imam’s brief and fleeting appearance, the *Malakût* of the Perfect Human Being (*Anthrôpos teleios*) began to manifest itself. This is a complete universe embracing the Throne (*'arsh*), the celestial firmament (*Korsî*), the heavens, the earth, and everything that exists.

Yet its full manifestation in this world will occur only with the return of the twelfth Imam, the Resurrector. At that very moment, the folding of our chronological time into the subtle time of the *Malakût* will be complete. For it is only with the twelfth Imam that human reality attains the full stature of the Complete Human Being. The end of this brief digression brings us back to the traditional accounts of the cosmos assembled by our commentator, and particularly to the forty worlds mentioned by the Imam at the point we have reached in the story of the White Cloud.

We cannot hope to bring such varied indications into a single system. There is, for example, a *hadith* in which the same Jâbir reports hearing the fifth Imam declare:

“Beyond this sun of yours are forty suns, and between every two suns there are forty universes. In those universes live multitudes of creatures who do not know whether God created Adam or did not create him. Beyond this moon are forty moons, and between every two moons there are forty worlds. There too live countless creatures who are indifferent to, or ignorant of, whether God created Adam.”

In short, the traditional accounts concerning these pre-Adamic universes are innumerable. Gathering and organizing them would require a lengthy investigation.

We can, however, already identify one feature they share, especially those traditions that give the number forty in one form or another. They tell us that our Adamic world—the world of humanity as we know it—is not the result of what is nowadays called evolution, an evolution whose duration science even claims to calculate in the millions of years needed to pass from a single-celled organism to a human being! According to the thinkers we are studying, our Adamic world, and the human condition belonging to it, result instead from a descent through successive worlds.

Each of these worlds still lies beyond Mount Qâf, beyond the physical universe perceived by our senses and which our scientific instruments aspire to conquer. This descent continues until it reaches the present human world, which marks both the end of the descent and the beginning of the ascent. We are thus invited not to forget that every achievement accomplished by physical machinery remains, by definition, on this side of Mount Qâf.

Among the traditions cited by Qâzî Sa'îd, one that has exercised the ingenuity of many thinkers speaks of forty mornings during which the mysterious formation of a cosmic Adam took place. On each of these forty mornings, the sun of divine Emanation rose. There were also forty nights, on each of which stars appeared, each star a divine Light cast upon the human receptacle that necessarily took the form of the Light it received. The succession of these mornings and nights signifies the emergence of forty worlds of humanity.

But in relation to the one we call “Adam our father,” the humanity inhabiting these worlds was both pre-Adamic and of a higher order. This explains the references to forty Easts and forty Wests. Each new world is a West in relation to the world preceding it, which is itself the East of the world that follows. In each of these worlds, at every level of pre-Adamic humanity, a pledge was given in answer to the question recorded in the Quranic verse: “*Alastu bi-rabbikum?* Am I not your Lord?” (7:171). One master of mystical knowledge even affirmed that he had seen most of these worlds and retained their memory.

Another claimed to perceive the very vibration of the question and its answer as something taking place in his own time—in the particular measure of subtle time belonging to him, of course.

“There is a tremendous secret here,” Qâzî Sa'îd remarks in passing, “which you may come to know to the extent that you are able to cast off the garment of earthly human nature (*nâsût*) and rise to the horizon of the *Malakût*.”

And in each of these pre-Adamic worlds, the same rhythm of forty is repeated. That is why we heard the Imam declare that each world is equal to forty times our universe. Only at the end of this cosmic process of formation did the world and humanity of the “little Adam” (*Adam al-saghîr*) emerge: the Adam who is “our father.” As another *hadith* puts it, in words addressed by the fifth Imam to one of his close companions:

“God has created millions of universes and millions of Adams. You live in the last of these worlds and belong to the last of these Adamic humanities.”

What, then, are we to make of the narrowly bounded cosmos in which humanity was supposedly confined before the so-called modern age? But now, of course, we can understand why all these worlds lie “beyond Mount Qâf.” For Mount Qâf itself, the mountain with the emerald cities, is the *Malakût* of our own human reality, the spiritual world corresponding to the human condition that is ours. All this is implied in the Imam’s reply to Salmân the Pure at this moment in the story of the White Cloud.

And now the Imam—not simply the first among the Twelve, but the eternal Imam who represents the complete theophanic assembly of all Twelve—utters what sounds like a solemn psalm. Many sayings from the *hadiths* return within it as echoes and allusions. The twelve Imams appear as the complete assembly of the divine energies through which the cosmos comes into being. The visible phenomena of our world are their traces and manifestations.

“O Salmân! Our Names—the Names of the Imams—are written upon the nights, and so there is darkness. They are written upon the days, and so there is light. I am the ordeal that falls upon our enemies. I am the Great Upheaval (Quran 79:34). Our Names are written upon the Throne, and so it stands supported. They are written upon the heavens, and so they rise. They are written upon the earth, and so it stands still. They are written upon the winds, and so they whirl.

“Upon lightning, and so it flashes. Upon light, and so it streams forth. Upon thunder, and so it roars. Our Names are written upon the forehead of the angel Seraphiel, whose one wing extends to the East and the other to the West, and who proclaims: ‘Worthy of the highest praise, most holy is the Lord of the Angels and of the Spirit’” (§ 26).

These final words are like an echo of Yahweh Sabaoth, the Lord of Hosts, and of the threefold cry of holiness sung by the Seraphim in Isaiah’s vision—a vision that was also one of the sources of Kabbalistic metaphysics. Qâzî Sa'îd offers this interpretation:

“The Names here signify the Lights of the Imams rising from the realm of the *Jabarût*, the world of divine power. All beings of light receive their light from the first Light that emanated from the First Principle. That first Light is the Muhammadan Light, the Light of the complete assembly of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. Everything that receives a share of this Light—which is being itself—receives it through the radiance of that primordial Light and the spiritual influx of that supreme Name.”

Earlier we learned that it was this cosmic, creative Imam who brought forth the angel entrusted with the darkness of the nights and the brightness of the days. This ordering and regulating activity does not occur without leaving something of its source within what it produces. That, Qâzî Sa'îd tells us, is what the “writing” of the Imams’ Names upon the nights, the days, and all the phenomena subsequently enumerated symbolically expresses. The idea that the structures and conditions of existence as a whole arise through the activity of the Imams, acting as a cosmic energy, is therefore gathered into a single image: their Names “inscribed upon the forehead of the angel Seraphiel.”

We encountered this angel at the very beginning of the story of the White Cloud. His forehead signifies the exalted metaphysical station of the twelve Imams. The East toward which one of Seraphiel’s wings extends signifies the rising place, the dawn of the lights of being (*matla' anwâr al-wojûd*). The West toward which his other wing extends signifies the world of matter in its material state, the world in which all beings of light live as exiles.[^EII4-210]

Thus the wing of Seraphiel that extends toward the East is the one through which he receives the influx from the higher worlds, while the wing extended toward the West is the one through which he pours that influx upon the lower worlds. Seraphiel thereby encompasses all beings that enter into the relationship of *robûbîya*, or divine Lordship. This relationship comes into being through the manifestation of the hidden God, the *Absconditum*. It makes the revealed God, the *Deus revelatus*, the Lord of beings through a reciprocal bond joining the Lord and the being over which he exercises Lordship.

The *rabb*, the Lord, and the *marbûb*, the one whose Lord he is, cannot exist in that relationship independently of one another. It would be unthinkable, however, for the *Absconditum*—the God beyond all description, of the theology that approaches God by negation—to enter into such a relationship. Hence Seraphiel’s cry of praise addressed to the one who is “the Lord of the Angels and of the Spirit.”

##### VI. The People of 'Âd

We now come to the dramatic episode that will bring the story of the White Cloud to its close. This episode offers a striking illustration of how our chronological time folds back into the subtle time of the *Malakût*. The particular kind of contemporaneity belonging to the *Malakût* allows visionary experience to witness events scattered throughout the past of our chronological history. This presupposes that the event taking place in chronological time presents us with only its outward face. Its true reality remains invisible and inaccessible to anyone incapable of entering the *Malakût*. There the companions will witness the destruction of the ancient Arabian people of 'Âd, who rebelled against the call of their prophet, as related in the Quran.[^EII4-211] Salmân the Pure resumes his account:

“Then the Imam said to us: ‘Close your eyes.’ We closed them. He said: ‘Now open your eyes.’ We opened them, and suddenly we found ourselves in a city larger than any we had ever seen. Its public places were crowded and bustling. Its inhabitants were taller than any human beings we had ever encountered. Each of them was like a palm tree.

“We asked: ‘Who are these people? We have never seen people of such extraordinary height.’ The Imam replied: ‘These are the people of 'Âd. They are unbelievers. They believe neither in the Last Day nor in the Prophet. ‘I wanted you to see them here, in this place of the *Malakût*, because in the lower world their time has passed. Their city, one of the great cities of the East, has been wiped away. ‘I have brought you here without your being aware of it. I wish to fight them before your eyes’” (§ 27).

Qâzî Sa'îd interrupts the narrative briefly to review several essential points of the metaphysics of time that we encountered at the beginning. The best course is to follow the central points of his commentary one by one.

1. Although their encounters with the prophet Sâlih and then with Solomon had already involved a folding back of time, our theosopher believes that what the companions had witnessed up to this point was primarily a transformation of our spatial world. What they now experience is a specific folding back of chronological time.

In other words, the Imam is initiating them into a vision of the *Malakût* of time itself, and of everything that exists in time (*zamânîyât*). The earlier episodes have already taught us what opening and closing the eyes means in spiritual initiation. Here, Qâzî Sa'îd explains, “closing their eyes means that the companions abandon their preoccupation with the *Malakût* of the Earth and the extraordinary things they have just witnessed there.” Opening them now means entering the *Malakût* of time, the horizon of everlasting duration (*ufq al-dahr*). Within that horizon, “all temporal things are like colored points threaded upon a string, or like shining pearls arranged along a necklace.

“Thus any being belonging to the *Malakût* (*malakûtîyûn*) can, whenever it wishes, choose whatever portion of time it desires.

“Earthly human beings, however, are confined within such narrow limits of perception that it would be useless to try to show them the whole. The Imam therefore shows his companions only a fragment of the *Malakût* of time.”

2. Everything we said at the beginning about Qâzî Sa'îd’s philosophy of time now finds its application in this final episode. Our author summarizes the question as follows:

“Understand that a being existing in time remains one and the same individual (*shakhs wâhid*) from the beginning of its existence until the moment when its visible presence comes to an end. It is a single, continuous reality. But because the particular measure that determines its form and appearance comes into view gradually, it appears to us in this world as something unstable, something that passes and flows away.

“Yet this in no way means that it is annihilated within the order of what actually exists, when we consider the thing as it truly is. Far from it! Such disappearance is impossible, for an individuality that constitutes a unity cannot both be annihilated and continue to exist. This decline and concealment are such only in relation to you, in relation to the imaginary representation (*wahm*) that dominates your intellect. Otherwise the person does indeed exist as one unified person (*shakhs wahdânî*), from eternity before time to eternity beyond time.”

There is also a common misunderstanding to guard against. None of this means that the whole of the past or the future is present within each fragmentary instant.

“I do not mean,” Qâzî Sa'îd clarifies, “that the totality of this unity constituted by a person exists within the present moment, the *nunc*.
