These proud words deserve to be quoted here, for they convey a whole spiritual atmosphere more vividly than any commentary could.[^EII4-237]

As for the writings of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i, they form a vast body of work whose study is indispensable to anyone wishing to penetrate the deeper mysteries of Shiite thought. Thanks to Sarkar Agha's work, we now possess a systematic and comprehensive catalogue. It lists no fewer than 132 titles, all Shaykh Ahmad's recorded writings being in Arabic. The true number is higher, since many titles refer to collections containing as many as ten or more individual treatises (risâla).

We must also remember that a considerable number of works have been lost: the shaykh did not keep copies of the treatises he wrote at the request of his correspondents and those who consulted him. Moreover, his library was kept in Karbala, in the house of his disciple and successor Sayyed Kazem, and that house was pillaged twice.

The catalogue is systematically arranged into nine sections: theosophy; Shiite doctrine; religious addresses and sermons; law; jurisprudence; Quranic commentaries; practical philosophy; literature; and collections (II, pp. 8–85).[^EII4-238] Approximately seventeen treatises remain unpublished. All the others appeared in lithographed editions, which are unfortunately now quite old. Particularly worth recalling are Shaykh Ahmad's extensive and highly individual commentaries on two works by Molla Sadra Shirazi. These are essential for understanding how Shaykhi theosophy relates to the "Eastern theosophy" (hikmat mashriqîya) of Suhrawardi as interpreted by Molla Sadra.[^EII4-239]

The Sharh al-Ziyârat al-jâmi'a is an extensive commentary on a text of "spiritual pilgrimage" honoring the Twelve Imams. With the Shaykhis, we may regard it as Shaykh Ahmad's most precious work: a veritable comprehensive statement of Shiite theosophy.[^EII4-240] The Fawâ'id ("Teachings") and the expanded version prepared by the author himself contain philosophical foundations of great importance.[^EII4-241] A large collection of ninety-nine treatises—actually more, for the reason already given—was published under the title Jawâmi' al-Kalim.[^EII4-242] We must reserve a more detailed discussion of all this for another occasion.

### Chapter II

#### The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i

##### 1. Sayyed Kazem Reshti (1212/1798–1259/1843)

The Shaykhi community enjoyed the good fortune of being led, after Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i, by a succession of figures as remarkable for their strength and nobility of character as for their truly extraordinary scholarly productivity.

Until now, anyone wishing to write the biography of the disciple whom Shaykh Ahmad expressly designated as his nâ'ib, his deputy and successor, had only incomplete sources at hand. The first was Sayyed Kazem's own account of his trials, especially his controversies and disputes with people whose names would otherwise have been forgotten.[^EII4-243] Further research has now enabled Sarkar Agha to discover two treatises (risâla) written by students of Sayyed Kazem, containing at last the material needed for a proper biography.[^EII4-244] We shall draw from them a very brief account.

Sayyed Kazem belonged to a noble family of Hosayni sayyeds—that is, descendants of the Third Imam—originally from Medina, which had settled in Iran two generations earlier. His grandfather, Sayyed Ahmad, had fled Medina during an outbreak of plague and taken refuge in Rasht, in the region southwest of the Caspian Sea. He settled there and established a family. His son, Sayyed Qasem, was born there, married there, and became one of Rasht's leading citizens. It was in the same city that Sayyed Kazem was born, in 1212 AH (1798).

His dreamy, contemplative childhood reveals dispositions strikingly similar to those we encountered in Shaykh Ahmad's own early life. A tutor was appointed to teach him the outward, or exoteric, sciences (zâhira). But the young man was consumed by two desires: to travel far from home and to be initiated into the higher forms of knowledge. Unfortunately, his family saw matters differently. Once again, a series of "initiatory dreams" strengthened his resolve and hastened his decision.

One fact deserves particular attention. It was Fatima, the Prophet's daughter and a central focus of Shiite devotion, who appeared to the young Kazem in a dream and revealed to him the existence of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i, the extraordinary nature of the man, and finally the place where he could be found: Yazd. We have already described the circumstances in which Shaykh Ahmad came to Yazd and remained there until 1229 AH (1814). Sayyed Kazem, then about fifteen years old, managed somehow to leave home and reach the city. His hopes and expectations were fully answered. He "committed every resource of his soul and heart" to absorbing the shaykh's teaching. From then on he became his inseparable companion and closest confidant. The shaykh was accustomed to saying: "My son Kazem understands me, but nobody else understands me" (pp. 147–148).

It was during the journey that took Shaykh Ahmad back toward the holy places, when he made his final stay at Kermanshah after the unhappy episode at Qazvin, that he advised his disciple to settle in Karbala. Sayyed Kazem appears indeed to have established himself there at about that time, devoting himself entirely to his twofold task of teaching and spiritual guidance.

Yet he must have returned several times to Iran, to his native Rasht, as we learn from one of his letters to the shaykh,[^EII4-245] unfortunately undated. During his years in Iraq he certainly suffered attacks and mistreatment at the hands of a small number of envious and troublesome individuals. But these hardships were offset by the friendship of eminent scholars who testified to his greatness of soul, the breadth of his learning and spiritual gifts, and the intensity of his inner life.[^EII4-246]

Nothing better conveys the impression he made upon those around him than the words of Mahmud Alusi, then the mufti of Baghdad and author of the Maqâmât alûsîya: "If the Sayyed had lived in an age when it was possible for a prophet (nabî) to be sent, I would have been the first to believe in him. For everything required—profound knowledge, moral conduct, sound doctrine, and spiritual gifts—is present in him."

In 1258 AH (1842), the people of Karbala rose in revolt against supporters of the Ottoman government. Terrible scenes of repression, pillage, and massacre followed. The sanctuaries and the Sayyed's house miraculously served as places of refuge. Afterward, however, the attacks against him—whose underlying motives are not difficult to guess—grew more intense. Eventually he decided to absent himself on a long pilgrimage to the sanctuary of the Kazimayn and then to Samarra.

But as he prepared to leave, he had a premonition that this would be his final journey. We have the testimony of Mirza Hasan Tabib, a distinguished physician and disciple of Sayyed Kazem, who recounts their last conversation:

"At the time of this journey, the revered Sayyed came to see me and said: 'Janab Mirza! Will you accompany me on the pilgrimage?'

"'I fear that will not be possible,' I answered, 'for I have several patients whom I am treating.'

"'Give them their prescriptions,' he said, 'and be sure to come with me. I have a feeling this will be my last journey.'

"'Agha!' I cried, 'may my life be devoted to you! God will not allow it. By divine grace, you are in perfect health and will remain so.'

"'Janab Mirza,' he replied, 'I know something that you do not know. Remember what I have just told you. Do not speak of it to anyone'" (pp. 153–154).

In fact, when Sayyed Kazem reached Baghdad on his return from Samarra, the Ottoman governor, Najib Pasha, who had applauded the killing and pillage at Karbala, invited him to visit and lavished every kind of honor and respect upon him. Nevertheless, he had a cup of "bad coffee" served to him. His friends hurriedly carried the Sayyed back to Karbala, where he died two days later, on the night of 11 Dhu'l-Hijja 1259 AH (1843). He was buried very near the sanctuary of Imam Hosayn, his distant ancestor.

Through Sayyed Kazem, the spiritual succession of the shaykhs belonging to the silsila shaykhîya—the Shaykhi chain of transmission—was secured. In the ijâzat, or formal authorization to teach and transmit knowledge, which he granted to Agha Mohammad Sharif Kermani, he mentions four such authorizations received from his own spiritual masters (mashâyekh). The authority of the fourth overshadowed the other three,[^EII4-247] for it came from Shaykh Ahmad himself.

Speaking of the relationship between the shaykh and his successor, Khwansari writes: "They were a single spirit manifested in two bodies."[^EII4-248] He emphasizes that, among his many disciples, Shaykh Ahmad designated no one but Sayyed Kazem as his nâ'ib al-manâb, his duly qualified representative and the spiritual leader of his companions and fellow disciples. Admittedly, Khwansari's testimony concerns only their outward relationship, for his great book sometimes shows that he had only an imperfect knowledge of the shaykhs and had little personal contact with them. Nevertheless, his testimony helps place this historical point beyond dispute (pp. 158–160).

The writings left by Sayyed Kazem (II, pp. 86–167) are likewise considerable. The catalogue lists no fewer than 172 titles—and the real number is even greater: entry 130 contains sixty-three separate treatises; entry 144 contains thirty-three; and entry 152 contains no fewer than eighty![^EII4-249] Unfortunately, many of these writings seem to have been lost beyond recovery. As already mentioned, the Sayyed's house in Karbala, where his descendants lived and his library was kept, was pillaged twice. A substantial number of Shaykh Ahmad's autograph manuscripts disappeared at the same time, since his library was also preserved in Sayyed Kazem's house (p. 157).

Fortunately, Sayyed Kazem had himself compiled a catalogue of his own works and those of the Shaykh, accompanying each entry with a short description of the book's contents.[^EII4-250] Thanks to this care, we can estimate the number of missing works at around sixty. Some thirty-five writings, on the other hand, still exist but remain unpublished; about fifteen of his works in all are in Persian. The others were printed at various dates, and copies have become rare. Much work will be required to recover this body of writing and thought, and to trace in detail how Sayyed Kazem developed and extended the ideas of Shaykh Ahmad. His commentaries on certain sermons (khotbat) and other texts attributed to the Imams reveal his particular aptitude for the highest reaches of speculative spiritual philosophy.[^EII4-251]

##### 2. Shaykh Hajj Mohammad Karim-Khan Kermani (1225/1809–1288/1870)

This shaykh[^EII4-252] was born in Kerman on 18 Moharram 1225 AH (1809) and died on 22 Sha'ban 1288 AH (1870) at Teh-Rud, three stages from Kerman, while making a pilgrimage to Karbala. His life seems short when measured against his astonishing achievement. He left no fewer than 278 works—some substantial volumes, others brief treatises—preserved in Kerman and for the most part still unpublished. He was an exceptional figure, whose learning embraced the whole spiritual culture of his setting and his age. The comparison that naturally comes to mind is with the universal minds produced by the European Renaissance.

Two great features define the course of his life.

The first was a conviction that he shared with Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i: the immense body of traditions transmitted from the holy Imams contains a complete spiritual philosophy, a whole body of knowledge concerning this world and the other worlds. Those responsible for the impoverishment of Shiism, in his view, were precisely those who turned to these traditions only to justify legal decisions or ritual practices. What was needed instead was direct study of this inherited body of teaching, without any intermediary authority.

This meant breaking with every legalistic conception of Islam. The break became all the more decisive because the seeker was now called to enter into a direct, personal dialogue with his Imams. We must always keep this in mind if we are to understand the difficulties the Shaykhis encountered at the hands of the official religious establishment.

The second defining event came when Mohammad Karim-Khan, at the age of seventeen, first heard of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i's teaching in Kerman itself. From this discovery came, one might say, the dazzling illumination that lit up his entire life. It happened in 1826. The date coincides with Shaykh Ahmad's final stay at Kermanshah and his return to the Shiite holy places in Iraq; it was at this time, as we have seen, that he instructed Sayyed Kazem to establish himself in Karbala.

Here again, Sarkar Agha's research has borne fruit. Among the mass of papers left by Mohammad Karim-Khan, he discovered several pages in the shaykh's own hand containing nothing less than the outline of an autobiography, reaching back into his childhood. It had been intended as the introduction to a work written in Arabic.[^EII4-253] Sarkar Agha provides a Persian translation (pp. 76–92). The document is so interesting that we hope, as in the case of Shaykh Ahmad's autobiography, to publish a complete French translation elsewhere. Here we can draw attention to only a few features.

Through his father, Ebrahim-Khan,[^EII4-254] the shaykh belonged to the reigning imperial family. From his own account we learn how his father founded the great religious college in Kerman that still bears the name Madrasa-ye Ebrâhîmî, furnishing it with a fine library that grew richer year after year. Ebrahim-Khan installed his son there, giving him a separate residence and his own household staff. The young man was thus free to devote himself entirely to his studies, sheltered from worries and intrigues, and ideally placed to attend the lessons of every visiting master.

His method of study was uncompromising: for every book he read, he wrote a book of his own. By the age of fourteen, he had already composed a treatise on grammar and another on logic. He then turned to the sciences, and afterward to the fine arts. Until his death, his father never ceased encouraging this almost feverish appetite for learning.

We can readily imagine the shock that the arrival of Mohammad Isma'il Kuhbena'i, a direct disciple of Shaykh Ahmad, must have brought to this young man whose hunger for knowledge was so consuming. Mohammad Isma'il came to Kerman and stayed for a year. At first, it seems, he took little interest in this privileged young scholar. Then a particular trait of the young man's character, reported to him by others, attracted his attention, and he wished to meet him.

When Mohammad Karim-Khan heard him speak of Shaykh Ahmad, and when Mohammad Isma'il gave him a glimpse of the broad outlines of the shaykh's spiritual philosophy and understanding of the Imams, his vocation was settled. He wanted to hear of nothing else.

Consequently, when his new friend had to return to Karbala, Mohammad Karim-Khan felt such an overwhelming longing that he overcame every obstacle. He too set out for Karbala, where, for eight months, he was an accepted disciple of Sayyed Kazem, already renowned as Shaykh Ahmad's successor. Sayyed Kazem was then twenty-eight years old; Mohammad Karim-Khan was about seventeen. The meeting of these two young men, both burning with the same spiritual enthusiasm, proved decisive for the future of Shaykhism and the spiritual life of Iran.

Pressing family obligations recalled Mohammad Karim-Khan to Kerman. Four years later, however, he returned to Karbala and spent another two years under Sayyed Kazem's guidance. In his teacher he saw the "mirror" of Shaykh Ahmad, just as he himself had now become Sayyed Kazem's "mirror." During this period he also made the pilgrimage to Mecca.

Then Sayyed Kazem instructed him to depart. He accompanied his disciple beyond the outskirts of Karbala and, at their farewell, said simply: "Return to Persia. From now on, you have no need of anyone among the olamâ," the religious scholars (p. 74).

The autobiography also gives us testimony of exceptional interest for understanding religious experience. Like Shaykh Ahmad and Sayyed Kazem, Mohammad Karim-Khan—especially in his youth—was granted visions in which the events he experienced gave symbolic form to the underlying patterns of Shiite spiritual consciousness. Even before his birth, his mother had experienced symbolic and prophetic dreams; one has the impression that her son's visionary experiences were, in a sense, a continuation of them.

We cannot examine these visions at length here, but several deserve particular mention. There was an encounter in a visionary dream with the Eighth Imam. In other visions, the familiar image of an object descending from heaven reappears in a different form: a mysterious device that enables the dreamer to ascend to heaven. Finally, and above all, there was a vision of the Ninth Imam, Mohammad Jawad (also called Taqi), which amounted to a personal initiation.

Following this experience, the shaykh says that he made a resolution, which he expresses in these words:

"From that time onward, I gave my attention to searching out hidden things. I came to perceive the holy Imams in my mind, to see them inwardly, and I felt myself guided by them. Henceforth, whenever I sought knowledge, I turned directly to them and to no one else. I profess nothing that is not founded upon them. I give my unquestioning allegiance (taqlîd) to no one else. All my knowledge comes from my inner vision, from the teaching of the Imams as it guides my spiritual search. From nothing else" (p. 83).

The same spiritual fearlessness, inspired by a direct relationship with the unseen world of the holy Imams, is already foreshadowed in a prophetic dream from his adolescence. He sees a strange apparatus rising toward the heights of heaven. It has a series of steps or platforms, but most people are content merely to take their places upon them. One of his companions tries to reach the summit and fails. In the intuitive certainty of the dream, the young Karim-Khan knows that whoever reaches the top will set the whole apparatus in motion and become the guide of everyone else. He succeeds in climbing to the summit and takes hold of the controls.

Such a dream gives us a sense of the strength of character that Shiite spirituality can impart to those who live it as fully and exemplarily as these shaykhs did, acknowledging no authority other than the inner authority of the Imams.

This pure inner authority would henceforth guide and inspire a labor that resulted in a body of work of overwhelming proportions. It is impossible here to follow the details of its development. Yet we should call attention to a few of the maxims that conclude the autobiography, addressed to the reader of the book for which it was intended to serve as a preface.

They reveal the exceptional strength of a personality that drew its very strength from the Shiite faith as he understood and practiced it:

"I have turned everything upside down, examined and tested everything, and have no aim other than to make the truth manifest.

"The two Angels merely write down what a human being dictates to them through his words, his thoughts, his tongue, and his other bodily organs. Beyond them, God perceives the secrets of our innermost consciousness, and on the Day of Resurrection He will bring forth the book in which they are recorded.

"Do not offer as an argument: 'We found our fathers following this path or that.' Perhaps your father knew nothing about it.

"Beware of finding comfort in agreement with beasts or with those who have lost their way. For the First Imam said: 'You will never know the sweetness of faith unless you keep company with the few and flee from the multitude. Whoever deserves the name of human being does not keep company with wild beasts.'

"Know that insofar as you love such creatures, you become like them. A human being takes the very form of what he loves. You will be resurrected in their likeness, for if someone loves a stone, God will resurrect that person in the form of that stone.

"Whoever lacks the Spirit of faith is dead. Avoid sitting and talking with the dead, for what teaching can be expected from corpses? If you happen to come into contact with them, you must purify yourself.

"If you have been tested as I have been, let only your outward person maintain such relationships, never your heart.

"Do not say: 'Other people do not speak this way; this person or that disapproves.' For I too am one of those 'others.' And you too possess authority, if God approves of you in His Book, the Prophet in his sonna—his exemplary practice—and the Imams in their transmitted teachings (akhbâr)" (pp. 85–91).

The question of the ijâzât, the authorizations received by Hajj Mohammad Karim-Khan, deserves closer attention. He received many of them, notably from Molla Hosayn Ganjavi and Agha Mohammad Sharif Kermani. But naturally their importance is somewhat overshadowed by the two detailed authorizations he received from Sayyed Kazem himself.

Curiously, because the preface to his great work Fasl al-Khitâb reproduces only the first two—his concern there being to emphasize the continuity in the transmission of the religious traditions (riwâyât)—certain people have claimed that he never received an ijâzat from Sayyed Kazem. Yet the texts of the two comprehensive authorizations granted by Sayyed Kazem are reproduced in the Tadhkarat al-Awliyâ (see above, note 38), and the autograph original, bearing the Sayyed's seal, is preserved in Kerman.

This is hardly a recent controversy. For reasons upon which we need not dwell here, certain people were already raising the question during Mohammad Karim-Khan's lifetime. He himself had given them a decisive answer simply by producing the documents (pp. 74–75, 92–93).

This resolves one of the questions raised chiefly among certain groups in Azerbaijan to which we have already referred. Sometimes these groups regard themselves as belonging to the Shaykhi spiritual lineage (silsila shaykhîya); at other times they place themselves outside it, while still claiming to be disciples of Shaykh Ahmad and Sayyed Kazem.

But another question concerns what Shaykhism regards as the "fourth pillar" of the Shiite religion, expressed in the term rokn-e râbi'. We shall attempt to give a brief account of this doctrine later (Chapter III). First, however, we must establish an important historical point.

It has been claimed that the doctrine is found neither in Shaykh Ahmad nor in Sayyed Kazem, but was a "creation" of Mohammad Karim-Khan. This is the origin of the names Roknîyeh and Hâjj-Karîm-Khânî, sometimes given to his disciples, who indeed regard these designations with pride.

This supposed objection can readily be answered in two ways. First, we can refer to the writings of the first two masters.[^EII4-255] Second, we can refer to two autograph documents written by Sayyed Kazem that settle the question definitively.[^EII4-256]

Besides confirming Mohammad Karim-Khan's authority as successor, these two documents help us understand why he insisted so strongly and so persistently on teaching this doctrine. There should be no room for doubt, were it not for what Sarkar Agha deplores as "ordinary people's unwillingness to receive the higher teachings of the Imams."

As for Mohammad Karim-Khan's bibliography, it is assembled (II, pp. 168–305) under fifteen broad headings, covering the following subjects: theosophy; Shiite doctrine and religious controversy; religious addresses and sermons; Quranic commentaries; traditions (akhbâr) of the Imams; sources of religious law; jurisprudence; treatises on prayer and devotion; medicine; studies of light, optics, perspective, and mirrors; treatises on color and music; astronomy, mathematics, and the astrolabe; alchemy; dream interpretation and geomancy; calligraphy, poetry, and grammar; and responses to questions on various subjects.

The catalogue contains 278 titles. As we have said, the actual number is higher, for the same reasons encountered in the earlier cases. Of these works, around fifty are in Persian, and barely fifty of the entire collection have ever been printed.

We can thus begin to form an idea of the vast quantity of unpublished manuscripts belonging to the Shaykhi spiritual lineage. The brief catalogue entries allow us to glimpse how, in this shaykh's writings, the spiritual philosophy grounded in the teaching of the Imams—whose foundations Shaykh Ahmad and Sayyed Kazem had already established—was extended, developed, and consolidated in every detail.

Unfortunately, virtually nothing of this work has yet become known in the West. Yet it is an essential monument of Shiite thought, and so long as we remain ignorant of it, our understanding of religious experience will lack something equally essential. We hope to devote to it the research it deserves.

There may be something arbitrary about selecting particular titles from the immense body of Mohammad Karim-Khan's writings. Nevertheless, let us mention the great Fasl al-Khitâb (II, p. 206), a systematic collection of traditions (hadîth and akhbâr), published in lithograph in Tehran in 1302 AH (1885), in a folio volume of 1,508 pages.

There is also the Tarîq al-Najât (II, p. 201), devoted to the knowledge of the spiritual path, published in lithograph in 1344 AH (1925), in a folio volume of 555 pages.

The Kitâb al-fitrat al-salîma (II, p. 193) offers a synthesis of spiritual philosophy built upon the "four pillars": the unity of God (tawhîd), prophethood (nobowwat), the Imamate (imâmat), and the Shiite community (shî'a). It was published in Tabriz in 1310 AH (1892), in a folio volume of 452 pages.

The author developed this synthesis further in a major Persian work entitled Irshâd al-awâmm (II, pp. 184–186), which may be translated as Spiritual Guidance for the General Community of Believers. It offers a complete and exceptionally accessible synthesis and is still read diligently by all Shaykhis.[^EII4-257] Its most recent edition was published in Kerman in 1355 AH (1936), in four parts bound as two folio volumes.

A collection of ten important treatises was also published in Kerman in 1354 AH (1935), in an octavo volume of 897 pages. All his scientific writings remain in manuscript: works on medicine and alchemy, and the great treatise on the color red, which more than once calls to mind Goethe's Farbenlehre, his Theory of Colours.

##### 3. Shaykh Hajj Mohammad-Khan Kermani (1263/1846–1324/1906)

We cannot recall this noble figure without a quiet sadness. It is almost as if, in striking at this shaykh, his persecutors had wished to wound the Shaykhi school itself.

Born on 19 Moharram 1263 AH (1846), Hajj Mohammad-Khan (pp. 56–71) owed his intellectual and spiritual formation chiefly to his own father, Hajj Mohammad Karim-Khan. Very early on, he became his father's collaborator, and it was from their close cooperation that the enormous, systematic collection of traditions known as the Fasl al-Khitâb, mentioned above, emerged.

This collaboration continued until Mohammad Karim-Khan's death. Thereafter, Mohammad-Khan in turn adopted the same method of instruction toward his younger brother, Zaynol-'Abidin-Khan, who would one day become his own successor. From an early age, the adolescent and his elder brother were intimate friends and collaborators.[^EII4-258]

Once the Fasl al-Khitâb was completed, Hajj Mohammad Karim-Khan granted his son, who had thus demonstrated his abilities, a comprehensive ijâzat, authorizing him to teach and transmit the tradition. Several witnesses also confirm the spiritual authority conferred upon the son at this early age.[^EII4-259]

In addition to the authorization received from his own father, by far the most important, Hajj Mohammad-Khan received a considerable number of others. Some are mentioned at the beginning of his Kitâb al-Mobîn, the largest of his works yet published. Among them were authorizations from Shaykh 'Ali Bahrani (see also §4 below), Molla Hosayn Ganjavi, and especially Shaykh Ja'far ibn Mohammad-Taqi.

We have already noted that this last figure was the son of Molla Barghani himself. Through his long friendship with the Shaykhis, he seems to have wished to make amends for his father's misconduct toward Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i.

As his writings attest, Mohammad-Khan Kermani's life was essentially that of a scholar and a man of spiritual devotion, wholly absorbed in research, teaching, and preaching. Although his works do not quite equal his father's in sheer extent, they cover all the same fields.

He was a kind and generous man. Sarkar Agha assures us that there was no one in Kerman who had not, at some time, benefited from his assistance or received some affectionate attention from him.

Yet agitation was stirred up against him—agitation which, beneath the cloak of pious religious pretexts, actually served very worldly interests. It was an artificial movement. If one questioned the people taking part in it, one discovered that they were unable to read Arabic, or even Persian, and knew absolutely nothing about the theological questions supposedly at issue. Their very ignorance left them all the freer to indulge in aggressive disturbances against the Shaykhis.

Here Sarkar Agha takes the opportunity to sketch what we might call a study of the spiritual and psychological character of this "resentment." His account lends to the life of Mohammad-Khan Kermani the significance of an exemplary biography.

Fundamentally, the Shaykhis had merely encountered, in modern times, the fate that true Shiites had always known. Their persecutors behaved no differently from the Umayyads and the Abbasids. Again and again, attempts had been made to appropriate Shiism and use it as the pretext for a political movement or revolution.

Those Shiites who refused such compromises inevitably found themselves, to a greater or lesser degree, at odds with the legalistic form of religion that such political enterprises tended to promote. Under these circumstances, Shiism sometimes had to conceal itself even from those who claimed its name. That is why the holy Imams themselves recommended to their followers the "discipline of secrecy" (ketmân, taqîyeh).

We shall see again later how dangerous it could be simply to appeal directly to the teaching and spiritual guidance of the Imams, without intermediaries—especially when doing so meant examining questions whose scope extended infinitely beyond matters of legal status. Too many established positions and interests were threatened for such an appeal not to cause alarm.

That is why the Imams descended from the Prophet have always stood as a challenge to the ambitions of this world.

Sarkar Agha concludes: From Adam down to our own day, there have always been minorities of this kind and majorities of that kind, in every religion and at every period. It is a law of nature: whoever differs from others arouses fear, and people turn upon him relentlessly, even if he is the most peaceful and silent of men (pp. 67–69).

Overwhelmed by sadness, Hajj Mohammad-Khan decided to move with his family to Tehran. But at Baghin, five farsakhs—about thirty kilometers—from Kerman, a solemn delegation caught up with him. It included prominent citizens, several of the most eminent shaykhs, bearing the title Hojjat al-Islâm, and even the royal prince Roknod-dawleh, then governor of Kerman and Baluchistan.

They came to offer their apologies and implore him to return to Kerman. Moved by these friendly appeals, the shaykh yielded.

A period of calm followed. The governor kept strict watch over the ruffians, troublemakers, and agitators. Yet, as we know, a mere handful of such people is enough to cause disturbances while leaving those responsible almost impossible to identify. The difficulty was all the greater because the shaykh insisted that his many followers must never answer violence with violence.

Finally, in 1323 AH, the shaykh chose to retire to Langar, some seven farsakhs south of Kerman. He died there the following year, on 20 Moharram 1324 AH (1906).

Taken as a whole, his writings form an imposing body of work and mark an essential stage in the history of the Shaykhi school (II, pp. 306–398).

These writings also cover the whole field of learning, giving pride of place in every discipline to the teachings handed down from the holy Imams. They comprise 204 titles (in fact more, for the reasons already explained). Sixty-five are works in Persian, and barely twenty have so far been printed.

Among them, we should single out the Kitâb al-Mobîn (II, pp. 344–347), a major work that systematically arranges the Imams’ traditions (akhbâr) according to the different branches of knowledge (published 1305–1324 AH/1887–1906, two folio volumes of 617 and 634 pages); Wasîlat al-Najât (II, p. 334, in Persian), an original investigation and synthesis organized around the four arkân, or “pillars”; Hidâyat al-mostarshid (II, p. 335, in Persian), conceived along the same lines; Misbâh al-sâlikîn (II, p. 339, in Persian; its title might be rendered Lampas viatorum, “Lamp of the Wayfarers”), organized around the triad also familiar from Sufism: sharî'at, tarîqat, haqîqât (revealed religious law, the mystical path, and spiritual realization); and Sharh al-Hadîthayn (II, p. 311), a masterly exercise in ta'wîl, or interpretation of the inner meaning, devoted to two traditions concerning Fâtima’s preeminence on the Day of Resurrection (published in Bombay, 1312 AH, 152 pages)[^EII4-260].

I would particularly like to mention the Yanâbî' al-Hikmat (“Sources of Theosophy and Philosophy”), a work that I know from personal study to be an invaluable summa, recently published in two volumes at Kerman (1965). For some fifteen years, moreover, the shaykh devoted an entire course of teaching to expanding upon this work. The collected lessons (dorûs) fill an unpublished Persian folio volume of some thousand pages. I hope to discuss it more fully elsewhere.

##### 4. Shaykh Hâjj Zaynol-'Âbidîn-Khân Kermânî (1276/1859–1360/1942)

The biography of his father, written with filial devotion by Sarkâr Âghâ (pp. 32–56), gives us an unusually vivid picture of the life of a spiritual community’s leader in the distant Iranian province of Kerman during the first half of this century. Its account is firsthand: Sarkâr Âghâ shared with his father the same spiritual intimacy that we have already seen among their predecessors.

Zaynol-'Âbidîn Khân, born on 7 Rajab 1276 AH (1859) and deceased on 5 Jomâdâ I 1360 AH (1942)[^EII4-261], was only twelve when his father, Hâjj Mohammad Karîm-Khân, died (1288 AH). His elder brother, Mohammad-Khân, who succeeded their father, took complete responsibility for his education and introduced him to the Islamic sciences. As we have already noted, a close friendship bound the brothers despite the difference in their ages. Zaynol-'Âbidîn accompanied his brother throughout his life and on his journeys.

Indeed, in his final years, burdened by trials and sorrow, the elder brother liked to say, “The visits of Zaynol-'Âbidîn-Khân are the only sweetness I still taste in this world.” Zaynol-'Âbidîn, for his part, valued nothing more than the long hours they spent studying together in their library. Their collaboration produced, among other things, the collection known as the Kitâb al-Mobîn, mentioned above. Shaykh Zaynol-'Âbidîn had a highly individual way of working.

When he spoke to his son about the difficulties he encountered, he offered remarkably perceptive observations on how an idea slowly takes shape before a discovery, and on how repeated attempts to put it into writing—even attempts that seem premature—can help bring the discovery about. His way of life reflected his character. Profoundly indifferent to prejudice and social convention, he regarded his entire person, like his predecessors, as devoted to the service of the holy Imams.

Five days each week he taught the higher divine wisdom, hikmat ilâhîya. On Thursday and Friday evenings, however, he delivered a lengthy sermon at the mosque. He spent eight to ten hours a day reading and writing, yet always found time for anyone who came with a question. He was a refuge to all, and no turn of events disturbed his even temper.

Journeys that interrupt a life of this kind could only be pilgrimages. The shaykh went once to Mecca (1305 AH/1888), three times to the Shiite holy places in Iraq, and four times to Mashhad in Iran, to the shrine of the Eighth Imam. Even while traveling, he went on working and writing.

During his lifetime there were still occasional attempts to stir up trouble against the Shaykhis, but it became clear that, whenever the authorities had the resolve to remove two or three agitators, peace and order quickly returned[^EII4-262]. The last seven years of the shaykh’s long life were overshadowed by serious illness. He watched events in the world, and Iran’s predicament in particular, with a clear-eyed pessimism: “It is not within human power to put things right.

“We must wait until people themselves become aware of their unbridled selfishness and their worship of this world, until they despair of it.” Until then, why be surprised “if even under the name of religious sciences ('olûm-e dînîya), people pursue nothing but worldly aims?” (p. 55). Shaykh Zaynol-'Âbidîn received numerous ijâzât, formal authorizations to transmit and teach. The most important came from his elder brother, Hâjj Mohammad-Khân.

Another was granted by Sayyed Hosayn, author of the great Qur’anic Tafsîr (commentary), and son of Sayyed Ja'far Yazdî. Both belonged to the Shaykhi line of transmission (silsila shaykhîya), and we have already had occasion to emphasize the exemplary case of Sayyed Ja'far. The wording of this authorization is of interest, since it was itself derived from Hâjj Mohammad-Khân—who listed his own authorizations and teachers (mashâyekh) at the beginning of his Kitâb al-Mobîn—and leads back through an unbroken chain to the earliest Shiite masters.

A third authorization, dated 19 Jomâdâ I 1311 AH (1893), is equally revealing of the care taken to establish a continuous chain of transmission back to the Imams. It was issued by Shaykh 'Alî Bahrânî, son of Shaykh Hasan, who had been among those who fled Bahrain for Iran and was a friend of Mohammad Karîm-Khân Kermânî.

Shaykh 'Alî Bahrânî had himself received one authorization from Mohammad Karîm-Khân and another from Mollâ Hosayn Ganjavî. The latter’s authorization, received from Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î, leads back link by link to Kolaynî (d. 329 AH/941), author of the Kitâb al-Kâfî, one of the foundational books of Shiism, and through him to the holy Imams. The writings left by Shaykh Zaynol-'Âbidîn-Khân form a body of work worthy of his predecessors (II, pp. 400–464).

There are 153 titles, about half in Persian, of which scarcely more than twenty-five have appeared in print. In particular, almost all the treatises on hikmat ilâhîya, divine wisdom—many of which explore symbols of Shiite theosophy drawn from the Qur’an and the Imams’ traditions—remain unpublished. His series of lectures on the nature of prophecy, covering prophecy in general (nobowwat 'âmma) and the specific prophetic mission (nobowwat khâssa), survives in several substantial manuscripts. Yet even these represent only part of what he taught; his disciples unfortunately disposed of the rest. 

##### 5. Shaykh Abû'l-Qâsem-Khân Ebrâhîmî, Sarkâr Âghâ (1314/1896–1389/1969)

The fifth successor to Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î as head of the Shaykhi community was Shaykh Abû'l-Qâsem-Khân Ebrâhîmî, better known by his honorific title, “Sarkâr Âghâ.” Born in Kerman in 1314 AH/1896, he was the son of Shaykh Zaynol-'Âbidîn-Khân and the grandson of Mohammad Karîm-Khân Kermânî. He died only recently, on 3 December 1969, in Mashhad, where he had gone on his annual pilgrimage.

We had met him barely a month earlier, on 9 November, during his stay in Tehran, little knowing that this conversation would be our last. Having benefited over many years in Iran from his teaching on the matters discussed here, I recall him with the respect inspired by the memory of his spiritual strength and profound learning. His writings reflect many of the challenges he faced, challenges scarcely different from those now confronting his son and successor, Shaykh 'Abdol-Rezâ Khân.

In a few pages of the major work to which we have been referring, a deep sadness breaks through. He wonders why, although “our mashâyekh [our shaykhs] have replied in hundreds of treatises, the same objections are endlessly repeated, and they still miss the point, for they never contain even the beginnings of an argument; they merely repeat suspicions, conjectures, accusations…” (p. 17).

Three of Sarkâr Âghâ’s major works in Persian deserve particular attention here.
a) Ijtihâd o taqlîd[^EII4-263]. — This substantial work raises such urgent questions that it calls for an extended analysis, which there is no room to undertake here. Its two title words can be understood only against the background of a controversy that has remained so fierce among Shiites that we must confine ourselves to a few cautious indications. It is the great dispute between the two schools known respectively as Osûlî and Akhbârî.

Vital questions are at stake: nothing less than how the whole body of Shiite traditions is to be interpreted. The dispute is generally treated as a matter for jurists, chiefly concerning fiqh, or Islamic jurisprudence. Sarkâr Âghâ’s great achievement is to restore the question to its proper level and show that, beneath the choice between these two schools, the whole of theosophy—and with it the whole of Imami Shiism—is also at issue.

The school of the Osûlîyûn, whom we may simply call the Osûlîs (from osûl, “foundations,” “principles,” or “general laws”), has become the larger school in numbers. Its adherents evaluate and interpret traditions from the Prophet and the Imams by applying rational principles and standards drawn from outside the traditions themselves; the traditions’ contents are then judged by those standards. This tendency probably first appeared in Shiism in a book by Abû Ja'far Tûsî (d. 460 AH/1067), who wished to demonstrate that Shiites were just as capable as Sunnis of using qiyâs—a word meaning both “analogy” and “syllogism”—even though the Imams had never accepted qiyâs, and Shiites could not recognize it as legitimate.

All the more so because, in the Osûlî view, certainty cannot be reached about the divine intentions expressed in the Qur’an’s words, the exact meaning of those words, the authenticity of traditions (hadîth) attributed to the holy Imams, or even what those traditions were precisely intended to mean.

In short, one can reach only an opinion, a conjectural form of knowledge (zann), and offer only a conjectural proof (borhân mazanna), as though by a kind of divination.

We can now understand why ijtihâd, closed in Sunni Islam for centuries, has remained open in Shiism. Ijtihâd means the painstaking, persistent effort of study, sustained over many years, by which someone seeks to master the religious Law and become qualified to issue a theological judgment carrying authority. Those who attain this office or dignity through their studies are the Mojtaheds. Their standing is broadly comparable to that of the four “imams” associated with the Sunni schools of law—the Hanbalite, Hanafite, Malikite, and Shafiite schools.

The philosophical assumption behind the Mojtaheds’ undertaking is that their rational intellect and reasoning ('aql) play a role equivalent to that of divine inspiration (ilhâm) in the Prophet (nabî) and the Imam. For the theosophers, by contrast, inspiration belongs to the holy intellect ('aql qodsî, intellectus sanctus), is fundamentally higher than ordinary reason, and can never be its equivalent.

The path of ijtihâd is open to any Shiite with sufficient time and resources. In practice, however, only a small number become Mojtaheds. Because their learning and judgments carry authority, most believers follow their opinions, freely choosing the Mojtahed they prefer. To follow, or conform oneself to, the opinion of one’s chosen Mojtahed is taqlîd. The two words in the title of Sarkâr Âghâ’s book should now be clear.

There is also the school of the Akhbârîyûn, whom again we may simply call the Akhbârîs. These are believers who accept the Qur’an, along with the entire corpus of hadîth and akhbâr in the Imami tradition, in its entirety and according to its literal wording. They can certainly claim a continuous Shiite tradition reaching back to the Imams, whereas the criteria used by the Osûlîs were codified comparatively recently (we shall return to this). Their leading figure in the Safavid period was Mohammad Amîn Astarâbâdî (d. 1033 AH/1623–1624)[^EII4-264].

Yet because of their literalism, they are generally thought of as people of uncomplicated spirituality, uninvolved in theosophy or mysticism, in hikmat or 'irfân (philosophical wisdom or mystical knowledge). This is not entirely fair. As we have already noted, the Akhbârîs include distinguished theosophers such as Mohsen Fayz, pupil and son-in-law of Mollâ Sadrâ (d. around 1091 AH/1680). His book Safinat al-Najât, “The Ark of Salvation,” shows that he knew perfectly well that interpreting the problem went far beyond the strictly legal sphere.

Another is Qazî Sa'îd Qommî, whom we have discussed at length above. We should also remember Mîrzâ Mohammad Neyshâpûrî Akhbârî (d. 1232 AH/1817), renowned for his knowledge of the occult sciences. The Shaykhis, then, reject the rationalism of the Osûlîs and stand much closer to the Akhbârîs.

Yet the two must not be confused, any more than Shaykhi theosophy should be confused with that of Mollâ Sadrâ’s school, or Shaykhi mysticism with Sufism. The Shaykhis hold that conjectural knowledge is not enough: spiritual life is impossible without certainty. No legal ruling, no system of jurisprudence, can provide that certainty.

The Qur’an and the traditions of the Prophet and the holy Imams are both necessary and sufficient. Just as there must be no intermediary between the Book of God and the believer, so there must be none between the Imams’ traditions and those who follow them. We have here something like a Shiite version of the Reformation principle Scriptura sacra sui ipsius interpres: Holy Scripture is its own interpreter.

We must add, however, that in this case Scripture’s self-interpretation first takes shape in the tradition, that is, in the inspiration (ilhâm) of the holy Imams. This does away, by that very fact, with the Mojtaheds’ role as intermediaries—a consequence unlikely to have made life any easier for the Shaykhi school. For the only legitimate or conceivable taqlîd is thus a direct adherence to the holy Imams themselves. This immediate relationship also accords perfectly with the Imams’ injunction not to resort to qiyâs, reasoning by analogy.

The task is to bring their traditions to bear on each individual case, discovering each time which tradition, or traditions, apply. Once again, the movement of thought is not dialectical but essentially interpretive—an exercise in ta'wîl, the search for inner meaning. The most fervent traditionalism thus proves capable of generating perpetual renewal: a new meaning may emerge every day. One must seek it out, and that is the very fruitfulness of esoteric knowledge.

Someone will no doubt ask: how, then, can the authenticity of these hadîth and akhbâr be judged? How can we know whether the Imams really said this or that? We shall return to this question. Put in those terms, it is the characteristic question of the historian who approaches the texts from the outside, a question that such a historian can hardly avoid asking.

But a phenomenologist, attending to religious experience as it is lived, discerns another question: where is the “place” from which the Imam speaks, and in which his words carry authority? The Imams are no longer physically present in this world. Their authority, which allows no intermediary, must therefore be inward. The “place” where it operates—and where the Imams’ words are heard, and were heard in earlier times—is Shiite consciousness itself. Without that consciousness, no one would even have cared to transmit the texts to us.

Is it not possible that, in the intensity of meditation, as the Imam’s presence becomes real to consciousness, his voice may be heard in words that take the form, on the lips or under the pen of the transmitter, of a sermon (khotba) or a narrative such as the story of the White Cloud? At that moment, we would say, whatever the name of the “secretary” (amanuensis) holding the pen, it is the Imam who speaks. (For this reason, the only adequate textual inquiry would be one concerned with the history of literary forms, or Formgeschichte.) Without this phenomenological understanding, we shall never understand the religious phenomenon of Shiism—or, indeed, religious experience as such.

Any criticism imposed entirely from outside, seeking to subject that experience to the laws of the external world, only breaks it apart. This has been our approach to interpretation throughout the present work. For the Imam’s real existence, his spiritual existence, is something other than the outward record of deeds accessible to external history. Nor is that real existence confined to the period of his visible appearance in history: if it were, there could be neither Shiite religion nor Shiite consciousness.

Shiite consciousness—the malakût, or spiritual realm, of the Shiite believer—is the only place where the Imam speaks and speaks with authority (recall the tradition of the White Cloud). The Imam is himself the history, the true history, of Shiite consciousness: a spiritual history whose events are inward visions. These observations should convey the weight of what is at stake in Sarkâr Âghâ’s major work and explain its exceptional interest. The questions it addresses reach far beyond jurisprudence into the realm of faith and religious experience itself—the res religiosa.

We can illustrate this here with only one example. A frequently debated question is whether a believer may, at least in matters of practical conduct, continue to follow a Mojtahed who has died, or whether that allegiance must be transferred to another. The usual answer is that it must be transferred to a living Mojtahed. The Shaykhis, however, make the following point.

Taqlîd, in the ordinary sense of the word and in the all-too-common way it is practiced, amounts to simply agreeing—to accepting a Mojtahed’s “authority” without any further personal grounds. Instead of truly conforming oneself to a teaching, one is merely conforming to others. Whether the Mojtahed is living or dead makes no difference: the practice becomes, quite simply, the same as that of the Sunnis.

But if we attend to the spiritual, true meaning of the conduct designated by taqlîd, we must recognize that it can only mean “conforming oneself” to the teaching of the Imams (as a tradition of the Seventh Imam, Mûsâ Kâzem, makes clear). Any taqlîd centered on the Mojtahed as a person has no foundation.

A Mojtahed cannot be said to speak by virtue of a rule-making authority vested in him personally. He interprets; he explains matters to those who have lacked the time or ability to “search” for themselves; he helps each person make the teaching his or her own (tashkhîs, an individual act of discernment and appropriation). The only voice that speaks with authority is that of the Imam himself, through a khabar, a transmitted teaching that brings out the hidden meaning of the revealed Book.

In that sense, a fatwâ, or legal opinion, is not different in kind from a khabar: it translates, develops, and deepens it. The value of a scholar who possesses this gift of interpretation therefore endures whether he is alive or dead, just as the content of a khabar endures whether its transmitter (râwî) is living or dead.

If the Shaykhis acknowledge such spiritual authority in their three great shaykhs, they do so because those teachers remained faithful in their interpretation and explanation of the Prophet’s and the Imams’ teachings. That is the sole reason. What may appear from the outside as an “innovation,” as the teaching passes from one shaykh to another, is in reality no more than the lifting of the veil of taqîyeh—the precautionary concealment of belief—on a point that might previously have required it.

Every Shiite, moreover, has a calling to ijtihâd, provided he possesses the necessary learning together with the moral and spiritual qualifications. The insistence on both conditions means that the very idea of “legal specialization” developing independently of the spiritual demands of religious life can only be a distortion. Likewise, because the Imam alone possesses authority, no “clergy” can claim it for themselves.

Finally, in practice, all Shiites, Mojtaheds or not, take the “Hidden Imam” as their guide in taqlîd, following the final instruction left to his last nâ'ib, or representative (329 AH/940). Since the Hidden Imam is alive and invisibly present, the question of giving one’s allegiance to a dead man cannot arise.

Yet that, in Shiite eyes, is unfortunately what Sunni scholars have done, piling book upon book on the writings of their four “imams,” who truly are dead (pp. 10–14).

b) Risâla-ye Tanzîh al-Awliyâ. — This substantial work[^EII4-265] is chiefly a commentary on the Irshâd al-awâmm, itself written in Persian by Mohammad Karîm-Khân Kermânî (mentioned above, § 2, p. 242). It answers sixty questions posed by various individuals about difficulties they encountered in reading that work, and consequently treats numerous essential points of 'irfân, or mystical theosophy[^EII4-266].

Here, however, we shall consider only one question of immediate relevance, a concern also visible in the first volume of the Fihrist (pp. 26 ff.): the unity, or reunification, of Islam and Muslims. In other words, the issue is certain contemporary attempts at a kind of “ecumenism” intended to bring together the Sunni majority and the Shiite minority.

Clearly, the question takes on an entirely different meaning depending on whether one understands Shiism simply as a legal tradition or experiences it as the authentic form of spiritual Islam. In the first case, it is enough to “unite” Shiism with the four existing Sunni schools as a fifth school of law.

In the second, for anyone who professes Shiism in its fullness, the walâyat—the spiritual guardianship and guidance—of the Twelve Imams is the “inner meaning of prophecy.” It is therefore implied, together with the Prophet’s mission (risâlat), in the very words of the profession of faith, the shahâdat. Their initiatory role in revealing the hidden, inward meaning of divine revelations makes them Guides upon the Way. At a higher level, they are ultimately understood to be the Way itself, and the meaning of that Way.

A Shiite who knows the level of reality from which his personal, inward obligation of fidelity to the Imams arises cannot help seeing such efforts at “reunion” as concealing worldly motives and political ideologies, pushing toward compromises he cannot contemplate. We have already seen how rigorously Shaykhi thought condemns this sort of confusion. Once we grasp what faith and trust in the “Hidden Imam,” whose invisible presence sustains Shiite life, truly mean, two characteristic attitudes become easy to understand.

First, the spirit of proselytism—missionary work or propaganda—is alien to this faith, for the invisible Imam alone can lead each consciousness inwardly to find the Way.

Second, these efforts at reconciliation appear to a Shiite to debase and endanger the very thing they claim to save, without even understanding what it is.

c) Risâla-ye falsafîya. — This final book is no less relevant to our own time than the preceding two[^EII4-267]. It answers twenty-five questions put to Sarkâr Âghâ by Mollâ Falsafî (8 Rabî' II 1369 lunar AH = 27 Bahman 1328 solar AH = 17 February 1950). The questions are searching, for they concern all the essential points of the four rokn (“pillars” or articles) that distinguish Shaykhi doctrine within Shiism.

The replies are equally pointed and define the positions of the two sides with some spirit. In truth, the questionnaire was not without a conciliatory intention. Mollâ Falsafî hoped that the answers, once submitted for consideration to the great Mojtahed of Qomm, might make it possible to stop using the name “Shaykhis,” thus removing every suggestion or suspicion of “dissent.”

But as we have seen, the Shaykhis are not at all troubled by the name given to them; and when one professes their fidelity to the holy Imams, it would be difficult to feel oneself a “dissenter.”

In short, the questions and answers were published, and matters went no further. From this necessarily brief sketch of the Shaykhi school’s history and literary productivity, two things emerge. We encounter a doctrine and a form of religious experience characteristic of Shiite consciousness in our own time; and we encounter an entire library hitherto unknown in the West.

Adding up the material examined above gives us about a thousand titles, in Arabic and Persian—and actually more if we take account of the way the majmû'a, or collected volumes, are put together. Barely more than a quarter of these works have been published, and for several reasons the rest can only appear gradually[^EII4-268].

### Chapter III

#### Some Points of Doctrine

##### 1. Tradition and Renewal

In these pages it is impossible to offer a detailed synthesis of Shaykhi doctrine, whose broad purpose embraces both a speculative understanding of the Imams and the spiritual regeneration of the believer. At the outset we recalled the Shiite tradition that Shaykhism was in fact bringing back to life, together with its representatives—not only in Safavid and pre-Safavid times but much further back, among those who surrounded the Imams themselves. It would be fruitless to judge this movement, or claim to “explain” it, from outside.

As we have also noted, its purpose has often been confused with that of schools from which it is in fact clearly distinct. Tonkâbûnî, for example[^EII4-269], describes the undertaking of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î—whom he acknowledges as an outstanding figure (sar-âmad)—as a synthesis of Shiite theology and philosophy, specifically the philosophy of Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî.

But such a synthesis had been accomplished long before, from Haydar Âmolî and Ibn Abî Jomhûr down to Mollâ Sadrâ himself. And although Shaykh Ahmad wrote systematic commentaries on two of Mollâ Sadrâ’s works, he did not do so simply to adopt the philosophy of the master of Shiraz. He had something quite different in mind.

Tonkâbûnî’s description would therefore make sense only if it pointed us toward a different kind of parallel: for example, the work of the great Ismaili thinkers Hamîdoddîn Kermânî and Nâsir-e Khosraw, especially the latter’s Jâmî' al-Hikmatayn, which seeks to bring together the two philosophies, Ismaili and Greek.

Yet their work would probably have provoked among philosophers who were strictly Avicennian a reaction much like that of the nineteenth-century philosopher Hâdî Sabzavârî toward Shaykh Ahmad.

What these two major forms of Shiite theosophy—Twelver and Ismaili—share is the very idea on which Shiism as a religious phenomenon rests: walâyat, the spiritual guardianship of the Imams, as the necessary counterpart of nobowwat, or prophetic mission. They share the conviction that the Qur’anic revelation, like every prophetic revelation, has both zâhir and bâtin: an outward meaning and an inward one; and that the role of the Imamate, and of the Imams’ teaching, is to guide people toward that inner meaning and initiate them into it.

Walâyat and nobowwat are joined in the person of the Prophet, but the prophetic mission as such is to reveal the outward meaning, whereas walâyat is concerned with teaching the inward meaning. The cycle of prophecy ends with the last Prophet; the cycle of walâyat begins with the first Imam. It is this teaching that is meant when we refer to the immense body of traditions (akhbâr) transmitted from the Imams.

But these traditions are not, in turn, literal commentaries on the Book and the Prophet’s hadîth. More often than not—especially where they concern the creation of the cosmos, the eternal preexistence of the fullness of the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones,” or the events of the last things—they speak in symbols.

Some are as long as an entire lesson. They invite ta'wîl, interpretation that reveals their inner meaning, and other hadîth and akhbâr teach how to undertake that very interpretation[^EII4-270]. In our discussion of ijtihâd and taqlîd above, we saw how and why Shaykhi interpretation could preserve the whole body of traditions from the Imams.

We also began to see how it responds to a question that the historian studying from the outside cannot help asking. It is a question that has given rise to several schools within Shiism: among the immense and not always clearly bounded corpus of hadîth and akhbâr, which traditions should be judged “sound” (sahîh) and which “weak” (za'îf)? Which should be accepted, treated with reserve, or set aside? The position of Shaykhism is remarkably firm.

More precisely, it insists on separating that question from another, more essential one: the meaning and content (ma'nâ) of a hadîth or khabar itself. To see exactly what is at issue, we need only recall that the Shaykhis have often been accused of accepting “weak” traditions as valid.

Sarkâr Âghâ replies (pp. 237 ff.) by asking: what exactly are these supposedly weak traditions? The technical terminology used to classify traditions and grade their reliability is no more than about six centuries old. Before it was devised, what standard did people use to accept or reject the traditions? They must have had one; it is inconceivable that the prophetic religion was ever without such a standard.

By what right, then, and in the name of what authority, should we abandon that earlier measure, whose origins go back to the Prophet and the Imams, in favor of a later critical terminology and the criteria it imposes? If a tradition agrees with the Book and with the Sonnât jâmi'a—the “complete Tradition,” meaning, in Shiite usage, the whole body of traditions tracing back to the Prophet and the Imams—what principle requires us to reject it, even when the newer terminology pronounces its historical chain of transmission “weak”? That weakness is more than compensated for by the agreement itself. One may certainly acknowledge that some narrators and transmitters (rowât, rijâl) are more trustworthy than others.

But these men were not prophets, whereas the Prophet and the Imams knew the invisible, suprasensory world. On the question of who may be trusted, specialists in the historical study of transmitters (rijâl) have filled books with conflicting judgments. Surely the assent of faith, the believer’s confidence in the Imams’ words, cannot depend on whether these critics approve or reject them.

Do these experts not place excessive confidence in their own discipline and its subject matter? Once we admit that someone might have been bold enough to fabricate a hadîth, why stop there? Why not admit that he might equally have fabricated an impeccable chain of authorities, all apparently beyond reproach, and so disarmed historical criticism in advance? (p. 240).

Here the same argument reappears that we encountered in the discussion of taqlîd. To accept the judgments of specialists in the study of transmitters would simply mean resting one’s faith on the human authority of the “transmitters,” rather than on the spiritual authority inherent in what the text teaches.

But the authority to which one turns and entrusts oneself is not that of a Mojtahed or a transmitter (râwî). It is the authority of the Imams—or, more precisely, of the “Imam who is invisible to the senses but present in the hearts of those who follow him.” From this point of view, there is no difference between the past and the present. The question of recognizing the Imam’s words and teaching remains the same then as now; time changes nothing.

The Imam’s presence is unchanged, and assent (tasdîq) depends ultimately not on any external human authority but on the testimony the Imam bears to himself in the heart of the believer. This is precisely what Shaykh Ahmad meant when he said he could “recognize an Imam’s hadîth by its fragrance.” There are no rational proofs to support such assent, but neither are there any that can disprove it. Negative philosophical criticism has no purchase here.

By contrast, philosophy’s task is without limit when it devotes itself to interpreting symbols[^EII4-271]. Sarkâr Âghâ expressly emphasizes that his purpose is not that of a historian: he does not claim to be practicing historical criticism. The point is precisely that assent to the beliefs of faith ('aqâ'id) can depend neither in principle nor in lived experience on criticism of that kind, for this would ultimately make it subordinate to some human authority (pp. 241–243). This shows how grave is the problem that Shaykhism has knowingly taken upon itself, fully aware of difficulties long familiar to Western theology and philosophy.

A revealing illustration is furnished by an anecdote, whether true or invented, about a certain Shaykh Mohammad Hasan at Najaf. A specialist solely in jurisprudence, but a formidable debater, he is said to have decided to test Shaykh Ahmad’s “sense of smell” (shamm), his capacity to recognize a tradition.

Tonkâbûnî recounts the episode; but, as we know, his sources are highly questionable[^EII4-272]. It also seems altogether improbable that the shaykh of Najaf would have allowed himself to behave in such a way[^EII4-273]. Whatever the truth, the story must be reported with scrupulous accuracy, not in an approximate version that tries to make it “more amusing” and, one fears, betrays an intention to ridicule Shaykh Ahmad[^EII4-274]. For here the inaccuracy leads to an utter confusion of two quite different questions.

Shaykh Mohammad Hasan supposedly “fabricated” a hadîth in elaborate Arabic, but supplied no isnâd, or chain of transmission. He then showed the paper to Shaykh Ahmad and said, “I have discovered a hadîth. Can you tell whether it really is a hadîth and understand its meaning (ma'nâ)?” It was the meaning and content that Shaykh Ahmad affirmed. His response is readily understood, since he had not been asked whether the chain of transmission was “sound” or “weak.”

To make a judgment using those labels, in the only sense to which they properly apply, no “divining faculty” is required: one simply has to identify the actual transmitters (rowât and rijâl). There are, in fact, two questions of entirely different kinds. One is a matter of historical criticism and belongs to the study of transmitters; the other concerns essence and spiritual meaning.

Or are we to assume that when a modern historian declares a hadîth “weak,” he does so because he finds its content unacceptable—for instance, a tradition concerning the ma'âd, the return in resurrection, or the “resurrection body”? If that is what he is doing, he should at least have the courage to say openly what standard he is using (pp. 251–252). Sarkâr Âghâ therefore sums up the problem in terms of decisive importance for every aspect of Shiite theology.

There are two paths, pursued by different people. 1) One may investigate the circumstances of the transmitters (rowât), as the Osûlîs do, and judge the “strength” or “weakness” of a “chain of transmission” according to the trustworthiness of those involved. This inquiry rests in turn on opinions expressed in historical works dealing with transmitters (rijâl) and traditionists (mohaddîthîn). It is the outward path, the external or exoteric method (râh-e zâhirî). It offers useful assistance, an auxiliary discipline, and enables one to form an opinion.

But it cannot lead to certainty about a truth of essence. 2) The second path aims precisely at that essential truth (râh-e haqîqî): the inward truth, the meaning and spiritual reality of what is said and signified. It asks whether what a hadîth or khabar says agrees with the explicit or implicit meaning of the Book and of the complete Tradition (sonnât) of the Prophet and the Imams.

Thus the shaykh consciously and unmistakably draws a distinction. On one side stands the knowledge produced by historical criticism, which remains external and is appropriate to a fides historica, a faith founded on historical evidence, but is insufficient in itself either to ground or to overturn the assent of lived spiritual faith.

On the other stands what we might call an intuition of essence—a phenomenological insight—which seeks to bring meaning and content to light and to perceive whether they harmonize with, or contradict, the whole symphony. Such perception admittedly presupposes a prior intuition of the meaning of that whole, and may be qualitative rather than quantitative. For this reason, it is explicitly said to be beyond the reach of just any learned person. It belongs only to those who possess spiritual capacity (qowwat-e qodsîya) and know the Imams’ way of speaking.

Indeed, a saying of the Sixth Imam states: “We do not recognize any one of you as learned until he has become able to recognize any of our hadîth that is presented to him” (p. 253). It is by this second path that meaning and content—significance and essence—are recognized, even where the Imam spoke in circumstances beyond the reach of external historical criticism. That, and nothing else, is what Shaykh Ahmad’s intuition could “recognize by its fragrance,” and what it did recognize.

This means that, even if the words had been invented by the person questioning him, they could still have agreed with the tradition; and in this case their meaning and content did in fact agree with the complete Tradition (sonnât jâmi'a). That said, it remains improbable that one of the religious scholars ('olamâ') would have indulged in such a game.

The fact that Shaykh Ahmad recognized the meaning is therefore all the less surprising, since it is even less conceivable that a scholar would have dared to fabricate a “false” saying that contradicted the Book and the sonnât jâmi'a (ibid.). The question put to Shaykh Ahmad thus amounted to something very simple. In any case, to recount the anecdote as though he had been asked to judge the validity or weakness of the historical chain of transmission, rather than the meaning and content, is—deliberately or not—to distort radically what happened.

We need not pursue the matter further. The saying of the Sixth Imam quoted a few lines above defines the position of Shaykhism and shows where it stands. That position requires, and gives a precise meaning to, a personal relationship of faith—and therefore a spiritual relationship—with the Imam as present now.

The certainty this relationship confers is of an entirely different order from anything that external historical research into the transmitters (rijâl) can provide. It gives that certainty a character independent of every external and temporal authority. The Imam, as the spiritual pole (qotb), gives the believer a “polar dimension.”

The frequent discussions of this question in Iran often leave one with the impression that the assumptions on either side have not been made sufficiently clear. Here, terminology developed in the West out of a comparable situation may help bring some clarity.

At the beginning of his own commentary on his book of *Teachings* (*Fawâ'id*), Shaykh Ahmad makes this declaration: “Whatever certainty I possess in my knowledge I owe to the Imams who guide us (*A'immat al-hodâ*). If my writings are free from error, it is because everything I affirm in my books comes from their teaching, and because they themselves are protected (*ma'sûm*) from error, omission, and missteps. Whoever allows himself to be taught by them can be sure of not going astray, so long as he follows them. This is the spiritual meaning of the Qur'anic verse (34:17): ‘Travel through them in safety, by night and by day’” (p. 246).[^EII4-275]

We stressed earlier that an authentic tradition continually gives rise to rebirth, and that the reverse is equally true. A tradition cannot really be handed down unless each person who receives it undergoes a new birth—a spiritual birth (*wilâdat rûhânîya*). Such a birth consists precisely in discovering and making one's own the spiritual meaning which, as we have just seen, our authors distinguish so firmly from the outward and passing circumstances that concern historical faith (*fides historica*).

Every new spiritual birth thus brings forth a new understanding of the tradition: it renews the tradition itself. This is what the opponents of the Shaykhi school failed to grasp. The journey “in safety, by night and by day” is what we might call the tradition's *hermeneutic expansion*: the continuing unfolding of its meaning. Innovation breaks with tradition. Renewal, on the other hand, is inseparable from it. There can be no tradition without perpetual renewal; the very idea of tradition carries with it the idea of rebirth.

##### 2. The Renewal of Metaphysics

We have just quoted a few lines from a work that Shaykh Ahmad gave the simple title *Teachings* (*Fawâ'id*). Some critics have suggested that he understood neither the aims nor the vocabulary of the philosophers. We have argued, on the contrary, that he knew perfectly well what was distinctive about his own teaching and terminology. It is therefore necessary to offer a brief account of his metaphysical doctrine. This cannot pretend to be a synthesis.

But a very concise summary of the first chapters of the *Teachings* will be enough to show that Shaykhi thought amounts to a genuine reform and renewal of metaphysics.

The *Teachings* has a history of its own. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î first wrote a twelve-chapter treatise under this unassuming title, around 1225/1810, as he returned from Isfahan to Yazd. Its extreme brevity makes it almost impenetrable to a reader who lacks the key. Some eight years later, a shaykh who was his friend asked him for that key as they traveled together on pilgrimage to Mecca. A journey may not have been the ideal moment to ask someone to write another book.

Yet the long stages of the pilgrimage evidently afforded ample opportunity for dictation, and Shaykh Ahmad rose admirably to the occasion. The result was a remarkable clarification, completed on 9 Shawwâl 1233 / 13 October 1818. The original text and its commentary together make up a large octavo volume of 290 pages.[^EII4-276] The shaykh divides his original work into short passages, or *lemmata*, of a few lines each, and follows each with a commentary resolving the difficulties presented by “those things which will seem strange in comparison with what theologians and philosophers (*'olamâ* and *hokamâ*) are accustomed to discussing nowadays, and which I am the first to take up, though our Imams and the foremost of their Shiites have always discussed them.”[^EII4-277] A Persian disciple of the shaykh, Mohammad ibn Mohammad Nâsir Gîlânî, had attended his lessons for several years.

We have so far been unable to discover anything about him beyond what he tells us himself. The twelve *Fawâ'id* formed part of the teaching he received, and he wrote his own commentary on them, insisting that he did no more than transcribe his master's oral instruction. We were fortunate enough to find the sole surviving copy of this commentary—which is also the author's own manuscript—in a private collection in Tehran, belonging to Mr. Soltânî.[^EII4-278] Neither teacher nor disciple seems to have known of the commentary that the other was writing. Comparing the two is therefore all the more revealing, and opens up far-reaching lines of inquiry. Shaykh Ahmad's own written commentary is clearer and more precise; the disciple's, however, preserves digressions to which the shaykh did not return in his own version.

With these two commentaries, the twelve chapters ultimately form a veritable summa of Imami metaphysics. We hope to publish a translation of Shaykh Ahmad's text and his own commentary elsewhere. For now, we shall confine ourselves to a short account of the first five chapters.

The first chapter sets out three kinds of argument or proof, each with its own intellectual, spiritual, and moral requirements: dialectical proof (*dalîl al-mojâdala*), supported by theoretical knowledge; exhortative proof (*dalîl al-maw'iza*), supported by the heart (*qalb*); and the proof of wisdom (*dalîl al-hikma*), supported by the innermost heart, its center (*fu'âd*). “The first condition of the proof of wisdom is that you act faithfully toward your Lord. For when you reflect and contemplate by means of that proof, you summon your Lord to appear before you, while at the same time He summons you to appear before the very center of your heart. As the First Imam said: ‘Our representations cannot encompass Him, yet He manifests Himself to them through themselves.

“But through those same representations He also withholds Himself from them, and summons them to appear before themselves.’ Your Lord then enters into contention with you. Weigh, therefore, with the just Balance. This is the best *ta'wîl*, the best spiritual interpretation (cf. Qur'an 17:37).

“The second condition is that you stop where evidence is evident to you, where understanding is intelligible to you, where the explanation is one you can communicate. This accords with the divine command: ‘Do not seek knowledge of what it is not possible for you to know: your hearing, your sight, the center of your heart—these are what will be called to account’ (17:38).

“The third condition is that you regard all these situations with God's eye, not your own [...]—that is, with the eye that is His own description of Himself to you and for you: as He makes Himself known to you, as He characterizes Himself for you. This means that your existing, considered as your act of being—your existence—is a trace and a light: the state of the knowledge you have of yourself ...” (§§23–27). Already in this first chapter the shaykh develops his fundamental positions: his doctrine of the forms of manifestation and the degrees of consciousness and knowledge. His vocabulary of being also begins to take shape, marking a break with the customary language of the philosophers.

Chapter II takes the demands and implications of Shiite *negative theology*—the refusal to attribute creaturely qualities to God—to their furthest limit. The source of being transcends every category of being. No attribute can be assigned to it, since every attribute belongs to the order of creatures; every description already presupposes being, and therefore always arrives too late. God is at once the Known and the Unknown, the Present and the Absent. The only way He can be known is through the very fact that He cannot be known. For any positive knowledge of Him comes through an act of knowing in which He is never the object, but always the active subject. He can be known only as He makes Himself known, each time, to the person who recognizes Him.
