The Throne upon which the Merciful establishes himself on the seventh day is the person of the Resurrector (*Qâ'im*), the last Imam, through whom and in whom the inward meaning of all Revelations will be unveiled. The last Imam himself is the “seventh day.” His person gathers together and sums up the “six days” of prophecy, just as the complete form of a physical solid gathers together its six faces. At different levels of meaning, both complete and recapitulate the “six days of Creation.”

The whole secret history of humankind—the six millennia symbolizing the cycle of prophecy—moves toward the appearance of this perfect Human Form, the Resurrecting Imam (*al-walad al-tâmm*, the Perfect Child). His millennium, the seventh in the cycle, is the seventh day of the creation of the sacred cosmos. For no one, not even one of the six great prophets, has yet received the fullness of everything. The seventh day has not yet dawned: “the day when no soul shall have power over another soul, and the command shall belong to God alone” (82:19).[^EII4-303]

There is, of course, a difference between the eschatology of Twelver Shiism and Shaykhism on the one hand and that of Ismaili Shiism on the other. I think we can express it most briefly by saying that Twelver teachings about the Imam correspond symbolically to the heaven of the fixed stars, the sphere of the twelve constellations of the zodiac, whereas Ismaili teachings correspond to the seven planetary heavens and their moving stars.

For Twelver Shiites, the last Imam is already here. He has already appeared, but his divine splendor is now hidden in a world beyond the senses until the hour of his manifestation or *parousia*. For the Ismailis, the last Imam is the secret of the future, the Form of superhuman perfection that humanity will bring forth on the Last Day. That day cannot dawn until the whole cycle of planetary revolutions is complete.

Yet on both sides the “time of the Imam” takes spatial form as an Earth beyond this Earth: among the Shaykhis, the mystical Earth of *Hûrqalyâ*; among the Ismailis, the Earth mentioned in the Qur'anic verse concerning the creation of the Heavens and the Earth. This cannot mean our present Earth, for Scripture says it is “illumined by the light of its Lord.”

Our Earth, by contrast, remains in Darkness, although the light of physical day shines upon it. No: the verse concerns the mystical *hexaemeron*, “that other Earth, still concealed in the night ... upon which, it is said, the esoteric community is already established through the steadfastness of faith, not through any material settlement ... and which is the Earth of light.” On that Earth the darkness of religions confined to the literal word and the Law will have been dispersed.[^EII4-304]

This, in the broadest outline, is how the texts of Shaykhi Twelver Gnosis and Ismaili Gnosis present the structural correspondence of time and space. I believe we could easily verify here the laws of “hermeneutic perspective,” the perspective opened by spiritual interpretation, which we sketched in Book I of the present work. At the same time, an intellectual undertaking comes into view.

Though it works specifically upon the forms of biblical or Qur'anic Revelation, it differs neither in scope nor in intention—only in method—from contemporary efforts to analyze and bring together the harmonic forms perceived throughout Nature, in every kingdom and at every level of the universe. It is as true to say that living beings grow and live in time but die and disappear in space as it is to say that they grow in space and likewise vanish in time.

The opposition between time and space, their separation and their power to destroy one another, is experienced as something demonic. That is the tragedy of every living creature: having to fulfill its task in time, only to surrender everything it acquired or won in space during that time—and the reverse is equally true.[^EII4-305]

Thus the *symmorphosis* of form in time and form in space, abolishing the law by which each destroys the other, is envisioned in Shiite spiritual philosophy as the “form of Resurrection,” the “perfect form of the Imam,” the “Earth of Light,” and the “seventh day of Creation.”

Seen in this light, Shiite eschatology offers its own resolution of the tragedy faced by every living being: thrown into time, yet feeling within itself an insistent presence that protests against its destruction by time. The Imam's space—the “Earth of Light of *Hûrqalyâ*,” where time becomes space—appears as salvation from chronological time.

This brings the Imam's person fully into view at the “supreme horizon” to which Shiite thought and spirituality raise him. It seems to us, then, that this work can end in no other way than by turning to the person of the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam. Century after century, his presence endures in Shiite consciousness, entering the lives of believers, the mighty and the humble alike, in moments of doubt, distress, and abandonment. Whether in dreams or in waking life, a fleeting vision shines with trust in the Unseen and the certainty that his presence is always near.

# *Book VII*

## THE TWELFTH IMAM AND SPIRITUAL CHIVALRY

### CHAPTER ONE

#### *The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam*

##### *I. The Completion of the Fullness of the Twelve*

We have spoken of the Twelfth Imam so often that any attempt to collect all those passages here would risk repetition. Readers wishing to keep in mind everything implied by the completion of the fullness—the *pleroma*—of the Twelve should refer to our earlier discussions of the doctrine of the Imams.[^EII4-306] With that groundwork established, we must now outline the portrait offered by the hagiography, or sacred biography, of the Twelfth Imam. This biography is still unfinished, for it continues throughout his “occultation” (*ghaybat*), the period of his hidden presence.

We shall then explore certain parallels between the ideas surrounding him and themes familiar in the West, grouping them chiefly under spiritual chivalry and the reign of the Paraclete.

Let us begin by recalling, first, some sayings of the Prophet concerning the Twelve Imams, and especially the Twelfth; and second, the law of sacred rhythm that determines their number. Both lead to consequences that meet in the person of the Twelfth Imam, as Shiite consciousness understands him.

Shiite writings about the Twelfth Imam are vast.[^EII4-307]

First come the traditions recorded in various collections of *hadîth*. They concern both his brief manifestation in the past and his future manifestation—his *parousia* at the end of our *Aeon*—as the Imam who announces the Resurrection (*Qâ'im al-qiyâmat*), the one from Mohammad's family “who rises” for the Resurrection (*Qâ'im âl Mohammad*).

Between these two manifestations, the “history” of the Twelfth Imam continues. It consists of a great body of narratives and testimonies from people to whom he has appeared, whether in dreams or while awake, always in circumstances that go beyond the ordinary laws of sense perception and the accepted standards of rational evidence.

As presented to Shiite consciousness in its collections of *hadîth*, neither the number of twelve Imams nor the completion of their fullness by the twelfth is an accident of history. In several traditions the Prophet solemnly announces that the Imams after him will number twelve, and no more. The last will be the Resurrector (*Qâ'im*), the Mahdi: the one who is guided and who guides others toward God.

Another interpretation, based on the expression *al-Mahdî ilay-hi*, understands him as the one *toward whom* people are guided and who then becomes their guide (*al-Mahdî al-Hâdî*). Usually the Prophet announces the coming of the Mahdi, the Resurrector, in relation to his own prophetic mission as the bearer of the revealed letter (*tanzîl*). The Mahdi will be master of *ta'wîl*, spiritual interpretation: he will disclose the complete inward meaning of all divine Revelations. This idea is shared by Twelver Shiite and Ismaili Gnosis.

In one *hadîth*, the Prophet calls the First Imam his brother and speaks of the Twelfth as though he were his own child. Someone asks him: “O Messenger of God, who is your child?” He replies: “The Mahdi, the one whom I was sent to announce.”[^EII4-308] Two other traditions deserve special mention.

In one, the Prophet declares: “If only a single day remained to this world, God would lengthen that day so that a man of my descendants might arise in it, whose name will be my name and whose byname will be my byname. He will fill the Earth with peace and justice, just as it is now filled with violence and tyranny.”

In the second, after announcing that exactly nine Imams will follow Hosayn ibn 'Alî, the Third Imam, the Prophet adds: “The ninth will be the *Qâ'im*. He will fill the Earth with peace and justice, just as it is now filled with violence and tyranny. He will fight to restore the spiritual meaning (*ta'wîl*), just as I myself fought to reveal the literal meaning.”[^EII4-309]

These texts—and many more could be cited—show how firmly Shiite tradition believes that the Prophet's own teaching contains the essence of its understanding of prophecy and the Imams. At its heart lies a balance of complementary realities: outward and inward meaning, *nobowwat* and *walâyat*; the prophets' mission of disclosing the outward Revelation and the Imams' spiritual gift of initiating believers into its inward meaning. The Imamate of Mohammad's line, taken as a whole, is the Seal of universal *walâyat*, the spiritual guardianship and authority of the Imams. The Twelfth Imam in particular is the Seal of Muhammadan *walâyat*, in whom all *walâyat* is gathered together.

Thus Shiite tradition believes it receives from the Prophet himself its deepest understanding of the Mahdi as the Seal of Muhammadan *walâyat*.

This differs fundamentally from the conception of the Mahdi widespread in Sunni Islam. There, the Mahdi cannot be organically linked to the Imam in the specifically Shiite sense, and therefore cannot be linked in the same way to the inward meaning (*bâtin*) of Revelation or its spiritual interpretation (*ta'wîl*). Nor can the idea carry the same sense of a future still open to human expectation after the coming of the Seal of the Prophets.

Here, by contrast, the last Prophet himself becomes the forerunner of the last Imam: the one who will interpret the Revelation the Prophet brought, and therefore the Imam of the Resurrection. As we have already emphasized, the fundamental difference lies in this way of envisaging the future. Shiism certainly agrees that Revelation is complete, that the cycle of divine communications has been closed and sealed, and that Mohammad was the Seal of the Prophets.

But Shiite tradition sees the closing of the prophetic mission as the signal for the opening of a new cycle: the cycle of *walâyat*, of spiritual initiation. Shiite consciousness has heard with particular anguish the declaration that humanity, in its distress, has no further prophet to await.

Yet the last Prophet himself announced the one who was still to be awaited: the Imam, Seal of Muhammadan *walâyat*, is the Awaited Imam (*montazar*).

Hence that restless serenity, that hidden movement, that union of radical pessimism with unconquerable hope which we have already recognized in Shiite consciousness and described as *desperatio fiducialis*: a despair that nevertheless trusts.

There is another consideration. Alongside these texts establishing the necessary bond between the Seal of the Prophets and the Twelfth Imam—the Seal of Muhammadan *walâyat*—and affirming the identity of their names and the symmetry of their missions, there are numerous *hadîth* insisting on the sacred rhythm that fixes the number of Imams at twelve. These traditions prevent us from explaining the end of the visible manifestation of the Imams' fullness on Earth as some historical accident comparable to the events that brought worldly dynasties to an end.

Their number is connected with the significance of twelve: the twelve signs of the zodiac, the twelve months of the year, the twelve hours of day and of night, the twelve leaders of the tribes of Israel, and so on. Likewise, within the scheme of Shiite sacred history, each of the six (or seven) great prophets was followed by twelve Imams.

We should also recall the *hadîth* of the “Twelve Veils of Light.” Represented as twelve millennia, these Veils express within Shiism the ancient theologies of the *Aeon*. Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî gave a remarkable commentary on this tradition. In discussing it, we even spoke of a *structural doctrine of the Imams*: the twelvefold structure of the Imamate corresponds to the cubic temple of the Ka'ba, understood anew as a spiritual temple.[^EII4-310]

But if the Prophet's own teaching about the Twelfth Imam implies that humanity's religious and spiritual history remains open—that sacred history, of which the facts of ordinary history are merely the chrysalis, is not yet complete—how can this be reconciled with the assertion that the Imamate is limited to twelve Imams and that the twelfth has already been born? Does that not mean that the Imamate itself is closed? Certainly not. Rather, it points to the profound idea at the heart of the Twelfth Imam's figure: the necessity of his concealment from this world, his *ghaybat*.

The Imamate of the Twelve spans the entire interval between the close of prophecy and the Last Day. Since eleven Imams have already appeared, the twelfth must exist and endure in a manner not subject to the ordinary laws of biology or chronological time. Consequently, to everyone who remains in this world under those laws, his presence must take the paradoxical form of an absence. None of his mysterious appearances to the faithful brings his *ghaybat* to an end.

But every such appearance suspends, for the believer who encounters him, the ordinary condition of human beings who cannot perceive the Imam's “hidden presence.”

This is why the time of the Hidden Imam is an interval, a time “between times.” His “history,” as it unfolds in the consciousness of his followers, is the ripening of that interval until *another kind of time* comes into being and brings the time of absence to an end. And this is why a believer who is granted a vision of him also finds himself “between times.” Such a vision is not an event *within* the time of this world, something that could be fitted into its history.

The Imam's hidden presence is a *not yet* whose fulfillment remains perpetually close: it is the “imminent Hour” spoken of in sura 54. The coming of the awaited Imam is expressed by a single word, “Joy” (*farah*). No Shiite speaks or writes the name of the Twelfth Imam without adding the customary prayer: “May God hasten the Joy for us.”

The complete history of the Twelfth Imam therefore embraces the events of his manifestation in both past and future. Here “past” and “future” belong to the objective time of chronology, while the present of his hidden presence belongs to lived, existential time, a time “between” the times of chronology. Each event in his history breaks through History, for it cannot be contained within what we ordinarily call history, governed by what we call historical causation. Examples abound.

To speak of Israel crossing the Red Sea is one thing; to speak of that same crossing as Israel's liberation from bondage to matter and entry into the supernatural spiritual world is another. Above all, we must follow the path shown us by our philosopher-theosophers, especially Qazi Sa'id Qommi, when they explain the time and place of the *malakut*, the spiritual world. The “history” of the Twelfth Imam is a sacred biography, and we shall try to set out its principal events.

But a warning is needed at the outset. Once we cross the threshold into this sacred biography, what is usually called historical criticism will seem to have lost almost all its authority. If, however, we leave its demands at the threshold, and approach what is before us through a genuinely phenomenological perception—attending to the reality as it presents itself—we may become capable, through the appropriate faculty, of perceiving and understanding what events “between times” mean. We may also recognize the higher order of reality they announce, precisely because they belong to it.

Every sacred biography can call upon witnesses, often many of them, as in the case of the Twelfth Imam.

Yet it cannot produce the certificates, attestations, and documents demanded by our fixation on outward, material historicity. That fixation has left us able to imagine only one acceptable level of reality on which an “event” can occur. To demand that sacred biography supply documents of the kind used in critical history is already to lower the level of reality to which its events belong. That reduction has undoubtedly been going on for a long time.

The less capable we are of perceiving that “events take place in Heaven,” the more insistently we demand proof of their material historicity. The more we lose our sense of events whose reality is essentially a *mysterium liturgicum*, a sacred mystery enacted in worship, the more festivals we erase from the calendar.

What is today called “historical materialism” has distant predecessors, even within theology. Everything we shall report about the sacred biography of the Twelfth Imam may therefore seem, to a historian, to rest upon documents without objective value. And yet the events did happen!

But documents preserving the only traces that events occurring in the *malakut* can leave are merely discarded husks, empty chrysalises, if we lack the key to them. For any philosopher who accepts even a minimum of “spiritual realism,” on the other hand, these documents are beyond price.

In other words, the faculty of perception required here is “that eye of the soul which never sleeps,” as Philo of Alexandria puts it. Events belonging to the time of the Twelfth Imam, whether recorded in documents concerned with past, present, or future, can be grasped only by the “spiritual senses” of which all our philosopher-theosophers speak. The Imam is absent from sensory perception; indeed, even if he stood physically before us, he would remain invisible *as Imam* to anyone who could see only as one sees ordinary objects in the external world. His epiphany, his coming into presence, cannot take place until human consciousness has awakened to it.

In the interval “between times,” it can occur only for the few whom he himself chooses: those capable of spiritual recognition (*ma'rifat*), rather than the merely outward awareness of which even an animal is capable. This is what the texts taught us when they spoke of “seeing the Imam in *Hurqalya*.” They implied that the suprasensory world of *Hurqalya* and the material world of the senses coexist, penetrate one another, and contain one another.

*Hurqalya* is above us, around us, and within us at the same time. If, through our ignorance, it is not within us, we can neither know nor recognize it “anywhere”; for we can know something outside ourselves only through a corresponding capacity within. To understand the Hidden Imam's concealed presence in this world, we might, outwardly speaking, compare him to the *bodhisattva* of Mahayana Buddhism, who renounces departure from this world and delays entry into *nirvana* until all those entrusted to him have been saved.

Inwardly speaking, we might recall Mulla Sadra's teaching that every soul, every spiritual being, carries its own heaven or hell within itself. These are only indications of a way of understanding, a *modus intelligendi*, with a rigor of its own. Without such a way of understanding, we might as well confess ourselves unable to comprehend sacred knowledge, the perception of invisible worlds, and the visionary events of which sacred history is made.

But for the seeker who “saves the phenomena” by approaching them as a pilgrim of sincere heart, these events will reveal, more fully than any theoretical account, the secret of the Shiite soul—a secret whose strength has withstood the powers of doubt and denial for ten centuries.

##### 2. From Byzantium to Samarra

The traditional account that opens the sacred biography of the Twelfth Imam begins with a young Christian princess of Byzantium. An Isolde-like love awakens in her heart, but hers is a love that calls her to give miraculous birth to a Divine Child. The theme of the Divine Child is well known in the history of religions; the Shiite texts concerning it, however, have received very little study. Here we shall present the essential story.

The Tenth Imam, Ali Naqi, became Imam at the age of seven and died in 254/868, scarcely into his forties. He suffered particularly from the suspicions and harassment of the Abbasid caliph, who had turned Samarra, about a hundred kilometers north of Baghdad, into a military city.[^EII4-311] The caliph kept the Imam there, more or less a prisoner, for twenty years. It was there that the Imam's son Hasan was born in 231/845, and it was for this reason that he was called Hasan Askari, from *askar*, meaning “army.” There too, on the fifteenth of Sha'ban in the year 255 (3 August 868), was born Hasan's son, the Twelfth and last Imam.

Granted divine foreknowledge, Imam Ali Naqi arranged matters so that his son could marry the woman destined to become the mother of the Twelfth Imam. Here sacred history begins. It unfolds through a supernatural correspondence between the Imam's foreknowledge and what can only be called the young Christian girl's initiation: a series of visionary dreams through which the future mother of the coming Imam must pass.

What we have already explained about the cycle of prophecy and the successive reappearances of the fullness of the Twelve enables us to understand the possibilities of a spiritual fellowship between religions at the esoteric level. At the same time, the way these events are presented reveals how Shiism understands its relationship with Christianity; and there is something deeply moving in it.

The accounts of the Twelfth Imam's birth and brief appearance on earth were gathered and organized by the first generation of great Shiite theologians. They trace back to contemporary witnesses who took part in the events.

We shall chiefly follow the version given by the great theologian Ibn Babuyeh of Qom, known as Shaykh Saduq.[^EII4-312] His account claims to reproduce, word for word, the testimony of Bashar ibn Solayman Nahhas, a close associate and intimate companion of the two Imams, Ali Naqi and Hasan Askari, during their enforced residence at Samarra.

One day, then, Imam Ali Naqi sent his servant Kafur to fetch Bashar. Once Bashar had taken his place before him, the Imam addressed him solemnly: “Bashar, you are our friend. You and your family have always shown the same devotion to the members of the Prophet's household. I wish to honor you with a privilege that will give you a place of friendship unequaled among our Shiites. I am going to entrust you with a secret and send you on a mission to bring a certain young woman here.”

The Imam then wrote a letter in Greek with his own hand, sealed it, and placed it in a red leather purse together with two hundred and twenty dinars. He gave Bashar the following instructions. Bashar was to go to Baghdad and, at the appointed hour, stand by the river at the harbor where ships carrying captive women came ashore. The only prospective buyers on the quay would be agents of the Abbasid caliph. Bashar was to spend the whole day watching, from a distance, what took place aboard a ship belonging to a man named Amr ibn Yazid.

At a certain moment, he would see this man presenting to the buyers a young woman of a particular appearance. She would be wearing two layers of silk to shield herself from men's eyes and hands. “You will hear her cry aloud in Greek from beneath her delicate veil. Know that she will be saying: ‘Accursed be the man who uncovers my eyebrows!’” One of the men, moved by the young woman's modesty, would declare how greatly he wished to buy her.

But she would answer: “Even if you possessed all the glory and riches of Solomon, son of David, I could never love you. Beware of wasting your wealth.” The shipowner, unwilling to force her, would admit his great embarrassment: the matter must somehow be settled. “Why such haste?” she would ask. “I must choose for myself the man who will buy me, so that my heart can find peace in the trust and fidelity I shall feel toward him.”

“At that moment, Bashar,” the Imam continued, “go up to Amr ibn Yazid and say: ‘I carry a letter, written in the Greek language and script (*rumiya*), by a noble man. It reveals his generosity, his loyalty, and his openhandedness. Give it to this young woman. Let her consider it and understand the character of its author. If she feels drawn to him and is satisfied, I am fully authorized to act on his behalf.’”

Everything happened exactly as the Imam had foretold, and Bashar followed his instructions. After reading the Imam's letter, the young woman let out an involuntary cry and told the shipowner that if he refused to sell her to the letter's author, she was prepared to take her own life.

But events turned out as she wished. All Bashar had to do was bring her to his residence in Baghdad before setting off with her for Samarra. He noticed how happy and smiling she was, and how often she drew the letter from her bosom to press it to her lips, her eyes, and her eyebrows. Unable to restrain himself, he said: “Your behavior amazes me. You kiss a letter when you do not even know who wrote it!” She answered: “You poor man, so weak in faith! May knowledge of the spiritual rank of the Prophet's descendants dispel the doubts in your heart.”

Now we come to the marvelous story itself. From the outset, we should note that the young woman's ancestry is exactly what the recurring fullness of the Twelve requires. She continues: “Know that I am, in truth, a princess. My father is Yeshua, son of the emperor of Byzantium. My mother descends from the apostles of Christ. Her lineage goes back to Sham'un, Simon Peter, the *wasi*—the spiritual heir, or Imam—of the Lord Christ. I shall tell you my extraordinary story. My grandfather, the emperor, wished to marry me to his nephew.

“I was thirteen years old. He gathered an imposing assembly in his palace: three hundred clerics and monks, seven hundred members of the high nobility, and four thousand officers, military commanders, and landed nobles—five thousand people in all. Within the palace he had a throne erected at the top of forty steps, encrusted with jewels and precious stones of every kind. He seated his nephew on the throne, and around it was arranged a great assembly of icons (*bot-ha*, ‘idols’). The Christian priests stood before the throne with the deepest reverence. The Gospels were opened.

“But suddenly the idols came crashing down, the columns of the throne shattered, and my cousin fell with the throne to the floor and lost consciousness. Fear seized the dignitaries and notables; their faces changed with terror. Their leader declared: ‘O King, spare us the sight of these dreadful omens! Such an event foretells the decline and disappearance of the Christian religion.’ Deeply disturbed, my grandfather gave his orders: ‘Raise the columns of the throne again. Gather the icons back onto its summit. Bring my unfortunate nephew to me, so that I may celebrate his marriage to this girl and turn these sinister omens away from us.’

“But as the man who was the ornament of the assembly took his place for a second time, the same catastrophe occurred. This time the terrified gathering scattered in every direction. Troubled and saddened, my grandfather the emperor abandoned his plan and withdrew to his private rooms.”

After these striking omens comes a series of visionary dreams through which the young Byzantine princess receives her spiritual initiation.

We can understand the first scene only if we remember the principle of correspondence that preserves the fullness of the Twelve from one era of prophecy to the next. Wherever this fullness appears, it carries the same secret of the same initiatory religion. What matters in the event as Shiite consciousness experiences it is that the passage from the Twelve of the Christian era to the Twelve of the Muhammadan era is completed and sealed through the mother of the Twelfth Muhammadan Imam. Through her, in the person of the young Byzantine princess, Christianity is initiated into Islam—or, more precisely, into Islamic gnosis, the inward knowledge of divine mysteries.

And this mediation is born of a mystical, passionate love that first blossoms in a dream. The same principle of correspondence, so fundamental to Shiite thought, will be illustrated once again by the simultaneous presence of Fatima, mother of the holy Imams, and Mary, mother of Christ. In this visionary dream, Fatima takes on the role attributed to her by the more radical forms of Shiite gnosis, which name her Fatima-Fatir, *Fatima the Creator*—using the masculine form of “creator.” She is Initiation itself, embodied in a person.

“The night following these events,” the young woman tells Bashar, “I found myself in the world of visions. I saw the Lord Christ with his apostles inside the emperor's palace. At the very spot where the throne had stood the day before, they raised a pulpit (*minbar*) made entirely of light. Then Muhammad entered the palace with his *wasi*, his spiritual heir, and his glorious descendants—the holy Imams. Christ stepped forward to meet him and embraced the Prophet Muhammad. Muhammad said: ‘O Spirit of God (*Ruh Allah*), I have come to ask for the princess, the daughter of your *wasi*, Sham'un (Simon Peter), in marriage to my own son.’

“And he pointed toward Imam Hasan Askari. Christ looked long at Sham'un and said: ‘An extraordinary honor and nobility have come to you. Join your family, then, to the family of Muhammad.’ Sham'un replied: ‘It is done.’ Then all together—Muhammad and his Imams, Christ and his apostles—they climbed the steps to the top of the pulpit of light. There Muhammad delivered a magnificent sermon celebrating the marriage of his son and myself. Muhammad and his descendants, the holy Imams, and the apostles of Christ were all witnesses to our union.”

One cannot help imagining the grandeur of this scene unfolding in the church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople.

The Shiite feeling expressed in this dream is the same one that inspired the great tenth-century Ismaili philosopher-theosopher Abu Ya'qub Sejestani to recognize the same meaning and structure in the Christian sign of the Cross and the Islamic declaration of the One God. Only those who penetrate to the hidden depths of religion seem capable of embracing this genuine fellowship across religious boundaries.

Remembering the conditions that have prevailed over the centuries of outward history, the student of religion may see in this dream an image as overwhelming as the vision experienced by Brother Marcus in the Goethe poem we shall quote later: the unfamiliar emblem of roses entwined around the Cross. The young Byzantine princess goes on: “When I awoke from this dream, I was afraid. I dared tell no one about it, for fear that my father and brother would kill me.

“I kept my secret so closely that my love for Imam Hasan Askari went on growing in my heart until I could no longer eat or drink. I grew thin, fell ill, and suffered terribly. There was not a physician in all the cities of the empire whom my father did not consult in the hope of curing me. One day, in despair, he said: ‘O light of my eyes! Is there any wish in your heart that I might fulfill?’ I answered: ‘The gates of joy are closed to me.

“But if you free the Muslim prisoners, perhaps Christ and his mother will come to my aid.’ When my father granted my wish, I showed some signs of returning health and began to eat again.

“Fourteen nights later, I had another dream. The sovereign of all womankind,[^EII4-313] Fatima the Radiant, came to visit me. Mary accompanied her, together with a thousand young women from among the houris of Paradise. Mary said to me: ‘Here is the Queen of Women, the mother of your husband, Imam Hasan Askari.’ I seized the hem of Fatima's robe and burst into tears. I complained that Imam Hasan had treated me so cruelly by refusing to let me see him.

“But Her Ladyship, Fatima, answered: ‘How could my child come to visit you while you continue to make God into many gods by remaining in the Christian religion? Here is my sister Mary. She has made herself free for God by leaving behind the religion you still profess.

“If you wish to please God, Mary, and Christ, and if you wish to see Imam Hasan Askari, then say: “I bear witness that there is no god but God, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God.”’ When I had spoken these two noble declarations, Fatima, Queen of Women, drew me to her and embraced me tightly. She said: ‘Now await my child's visit. I shall send him to you.’

“When I awoke, my tongue was still speaking those two noble declarations, and I waited to meet my Imam.[^EII4-314] When night came and I had returned to the world of visions, the sun of His Lordship's beauty rose before me. I said to him: ‘My beloved! Your love has made my heart its prisoner. Why have you withheld the sight of your beauty from me until now?’ He answered: ‘I was so long in coming to you because you were making God into many gods.

“Now that you have become a *muslima*, I shall be with you every night, until God brings us face to face, openly and without a veil, and replaces our separation with reunion.’ From that night until this very moment, not one night has passed without my beloved bringing me the drink of union to heal the pain of separation.”

Such is the secret entrusted to Bashar, the confidant of the holy Imams. He is familiar with the supernatural circumstances of life; those are not what he doubts. What troubles him is a thoroughly practical question. “How did you come to be among the captives?” he asks the young woman. She replies: “One night Imam Hasan Askari told me that my grandfather, the emperor, was about to send an army against the Muslims. He advised me to disguise myself so as not to be recognized, to take a few of my women with me, and to follow the army at a distance.

“I did as he said. Soon, as fortune would have it, a Muslim advance party came upon us and took us captive. That is how I came to be in the situation you now see. No one but you knows that I am the daughter of the emperor of Byzantium. When I was captured, an elder to whose share I had fallen asked me my name. Concealing my true name, I answered: ‘My name is Narcissus (*Narkes*).’”

Confronted with the wondrous story of a woman supernaturally called to become an Imam's companion, who had exposed herself to captivity out of pure love, Bashar can only remain respectfully silent.

Yet one last practical question concerns him, and he ventures to ask it: “You are Greek. How is it that you speak Arabic so well?” Narcissus explains: “My father took great care to give me an excellent education. He entrusted me to a woman highly skilled in several languages. She taught me Arabic morning and evening, until I became thoroughly proficient in it.”

Here ends what we might call the prologue to the mystery of the Twelfth Imam's birth. Now we enter the mystery itself. When Princess Narcissus (*Narkes Khatun*) is presented to Imam Ali Naqi at Samarra, the following dialogue takes place.

*Imam Ali Naqi:* In what way has God made known to you the glory of the Islamic religion and the error of the Christian religion, the exalted station of the Prophet and the members of his household—the holy Imams?

*Narcissus:* How can I describe to you, O descendant of the Messenger of God, something you know so much better than I do?

*The Imam:* I wish to receive you with every honor due a guest. Tell me which you would prefer: that I give you twenty thousand dinars, or that I bring you good news accompanied by everlasting glory?

*Narcissus:* It is the good news I desire. I have no need of wealth.

*The Imam:* Then hear the good news: a son will be born to you whose reign will extend over East and West, and who will fill the earth with peace and justice, just as it is now filled with violence and tyranny.

*Narcissus:* Who will be the father of this child?

*The Imam:* The man for whom, on a certain night, in a certain month and year, the Prophet Muhammad asked for your hand in marriage. To whom did the Lord Christ and his *wasi* agree to give you?

*Narcissus:* To your son, Imam Hasan Askari.

*The Imam:* So you know him?

*Narcissus:* Since the night I professed Islam at the hands of the Queen of Women, Fatima, I have not known a single night without the sight of his beauty and the consolation of his love.

Then the Imam called his servant Kafur: “Go and ask my sister Hakima Khatun to come here.” Her name means “the wise woman,” Sophia; a variant calls her Halima, “the gentle woman.” When she entered, the Imam said: “This is the young woman of whom I spoke to you.” Hakima embraced Narcissus tenderly. The Imam continued: “O daughter of the Messenger of God, take Narcissus home with you. Teach her our traditions and everything that the wife of Imam Hasan Askari, the mother of the One who will rise again, must know.”

It is through the testimony of this venerable woman, Hakima Khatun, sister of Imam Ali Naqi and aunt of the young husband, Imam Hasan Askari, that we learn the circumstances of the birth of the last Imam, the Imam who is yet to come. According to tradition, she related the following: “On the Thursday night of mid-Sha'ban, in the year 255 AH (3 August 868), I went to the house of my noble nephew, the Imam of the time, Hasan Askari.

“When I was about to leave, His Lordship said: ‘Aunt, stay with us tonight. This very night the most noble child will be born, through whom God will bring the earth to life with knowledge, faith, and spiritual uprightness, after it has died through error and monstrous wrongdoing.’ I asked: ‘My lord, to whom will this child be born?’ ‘To Narcissus, of course!’ I looked at Narcissus, but I could see no sign whatever that she was expecting a child.

“I was astonished. His Lordship the Imam smiled and said: ‘Aunt, when morning comes, the sign will become visible. It will be as it was with the mother of Moses, who showed no sign of her condition until the hour of birth, so that she might escape the measures decreed by Pharaoh, who was putting women in her condition to death.’[^EII4-315]”

But this is not simply a matter of escaping Pharaoh—or the Abbasid caliph, who represents him well enough. Rather, escaping Pharaoh means escaping all the consequences that would follow from confusing the divine taking on human form in the person of the Imam with a material embodiment of the divine in flesh and in history. Every detail that the venerable Hakima is about to recount shows us how Shiite teaching about the Imams reproduces the essential features of a Gnostic understanding of Christ.

What is at issue is a theophany, a manifestation of God—not an Incarnation, nor a hypostatic union that fuses two utterly different natures. The Imam as envisioned by Shiite consciousness therefore has features corresponding to a Christology other than the official one: the Christology which, from the Valentinian Gnostics to Master Valentin Weigel, would have regarded any conception other than a *caro Christi spiritualis*, the spiritual flesh of Christ, as blasphemous. One might call this docetism.

But docetism, whether in Marcion or elsewhere, does not abolish the reality of the event. It does not reduce it to a myth or a ghostly appearance. It perceives the event on a spiritual level of reality where materialization and secularization—that is, reduction to what can be established through ordinary experience—are radically impossible. Precisely because they belong to a level beyond ordinary evidence, the features of such a vision appear as paradoxes. It is through these very features that Shiite teaching about the Imams reveals its Gnostic inspiration. Many illuminating comparisons could be drawn, but here we shall confine ourselves to presenting texts that have received little attention in the general history of religions.

The venerable Hakima Khatun gives the following account in full:[^EII4-316] “Imam Hasan used to tell me: ‘We, the spiritual heirs (*awsiya*) of the Messenger of God, are carried by our mothers not in the womb but in the side. We come forth not from their womb but from the thigh, because we are the Lights of God Most High, and he has kept all stain and impurity far from us.’

“I went to Narcissus and spoke to her of these things. She said: ‘O Khatun, I feel no sign of anything within me.’

“Yet I decided to stay the whole night. I ate the evening meal and slept near Narcissus. Every hour I checked on her condition. That night, more than on other nights, I repeated all the prayers of the night vigil. When I reached the *witr* prayer, Narcissus awoke. She performed her ritual washing and recited the dawn prayer. While I watched her, the false dawn had appeared. I almost began to doubt that His Lordship the Imam would fulfill his promise within the time he had set. Suddenly, Imam Hasan called to me from his room: ‘Do not doubt, for the hour has come.’

“At that moment I noticed a certain restlessness in Narcissus. I took her in my arms and invoked the divine Name over her. The Imam called out: ‘Recite over her the sura beginning, “We sent it down on the Night of Destiny”’ (97:1 ff.).[^EII4-317] Then I asked Narcissus what she felt. ‘I think,’ she told me, ‘that the sign my lord foretold is beginning to appear.’ As I began reciting the sura *We Sent It Down on the Night of Destiny*, I heard the child within his mother reciting it with me and greeting me.

“I was frightened. Again the Imam called to me from his room: ‘Do not be amazed at the divine power that has enabled us to speak its wisdom and made us its witnesses and guarantors on earth.’ When the Imam finished speaking, Narcissus vanished from my sight. It was as though a veil had fallen between us. I ran to the Imam, crying out in distress. He said: ‘Aunt, go back. You will find Narcissus where she was.’

“When I returned, the veil had disappeared, and Narcissus shone with a light so brilliant that it dazzled my eyes. And there I saw His Lordship, the *Sahib al-Amr*—the Twelfth Imam, newly born through a supernatural birth.

“Facing the *qibla*, the direction of prayer, he was kneeling on the prayer rug, with both index fingers raised toward Heaven. He was reciting: ‘I bear witness that there is no god but God; that my ancestor is the Messenger of God; and that my father, the Commander of the Faithful, is the Guide toward God (*Wali Allah*, the Friend of God).’ He then named all the other Imams, one by one, until he came to himself. Then he said: ‘O my God, be faithful to your promise to sustain me. Bring my office as Imam to its perfection, make my steps firm, and through me fill the earth with justice.’

“At that moment Imam Hasan called out to me: ‘Aunt, take the child in your arms and bring him to me.’ When I lifted him, I found that he was already circumcised, his umbilical cord severed, and his body perfectly clean and pure. On his right arm were written the words: ‘Truth has appeared and falsehood has vanished; falsehood was destined to vanish’ (17:83).

“When I carried this blessed child to his father, the child fixed his gaze upon him and spoke a greeting. His Lordship the Imam took him into his arms and pressed his blessed lips to the child's two eyes, his mouth, and his two ears. He traced a sign in the palm of the child's left hand, laid his pure hand upon his head, and said: ‘My child, speak by divine power.’ Then His Lordship the *Sahib al-Zaman*—the infant Imam, the ‘Master of this Time’—pronounced: ‘In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful!

“We shall bestow our favor upon those whom tyrants have oppressed on earth. We shall make them Imams of the religion. We shall make them the heirs. We shall establish them securely on earth, and We shall show Pharaoh, Haman, and their armies what they feared’ (28:4–5). These verses of the Book corresponded perfectly to our *hadith*, the transmitted accounts concerning His Lordship and his forefathers.

“His Lordship then called down blessings upon the Prophet, the Commander of the Faithful, and all the Imams down to his noble father. At that moment a flock of birds appeared above the child's head. Imam Hasan called one of them and said: ‘Take this child, care for him well, and bring him back to us every forty days.’ The bird took the child and flew up into the sky.[^EII4-318] The Imam gave the same instruction to the other birds, and they took flight. Then he said: ‘I entrust you to the same one to whom his mother entrusted Moses.’ Narcissus began to weep.

“But the Imam told her: ‘Be at peace! He will drink no milk but yours. Soon they will bring him back to you, as Moses was returned to his mother. As the verse says: “We restored Moses to his mother, so that her eyes might be filled with light through him”’ (28:12). ‘Who is this bird,’ I asked, ‘to whom you have entrusted the child?’ The Imam answered: ‘It is the Holy Spirit, to whom the Imams are entrusted. He gives them divine help, preserves them from every error, and adorns them with higher knowledge.’

“Forty days later I visited my nephew. When I entered the house, I saw a child walking about. I exclaimed: ‘My lord! This child looks two years old!’ The Imam smiled and said: ‘The children of prophets and their spiritual heirs (*awsiya*), when they are Imams, grow differently from other children. One month for them is equal to a year for others. They speak while still in their mothers' wombs; they recite the Quran and perform their worship before their Lord. Even in their earliest childhood, the angels teach them every morning and descend to them every evening.’

“I came to see him every forty days throughout the lifetime of Imam Hasan Askari, until the last days before his death. Once I met the child, the Twelfth Imam, bearing the appearance of a Perfect Man (*mard-e kamil*).[^EII4-319] I did not recognize him and asked my nephew: ‘Who is this man beside whom you invite me to sit?’ ‘Why, it is the child of Narcissus,’ he answered.

“‘He will succeed me when, very soon, I have left you. You must accept his word and obey his commands.’ Only a few days later, Imam Hasan departed for the holy world. And now, every morning and evening, I attend upon the Imam of this time. He instructs me in everything I ask. Sometimes he answers a question before I have even spoken it.”

Clearly, these last words of the venerable Hakima refer to certain privileged ways in which the Hidden Imam makes himself known, especially during the time of the Greater Occultation.

But what we should notice first is the reference to the final days of Imam Hasan Askari, who died while still very young, barely twenty-eight years old, in 260/873–74. We owe the account of those final moments to Isma'il Nawbakhti; Nawbakhti is the name of one of the oldest Iranian Shiite families. This account is of the greatest importance to Shiite religious consciousness. Alongside the collected *hadith* in which, over approximately five years, Imam Hasan is shown presenting the child himself to an elite group of some forty Shiites, the account of the Eleventh Imam's death offers a twofold testimony: to the existence of the Twelfth Imam and to his investiture as successor.

As his departure approached, Imam Hasan explicitly invested his young son, Imam Muhammad, as his successor. “Isma'il ibn Ali Nawbakhti related the following:[^EII4-320] I went to visit Imam Hasan during his final illness and took a seat beside him. He said to his servant Aqid: ‘Prepare me an infusion of mastic resin.’ Meanwhile the mother of the *Sahib al-Zaman*, the Master of the Time, brought the bowl and placed it in Hasan Askari's hands.

“But when he tried to drink, his hand trembled so violently that the bowl struck his teeth. He put it aside and said to Aqid: ‘Go into the next room and bring me the Child who is praying there.’ ‘When I entered the room,’ Aqid said, ‘I saw the Child on his prayer rug, both index fingers raised toward Heaven. When I greeted him, he brought his prayer to a close and said to me: “Peace be upon you.” I said: “My master asks you to come to him.”

“Just then his mother came, took him by the hand, and led him to his father.’ The child's grace shone with light. His hair was curly, and a smile parted his lips. When the dying Imam fixed his eyes upon him, he wept and said: ‘You who are now to become the head of the Prophet's household, give me something to drink with your own hands, for I am about to return to my Protector.’

“The child took the bowl of mastic infusion (*ab-e mastaki*), moved his lips in an invocation, and gave it to his noble father. When Hasan had drunk, he said: ‘Prepare me for prayer.’ A towel was brought. The Child performed his father's ritual ablutions for him and anointed his head and feet. Then the dying Imam said: ‘O my noble Child! You are now the lord of this time. You are the Mahdi, the Guide, the Guarantor of God upon this earth.

“My child, my *wasi*, my spiritual heir, you are born of me. You are MHMD ibn Hasan. You are a child of the Messenger of God. You are the Seal, the last of the Immaculate Imams. The Messenger of God announced your coming to humankind. He spoke your name and your customary name (*kunya*). The promise made to my father and my forefathers has come down to me.’ With these words the Imam passed into Paradise.”

Such is the account of Isma'il Nawbakhti, now found in all Shiite works of theology and religious instruction. And it was very shortly after the death of his young father, Imam Hasan—perhaps within hours—that the child Imam also disappeared. We should not demand too much material detail here. The Shiite books say little, and on this point they can hardly do otherwise.

For if entering the state of occultation (*ghaybat*) by its very nature removes all traces from the physical space of the material world, how could we search that world for traces of the transition? In fact, there are two occultations, or two degrees of occultation. The first is what Shiite theologians call the “Lesser Occultation” (*ghaybat sughra*). It began in the year of Imam Hasan's death (260/873–74) and lasted until 329/940–41.

The second began at that very point. This is what Shiite theologians call the “Greater Occultation” (*ghaybat kubra*), and it continues to this day.

##### 3. The Seal of Muhammadan *Walayat* and His Occultation (*Ghaybat*)

The period of the Lesser Occultation thus began at about the time the Eleventh Imam, Hasan Askari, breathed his last. The child Imam vanished within his own home in Samarra, the house he inherited from his father, who had just died there. He disappeared into an underground chamber reached by a staircase of several steps. We seem to be presented here with an archetypal image. The chamber served as an oratory for the child Imam and his father. They were accustomed to retreat there for meditation and prayer, and also to escape intruders, especially the watchful agents of the Abbasid caliphate.

We can easily calculate that the young Imam was five years old at the time of his disappearance, though some traditions give a slightly greater age.

During the roughly seventy years of the Lesser Occultation, the Imam would be invisible not only to ordinary people but also to his own followers. He would nevertheless communicate with them through four successive *na'ibs* or *wakils*—deputies or authorized representatives. Shiite books preserve detailed accounts of their names and lives. The first was Uthman ibn Sa'id, who had already served as secretary and trusted associate to the Tenth and Eleventh Imams. He was succeeded by his own son, Abu Ja'far. Then came Abu'l-Qasim Husayn ibn Ruh Nawbakhti,[^EII4-321] and finally Abu'l-Hasan Ali al-Samarri.

Through these intermediaries a number of Shiite figures, whose names are likewise preserved in tradition, were even brought into the presence of the Twelfth Imam.[^EII4-322] Apart from such occasions, the Imam appeared only sporadically: at his father's funeral and during the division of the inheritance, for example, to put an end to the unfounded claims of his uncle Ja'far, brother of Imam Hasan Askari.[^EII4-323] Other manifestations already resembled those that would occur in the time of the Greater Occultation, as we have heard in the testimony of the venerable Hakima.

At the end of those seventy years came the momentous decision that inaugurated the Greater Occultation, which continues still. Here, above all, we can do no more than present the Shiite documents. The great theologian Ibn Babuyeh, Shaykh Saduq, whose authority we have already invoked, records what he was told in person by a witness involved in the events, a certain Abu Muhammad Hasan ibn Moktib.[^EII4-324] This man was in Baghdad in the very year, 329/940–41, when the Hidden Imam's last deputy, Abu'l-Hasan al-Samarri, died. He was visiting him a few days before his death when a sealed message suddenly arrived, sent by the Imam. He was allowed to make a copy. This was its content:

“In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful. May God show your brothers his generosity in recompense for the ordeal your departure will bring them. Within six days you will meet death. Put your affairs in order. Do not appoint a successor to take your place as my *wakil* after your death, for the time of the Greater Occultation has now come. I shall no longer show myself to anyone, except when divine permission is given.

“But that will not take place until a long time has passed. Hearts will become closed to compassion. The earth will be filled with tyranny and violence. Some among my Shiites will arise and claim to have seen me with their physical eyes. Beware! Anyone who claims to have seen me physically before the events of the end[^EII4-325] is a liar and an impostor. There is no help and no strength except in God, the Most High, the Exalted.”

Shaykh Saduq's informant completed his story: “Six days after that visit, when I had copied down the Imam's message, I went once more to Abu'l-Hasan Ali al-Samarri. I could see that his final hour was indeed approaching. One of the intimates gathered around him asked: ‘Who will be your *wasi* after you—that is, your successor, the new *wakil* of the Hidden Imam?’ He replied: ‘The matter now belongs to God alone. It is for him to bring it to its fulfillment.’ These,” adds the witness, “were the last words anyone heard him speak.”

But it is now that the secret history of the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam, begins. What an extraordinary thing it is! In the starkest contrast to our obsession with the “material historicity” of facts, without which we can scarcely imagine that there might be “real facts” at all, the figure of the Twelfth Imam passes through history as lightly as a ray of light passes through stained glass.

Yet for more than ten centuries he has dominated the whole of Shiite religious consciousness. Indeed, he is the very history of that consciousness, which for more than ten centuries has lived, in the secrecy of ardent devotion, in the company of the Twelfth Imam's mysterious person. The last words of his final message warned Shiite consciousness against adventures and impostures of every kind. That is why every attempt—and there have been several—to bring its end-time expectation of his coming to an end has been rejected, sometimes fiercely, as an intolerable blasphemy.

Here, then, we must keep in mind all the distinguishing features of the Twelfth Imam that we have encountered throughout this work.

Above all, we must recall the structure of Shiite teaching about the Imams and its sacred history: (1) the cycle of prophecy and the cycle of *walayat*, the latter being the cycle of the Imamate, or initiation into the spiritual meaning of divine revelations; (2) the double Seal of *walayat*: the Seal of universal *walayat* in the person of the First Imam, and the Seal of specifically Muhammadan *walayat* in the person of the Twelfth; (3) the perfect symmetry of the two cycles, in which each “Friend of God” in the cycle of *walayat* stands in relation to its Seal, the Twelfth Imam, just as each earlier *nabi*, or prophet, stands in relation to the Seal of prophecy; (4) the reasons why *walayat*, after the Seal of the prophets, corresponds to the simple prophetic vocation—that of a *nabi* who is not a messenger—in earlier periods of the cycle of prophecy; and (5) the reasons why Haydar Amoli opposed Ibn Arabi so firmly over the double Seal of *walayat*, and why his work has appeared to us as a great moment in “prophetic philosophy.”

For, as we have said, it is through the figure of the Twelfth Imam that Shiism intimates its deepest secret. This theme crowns the entire structure of its theology and theosophy. We have already noted the fundamental feature through which the theology of the Twelve Imams recalls the ancient Hellenistic and Zoroastrian theologies of the *Aion*, the eternal age. It is the idea of a twelvefold whole whose fullness has already been given, even though its final manifestation is still to come.

For eleven of the Imams, the time of earthly appearance is over. Suspended in this way “between times,” the Twelver Imamate is therefore something other than what is called a “dogmatic teaching authority.” It would be a mistake simply to transfer to it the Western idea of a “religion of authority.”

Yet two things remain true. On the one hand, the Imams' enduring teaching, which reveals the hidden meanings of the Quran, is indeed the authoritative source. On the other, their persons, in their heavenly or metaphysical state, are themselves centers of Shiite devotion, because they are the Guides.

This idea reaches its fullest expression in the notion of the personal Guide (see below, III, 4): the Imam who, though withdrawn from the sight of this world, remains present in the hearts of his followers, and whose supernatural invisibility protects them against any attempt to turn spiritual life into a social institution.

The moving accounts of the Twelfth Imam's sacred life, and of the mystery of his two periods of “occultation,” are certainly not texts that can be subjected to historical criticism in the ordinary sense. That is why we have insisted that the phenomenological approach—an approach that seeks to understand a religious experience as it is lived—is the most fruitful for the scholar of religion.

For more than ten centuries, the Twelfth Imam has lived a mysterious life in a region “which no mortal can approach,” a region whose coordinates cannot be marked on our maps. There he is surrounded by companions who, like him, remain hidden from our world. Many testimonies tell of occasions when he himself, or one of his companions, has appeared, but in such a way that those who encountered them generally understood what had happened only afterward.

And these encounters are not reserved for exceptional people. They may happen to ordinary men and women whom great suffering, for instance, has shaken free of the certainties and comforts of everyday life. To understand such things, we need a conception of reality that has room for the “eighth clime,” the world beyond the seven regions of ordinary geography. An analysis that dismissed them as daydreams, imaginary inventions, or schizophrenic delusions would merely be confessing its own inability to understand them.

Because the Twelfth Imam's time lies “between times,” the Imams who were his ancestors and predecessors lived in spiritual union with him. Together, the Twelve form a single Essence, given distinct existence in twelve persons. Everything that will happen at the end—the words the Twelfth Imam will speak, the deeds he will perform, the battles he will fight—is known to us through the Imams who preceded him. They themselves perceived these events through their sacred knowledge (*hierognosis*), a possibility fully accounted for in the theory of prophetic knowledge.

One striking expression recurs in accounts of their visions of the last things: “It was as though I stood before the Resurrector” (*ka-innî bi-Qâ'im ahl baytî*; literally, “It was as though I stood with the member of my family who will be the Resurrector, the *Qâ'im*”), as though I were looking upon him. The same is true of the Prophet, who spoke on several occasions of the Imam yet to come.

Thus the Prophet could speak of the day that God would prolong, if necessary, until the appearance of “the one who will fill the Earth with peace and justice, as it had been filled with violence and tyranny.”

For Shiite theosophical interpretation, the day that God prolongs until the appearance of the Resurrecting Imam (*qiyâm al-Qâ'im*) is precisely the time in which the Imam's followers are living now. It is the time of their own existence, the time “between times”: the Imam's occultation, the age of the Hidden Imam, who is therefore called *sâhib al-zamân*, the one who holds sway over this age. Haydar Âmolî explains it through an image. The cycle of prophecy that brings divine law began at sunrise with Adam and reached its noon with Mohammad. After Mohammad it was closed and passed out of sight, like the sun after setting.

But the *walâyat*, the inner or esoteric prophecy that rose at the beginning of this night, began with 'Alî, the First Imam. It advanced from Imam to Imam like the moon traveling through the darkness, until dawn, rising with the twelfth and final Imam, would dispel the night. This night, then, is what we experience as “our time,” the time “between times,” the age in which the Imam remains hidden. It is the night of symbols, the night in which esoteric understanding is indispensable.

We may therefore say that the mystery embodied in the person of the Twelfth Imam points to a secret of expectation: the waiting for the end of time that was already a feature of ancient Zoroastrian Iran. With Islam as a whole, this expectation accepts that the cycle of lawgiving prophecy is closed; yet it also affirms that something continues, and that something is still to come. We have already seen how the idea of a new cycle following the cycle of prophecy—a cycle of initiation into the hidden spiritual meaning of divine revelation, administered by the holy Imams—refuses to let religious life become fixed in a moment of the past, sealed forever.

Shiite consciousness does not strain toward an indefinite future; it awaits an end of time, an eschatological fulfillment. That very expectation calls for a release from the merely literal reading of revelation, and from the imprisonment of its meaning in a past that literalism keeps closed. Conversely, no such expectation could exist without *gnosis*: some knowledge, or at least some intimation, of revelation's inward, hidden, *anagogical* meaning—that is, a meaning that carries the soul upward. This inward, upward-leading meaning, which holds the soul in a state of supreme expectation, is the very secret of the Imamate, of the complete spiritual assembly—the *pleroma*—of the Twelve.

The coming of the Twelfth Imam brings the Integral Human Being, the Perfect Human (*al-Insân al-kâmil*), to completion. It reveals what other traditions of gnosis call the mystery of the *Anthropos*, the primordial or archetypal Human. This is why the doctrine of the Imams performs a role comparable to that of Christology in Christian theosophy.

What other traditions call the pre-existent Logos is here called the Muhammadan Light (*Nûr mohammadî*), or the eternal Prophetic Reality (*Haqîqat mohammadîya*): the first creation, through which being is eternally summoned into existence by the imperative “Be!”—the *Esto* (KN) of the primordial Will that creates from itself. This Light has two intelligible “dimensions”: the outward one, revealed through prophecy, and the inward one, represented by the twelve Veils in which the Prophetic Light dwells during its descent and its ascent back to its origin.

Together with the woman who is called “the mother of her father,” they constitute the complete spiritual assembly of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. With the twelfth of the Imams, the fourteenth member of this assembly, the Light reaches its full growth, and the mystery of its enthronement is fulfilled. Should we ask what would have happened if Islam as a whole had followed the teachings and doctrines of the Shiite Imams? What form would historical Islam then have taken? Perhaps the question is mistaken from the outset.

For what we ordinarily call “historical” reality is only the outer shell, the ambiguous appearance, of a hidden sacred history whose events possess the reality and permanence of a *mysterium liturgicum*, a mystery enacted in sacred worship. That is why we have had to say that every attempt to explain Shiism solely through social or political causes, in terms of the laws of historical causation, misses the very essence of Shiite thought and consciousness.

The time of the Imamate remains “between times.” This is not a question of political legitimacy or social utopia. It concerns the mystery of the Imamate itself, which began at the dawn of humanity with Seth, son of Adam, the first Imam of the first prophet, and will end with the appearance—the coming into presence—of the final Imam of the final prophet.

We can then understand the passionate devotion that Shiite belief and practice center upon the Twelfth Imam, who for ten centuries has been the Hidden Imam, the Awaited Imam.

The sacred biography recounted above tells us when and how this period of concealment began. More precisely, Shiite theologians distinguish two periods of occultation. The first began when the Eleventh Imam, Hasan 'Askarî, departed this world at Samarra at the age of twenty-eight (260/873–74). On that day, the child Imam, Mohammad al-Mahdî, also disappeared. His father had invested him with the Imamate in what was the last act of his earthly life, and it was as though Imam Hasan had taken the child of his soul away with him. This first period, called the Minor Occultation (*ghaybat soghrâ*), lasted seventy lunar years (until 329/940–41).

During it the Imam remained unknown to the general public and communicated with the body of his followers only through four successive deputies, whose names we recalled earlier. A very small number of followers, however, were brought into his presence.

The second period begins with the letter addressed to 'Alî al-Samarrî, whose text we translated earlier. This is the Great, or Major, Occultation (*ghaybat kobrâ*).

Yet in this period, no more than in the first, does the Imam cross the threshold that irrevocably separates our world from the world beyond. His situation is like that of those who were taken from the visible world without passing through death: Enoch, Elijah, and Christ himself, according to the teaching of the Quran. Earlier we referred to the *bodhisattva* who refuses to enter *nirvana* until every being has been saved.

The expectation focused upon the Twelfth Imam also has its counterparts in Mahayana Buddhism's expectation of Maitreya, the future Buddha; in Zoroastrianism's expectation of the Saoshyant; and in Christianity's expectation of Christ's Second Coming. There are also the hidden heroes of epic tradition: King Arthur in the Celtic epics[^EII4-326], and Kay Khosraw in the Iranian epic.

All these figures belong to the same family of heroes associated with the end of time. With their companions, they live mysterious lives upon an Earth close to ours, yet not our own. Here the *mundus imaginalis*—the imaginal world—is of decisive importance. To do justice to the phenomenon, the phenomenologist must embrace what we have called the “reality of the imaginal.” There can be no meaningful interpretation of the Great Occultation without acknowledging this world that exists alongside our own: a world containing all the forms of the sensory world, the world of mystical cities “where spirits take on bodies and bodies become spiritual,” as Mohsen Fayz so aptly defines it.

A few privileged people enter this world and return, without any distinction of social class. Unless we allow for its existence, every attempted explanation risks destroying the very thing it seeks to explain. There have, of course, been naïve minds for whom the Imam must exist exactly like the people we meet every day. Some have even seriously discussed extraordinarily long-lived persons and the biological possibility of surviving for centuries.

But let us remember that the last knights of Kay Khosraw also tried to seek him in this way. Where, then, were they actually looking? The Imam's invisible presence, his perpetual contemporaneity “between times,” means something else. It is neither a moral allegory nor a mythological representation. It is precisely the reality of that *mundus imaginalis* which Suhrawardî and the Platonists of Persia were compelled to affirm in their prophetic philosophy, because they knew that without such a world they could not account for the reality of spiritual, metaphysical, and supernatural events.

Until the hour of his appearance, the Hidden Imam becomes visible only in dreams or in certain personal manifestations that have the character of visionary events. These do not interrupt the period of *ghaybat*, of occultation: they take place within this very time “between times” and do not become part of the stream of material historical events that any observer might record and verify. Shiite books contain numerous accounts of such theophanic visions, manifestations of the divine; they deserve a classification by type.

Most often the Twelfth Imam appears as a very beautiful child or young man. He reveals himself to those in material distress or spiritual torment, perhaps at a bend in the road, or in a mosque where a believer stands alone. Usually it is only afterward that the person realizes the Imam was the one who appeared. Every Shiite believer knows that he may call upon the Imam for help. People even speak of the geography of the secret place where he dwells: the mysterious territory of the Green Island, for example (see below, II, 2). Later we shall note its curious—though purely nominal—resemblance to the name of the Strasbourg Knights Hospitaller's residence.

But does not the Imam's last message also bear some resemblance to the last message of the “Friend of God” of the Oberland? (See below, III, 1.) Indeed, there is such certainty that life is not confined to the conditions of our visible material world that some traditions recount events from the Twelfth Imam's life in the invisible world. They even speak of his five sons, governors of mysterious cities (see below, II, 3).

To meditate upon the invisible person of the Twelfth Imam is to enter the “Celestial Earth” of Hûrqalyâ, which bears so striking a resemblance to the Land of Light, the *Terra lucida* of Manichaeism. To “see the Imam in Hûrqalyâ,” as an eminent Shaykhî master put it, is to see him where he truly is: in a world that is both *concrete* and *beyond the senses*, perceived through the organ suited to a world of that kind—a world parallel to ours, yet different in nature.

We can now understand the force with which Shiite consciousness rejects two errors that it regards as fatal. The first is the error of those incapable of theophanic perception, who blandly declare that the future Imam has not yet been born.

Yet we have already seen why, through the spiritual significance of the number twelve, the Twelfth Imam must be both *already here* and *not yet*.

The second, still graver, error is the skeptic's objection: the Imam was born, but he died while his father was still alive. For Shiite consciousness, assenting to such a claim would be like accepting an echo or anticipation of the declaration that “God is dead.”

The reason is that the Twelfth Imam embodies the same deep spiritual longings expressed in Christianity by the doctrine of the *caro spiritualis Christi*, the spiritual flesh of Christ. Such a being neither appears nor disappears according to the laws of biology and material history, the laws of physical birth and death. He is a supernatural being whose appearance to human beings—or withdrawal from their sight—depends upon human beings themselves. His appearance is the very sign of their renewal. That is the deepest meaning of the Shiite conception of *ghaybat* and of the Imam's return.

As the shaykh to whom I referred a few lines ago explained to me (see also Book VI above, pp. 280 and 291), it is human beings who have imposed concealment upon the Imam: he is hidden because they have made themselves incapable of seeing him. He cannot manifest himself because he cannot be recognized. His coming into presence is not merely an event that will occur one fine day; it is something that takes place, day by day, within the consciousness of faithful Shiites.

From this perspective, the distinction between those whom the traditions call the “companions of the Hidden Imam” and those they call his adversaries becomes strikingly clear. We also see the entire cycle of Initiation succeeding the cycle of Prophecy, carrying within its movement the mystical hierarchies that remain present among us, although unseen.

To break this cycle of Initiation would therefore be to break the expectation of the end of time, and the reverse is equally true. We said earlier that Shiite consciousness could conceive of such a rupture only as an unbearable blasphemy.

Let us recall once again the terms of the Imam's last letter to 'Alî al-Samarrî: “People will arise who claim to have seen me in the flesh. Beware! Anyone who claims to have seen me physically before the events of the end will be a liar and an impostor...” There is something graver still. According to a *hadith* reported by Mofaddal (Mofazzal), because the Imam is hidden, the entire esoteric hierarchy is also concealed, beginning with the *Bâb* (the “Threshold,” the rank nearest to the Imam).

We have already had occasion to say this: not only anyone who claimed to be the Imam in person, but anyone who presented himself as the Imam's authorized representative (his *Bâb*), claiming personal investiture in order to preach publicly, would destroy the expectation essential to Shiite awareness of the end of time. By attempting to anticipate the Imam's coming, he would place himself, by that very fact, outside Shiism. Such a thing has happened, as we know: it was the tragedy of Babism, and then of the Bahá'í faith.

But that gives no one the right to hold a school responsible for doctrines that negate its own teaching and that it experiences as blasphemy. None of this means that the Imam abandons his followers, however long the Great Occultation may last. They may see him not only in dreams, as we have said, but also in ways and circumstances more mysterious still.

We shall now consider a few such cases, chosen from many others. First, however, we must set out three principles of interpretation that summarize what has gone before.

To understand the accounts that follow, we must keep three things in mind—three things that followers of the Imam take for granted.

**First**, the Imam lives in a mysterious place that does not belong to the space mapped by empirical geography. It has no coordinates on our maps. Yet this place “outside place” has a geography of its own (see below, II, 4).

**Second**, life is not limited to the conditions of our visible material world and its familiar biological laws (the carbon cycle). Events occur in the Twelfth Imam's life during his Great Occultation. We have already mentioned his five sons, governors of mysterious cities that one of our accounts will allow us to visit. These sons have descendants of their own. Here we would do well to recall the way beings are engendered in Yima's paradise, in Êrân-Vêj[^EII4-327].

**Third**, we must grasp the exact meaning of the final lines of the Imam's last letter. Shiite theologians have always emphasized that the strict invisibility decreed and announced by the Imam is meant to discredit in advance every agitator or adventurer who might claim to be a *nâ'ib*, a deputy of the Imam, in order to legitimize a political ambition. Every such claim is, by its very nature, fraudulent.

What matters to Shiism is the final Event of our *Aeon*, our age of the world: the ultimate reign of the Imam, who will restore all things to their rightful place and their truth—a universal restoration (*apokatastasis*)—and who for this reason is called the *Qâ'im*, the Resurrector. Shiite theologians agree, however, that the Imam never ruled out appearing “privately” to help a follower suffering material or moral distress: a lost traveler, for example, or a believer overcome by despair[^EII4-328].

Although Shiite sacred history abounds in such visions of divine manifestation, they occur only at the Imam's initiative. Almost always he appears as an extraordinarily beautiful young man; and almost always, with rare exceptions—we shall encounter one below—the person granted the vision realizes only afterward whom he has seen. A strict anonymity ordinarily surrounds these appearances: the very anonymity that protects religious experience from being turned into a social institution.

“Many men,” writes one of our theologians, 'Alî Asghar Borûjardî[^EII4-329], “have seen the perfect beauty of this Chosen One [the Twelfth Imam], but they recognized him only later, after he had left them.” They understand because the help they received, whether material or spiritual, could only have come from the Imam. Some have seen him during the pilgrimage to Mecca; others in the mosque of Kufa, the ancient Shiite city par excellence; still others in one or another Shiite holy place.

But the experience is never a collective vision. Even when people “see” him, they are incapable of recognizing him. That is exactly what the Great Occultation means. The Imam comes and goes everywhere in the world without being present *as a part* of any one place, without being fixed or contained within it.

The same anonymity surrounds his companions, a word that has both a broad and a narrower meaning. In the broad sense, it refers to the esoteric hierarchy we have discussed several times, whose membership is determined by symbolic correspondences. Its members remain unknown among us, generation after generation; whenever one departs, a companion from the next lower rank is raised to take his place. We have seen this same idea in Sufism. In the narrower sense, the companions of the Hidden Imam are an elite within the elite, young men or “knights” (*javânmardân*) who serve him constantly in his immediate company.

We shall encounter them in the account of the “Journey to the Green Island” translated below.

Yet both groups are hidden under the same veil of anonymity: the first for the reasons already given (Book VI, pp. 278 ff.), and the second because even the few chosen people who have met them “in the land of the Hidden Imam” cannot recognize them any more readily than they could recognize the Imam himself.
