As the theologian just cited writes: “No one knows them, and they make themselves known to no one. Just as men cannot recognize the Imam, they never recognize a single one of his companions or pages. These companions do not frequent men's houses. Their activities and occupations are unknown.

“Sometimes they come into contact with human beings, but no one knows their true state or condition. In deserts, on islands of the Ocean, in the heart of mountains or the depths of valleys, they sometimes pitch their tents. And so many travelers, caravaneers, and wanderers who have lost their way have seen tents, dwellings, castles, and enchanting green places rise before them in the middle of arid deserts... Some have been allowed to enter. They saw and understood. They returned, but could never again find the way back, or show anyone else how to get there.”

Because both groups remain hidden in the same way, there is in fact no definitive criterion by which to distinguish their members. Nor would it serve any purpose to try. Since the Imam's “place” is everywhere, we can say of all of them that their own “place” is near him. Together they form that elite, that “knighthood,” through which the higher world communicates with the lower—and without which humanity could not continue to exist. Through them runs a continual selection of beings who transcend ordinary humanity, from Adamic humanity (the three hundred who bear the likeness of Adam) to seraphic humanity, embodied in the Supreme Pole (the one who bears the likeness of Seraphiel).

Every devout Shiite longs to be counted among them, or raised from the dead in their company, at the Imam's side in the final battle (see the pilgrim's prayer translated here, pp. 458 ff.). In developing this theme, Shiite theosophy has given vivid expression to something that both distinguishes it and reveals its deep kinship with other spiritual traditions. Later we shall try to make these resonances felt by developing the theme of “spiritual knighthood.”

The anonymity required of the mystical knighthood surrounding the Hidden Imam, in either sense, is as strict, as we noted earlier, as that of the knights of the Grail: one cannot reach them unless they themselves lead one to them. Suhrawardî's work gave us the opportunity (in Book II) to trace the signs that lead from Iran's heroic epic to its mystical epic, along a tradition parallel to the adventures of Parsifal and pointing likewise toward the realm of the Grail.

Later we shall show how Shiite literature about the Hidden Imam guides us along a converging path. The same ethical rule governs both the anonymity of the mystical knighthood that forms the esoteric hierarchy and the *kettnân*, the discipline of keeping sacred secrets imposed by the Imams. It is observed by every believer who has been tested (*momtahan*), that is, initiated into the spiritual meaning of Imamism.

Since 'Alî al-Samarrî's final words—“From now on, the matter belongs to God alone”—this spiritual attitude, this *ethos*, has been marked by *desperatio fiducialis*: a despair that nevertheless trusts, an unshakably confident pessimism sustained by the coming dawn of the Imam's appearance. Through it, every follower who has “proved himself” answers and corresponds to the watchfulness of the Unseen Ones. This is how the dawn draws near; this is what it means to “be a companion of the Imam.”

We can understand all the more clearly why anyone who publicly claimed to be a “companion of the Imam” and presumed to speak in his name would be committing a betrayal, and could only be an impostor.

We shall not try to pierce that veil of anonymity here. Instead, we shall translate a few accounts from witnesses who “were led there and saw.” Even if they cannot guide us back along the path they took, they can at least tell us what they saw when they left the outer world and entered, “between times,” what we can only call by the name Suhrawardî himself coined in Persian: *Nâ-kojâ-âbâd*, the “Land of No-Where.” It is an inner place, genuinely a land (*âbâd*), yet one cannot say *where* it is, because no direction toward it can be found by using the cardinal points of the sensory world. It is the land of “theophanic visions,” and belongs to what Suhrawardî also called the “eighth clime.” The universe of the *Malakût*, the spiritual realm parallel to the sensory universe, has its own space and its own arrangement of places.

We can begin to imagine how that space relates to the space of our world only when we understand, with our philosophers, how a spiritual substance “envelops” a material one—how the soul is the body's “spiritual place.”

Among the many accounts of the Imam's appearances “during the Great Occultation,” the four texts translated below belong to different types. Two of them—the first, concerning the founding of Jam-Karân, and the fourth, concerning an encounter in the desert—bring the believer directly into the presence of the Imam himself. The other two—the journey to the Green Island and the journey to the five islands—bring the believer into the presence of the Imam's companions or sons. In every case the meeting follows a secret decision by the Imam. A person must become capable of receiving such a meeting; but no one can decide to meet the Imam, still less bring the meeting about by force of will.

An anecdote below will remind us of this. Sometimes the Imam's presence breaks into the very place where a believer or pilgrim is standing, and there transports that person into his presence (the fourth account). Sometimes the visionary experience begins when figures “belonging to the Imam's world” appear and gradually lead the pilgrim into that world (the first and second accounts). At other times it begins with an initiatory prelude—such as a sea voyage—that, without the travelers' knowledge, carries them into an unknown world (the third account).

All these accounts share one remarkable feature: the passage from the geography of the sensory world to that of the unknown world occurs without the travelers being aware of the precise moment of transition. They recognize it only when they are already “somewhere else.”

Another striking detail is that the Imam's world may break into ours and leave a material trace behind, such as a building erected at his command. More unsettling still, the pilgrim may bring back an object as evidence of the encounter: a book or a purse, for example. Sometimes the event makes the account into a genuine narrative of initiation—initiation into Shiite teaching, into the mystery of the Imamate (the second and third accounts).

Yet there is something, as the account of the journey to the Green Island warns us, that we shall never know, because the discipline of sacred secrecy forbids—or at that time forbade—it to be put in writing. These accounts suggest that the spiritual place outside ordinary space is present everywhere: what we might call the ubiquity of *Nâ-kojâ-âbâd*. In relation to the bounded, enclosing space of the sensory world, the spiritual place is nowhere precisely because it is equally everywhere (see below, II, 4).

Finally, these accounts, together with the many others like them, must be read as a continuation of the sacred biography of the Twelfth Imam. When we say that the Twelfth Imam has, for ten centuries, been the history of Shiite consciousness, we are speaking neither metaphorically nor by some trick of naming things. We mean it in the thoroughly “realist” sense of the *mundus imaginalis*.

The point in our world where the Imam's place becomes visible is the *mazhar*: the *theater* and *mirror* in which his place appears. It is therefore not within that mirror that we should afterward look for the Imam himself. Suhrawardî explains this admirably, in complete agreement with what Swedenborg would later teach concerning the world of visions. In the mystical study of mirrors, the faculty that perceives appearances in them is the imagination itself—a *katoptron*, a mirror, and specifically the mirror of consciousness.

To call these visions, these manifestations, the biography and history of the Twelfth Imam is therefore to say that this history takes place in the parallel world. Compared with history as the word is ordinarily understood, it is an *anti-history*. It does not enter ordinary history any more than a reflected image enters into the substance of a mirror, as black pigment, for example, enters into black wood.

The place in which it unfolds is spiritual, just as its time lies “between times.” These manifestations free the human being from the laws of history and from the space in which ordinary history occurs. They are not subject to the laws of historical causation; the Hidden Imam's secret history cannot be “explained” by the workings of those laws. The principle underlying these manifestations is a principle of release from historical causation. It moves against the current of our religious theologies and philosophies that “seek God in history.” The Twelfth Imam's “history” is an escape from History. Unless we understand this, we cannot enter the Imam's world.

We will fall back upon “scientific” explanations whose clearest result may be to abolish the very reality they set out to explain.

### CHAPTER II

#### *In the Time of the “Great Occultation”*

##### I. *The Sanctuary of Jam-Karân*

The accounts translated here will confirm that, although the Hidden Imam's return dominates the whole of Shiite consciousness, the Shiite community's relationship with its Imam necessarily remains within the *dimensio mystica*, the mystical dimension.

Indeed, it would be hard to find a book about the Imam that did not devote a chapter to testimonies from people who have seen him, whether in dreams or while awake. These accounts together constitute the “history”—more precisely, the sacred history—of the Twelfth Imam during the Great Occultation, a time “between times.” We have therefore said that this history itself unfolds “between times.” The duration of an experience of this kind has its own measure: it cannot be fitted into the sequence of chronological time or measured in its units.

We can establish the visionary's place in ordinary chronology before and after the experience. But compared with the event itself, all we possess then is the chrysalis, the empty shell: for *during* the event, the visionary was not there, in ordinary time and space.

Many anecdotes illustrate that such an event depends neither on human initiative nor on a person's decision. Their origins may be difficult to trace, yet they remain eloquent because they say exactly what they need to say. I shall recount one particularly characteristic story, as an Iranian friend told it to me some years ago[^EII4-330]. A *mojtahed*—one of those scholars who devote their whole lives to studying and interpreting the Shiite traditions—longed passionately to see the Hidden Imam. To this end he performed every kind of pious act.

Then one night he dreamed of a figure who told him that he would see the Imam at dawn on a particular morning, at the workshop of a particular craftsman near one of the gates of Isfahan. He hesitated, but the same dream came to him on three successive nights. So he went to the place indicated. Just as he was about to enter the craftsman's house, a young man came out. The scholar went inside, introduced himself, and carefully explained at length why he had come so early.

“But the Imam was here only a moment ago,” the craftsman replied, “just as you were coming in.” My Iranian friend explained the story this way: the Imam can take on any outward appearance. It is not for you to seek a vision of him. It is for him to decide whether you have the *capacity* to see him—whether you truly are one of his companions, whether you belong to *his* world. To belong to the world of the Imam's companions is to have the capacity to perceive spiritual Forms, to “see things in Hûrqalyâ.” Neither human effort nor human learning can create or activate this capacity. An ordinary person may be granted it just as readily as a shaykh, a great spiritual master, or a learned scholar. The initiative belongs to the Imam.

That is how Shiite consciousness understands it, and the origin of the sanctuary of Jam-Karân offers a striking illustration. The sanctuary of Samarra in Iraq marks the place where the Imam became hidden from human sight, from the eyes of the flesh. The sanctuary of Jam-Karân in Iran is one of the places where he appears to a different, subtle faculty of vision.

Without recognizing this faculty, any account of what a human being is remains incomplete. It will either treat concrete spiritual reality as though it were material, or reduce it to fantasy, hallucination, or a mere idea[^EII4-331]. That is why we have already connected the study of visionary consciousness with Suhrawardî's account of reality. More than any other, his philosophy established a place in the order of being for the “world of visions,” and his influence in this respect has endured over the centuries.

Thus a pilgrimage to Samarra or Jam-Karân, whether made physically or inwardly, presupposes for every pilgrim a passage beyond sensory perception into a higher mode of perceiving[^EII4-332].

Jam-Karân is an oasis about a league and a half southeast of the city of Qomm, in the desert, near mountains that at dusk take on shapes as fantastic as the fragile mud-brick buildings of the little settlement. There, in the fourth/tenth century, following an appearance of the Twelfth Imam to a shaykh who lived in the village, a sanctuary was built that became a place of pilgrimage for all Twelver Shiites. We are especially concerned with the circumstances of that appearance.

Our information about the founding of the mosque at Jam-Karân by order of the Twelfth Imam goes back to one of Ibn Bâbûyeh's many works. That book has been lost, but fortunately the account was preserved in a *History of Qomm* written by one of his contemporaries. We found it in one of the learned compilations assembled by the eminent Iranian Shiite scholar of the preceding century, Mîrzâ Hosayn Nûrî[^EII4-333].

The account is told in the first person, in the words of the shaykh who, one night in Ramadan 373/February 984, was granted the privilege of speaking with the Twelfth Imam. This date—an entirely external marker, of course—is only about forty years later than the date assigned to the beginning of the Great Occultation. The opening of the story contains details particularly worth noting because they recall symbolic practices familiar from rites of initiation.

First comes the changing of clothes. We find the same feature in other accounts that likewise resemble initiation narratives. In the “Story of the White Cloud” (above, Book V, Chapter III, 3), for example, we saw the Imam appear at one point wearing two robes whose symbolic colors announced that the participants had crossed into the *Malakût*, the spiritual world. There, too, an episode included by Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî in his interpretation showed the Fifth Imam, Mohammad Bâqir, entering an oratory to change his robe before leading his disciple into the *Malakût*, then putting his original robe back on upon returning.

The successive putting on of robes corresponding to the stages of mystical ascent is also a well-known feature of the rites of the Mithraic mysteries. Putting off one garment and putting on another is, in fact, a ritual that necessarily accompanies passage from one world to another. It signifies that one cannot enter a higher world with the nature and faculties one possesses in a lower world.

As we shall see from the opening of the story, the gestures made by the shaykh of Jam-Karân, confused and alarmed by the extraordinary summons he has received, correspond point for point to familiar rites of initiation. Although there is no formal liturgical ceremony, the meaning is the same. Twice the shaykh tries to put on his ordinary clothes, and twice an insistent voice warns him that he is mistaken. Those clothes are not his. They belong to his outward, everyday life, not to his soul. Only the soul's garments can be worn for a temporary entrance into the *Malakût*, because they alone truly belong to him.

The everyday garment is neither genuine nor his own; the sacred garment belongs to the soul, like the garment worn by the initiate at the moment of initiation. Here, too, when the shaykh is warned of his error, he finds the garment that is truly his and that alone allows him to appear at the place to which he has been summoned. Precisely because it is his own garment, he now finds it spontaneously, without having to search.

Another detail: the shaykh searches in vain for the key to his house so that he can leave. The same voice tells him that no key is needed to go out and enter the world where he is expected. Nor does the exile in Suhrawardî's initiation narratives need a key to leave his prison and set out to meet the Angel; others have already opened the door for him.

Finally, when his mysterious visitors bring the shaykh into the Imam's presence, he sees him surrounded by dignified figures whose clothing reveals them to be among the Imam's companions. Close to the Imam sits a venerable sage reading aloud. The visionary recognizes Khezr (Khadîr), the mysterious prophet always encountered near the Spring of Life, the initiator of all who have had no human master—or no master other than the Imam. He has appeared often and will appear again in the texts presented here.

A companion of the Twelfth Imam, he is even identified by some with the Imam himself. Every detail thus seems to be in its proper place, showing us that the Imam's presence takes a person out of the world of ordinary perception and suggesting where the visionary is brought, where the meeting with the Imam takes place. Let us now follow the text.

“The shaykh 'Afîf Sâlih Jam-Karânî (called simply Hasan later in the account) related the following: On the night of Tuesday, the seventeenth of Ramadan in the year 373 of the Hijra (22 February 984)[^EII4-334], I was sleeping in my house when several men knocked at the door. It was past midnight. They woke me, calling, ‘Get up, and answer the summons of Imam Mohammad al-Mahdî, *Sâhib al-Zamân*, the Lord of the Age, who is calling you.’ I got up, somewhat anxious, and began to prepare myself. ‘They will surely have left before I am ready,’ I thought. I put on my shirt.

“But a voice said, ‘Take off that shirt; it is not yours.’ In my confusion I tried to put on my *sarâwîl*, my breeches. Again the same voice said, ‘Those do not belong to you. Take the breeches that are yours.’ So I put aside the garment, took my own, and put it on. Then I began looking for the key to my door so that I could go out. Again I heard the voice: ‘The door is open!’ When I reached it and found that it was indeed open, I saw a group of noble-looking men standing there. I greeted them; they returned my greeting and said, ‘Welcome!’ Then they led me to the place where the mosque now stands.

“As I looked around, I saw a throne (*takht*) with splendid cushions arranged upon it. A young man of about thirty was reclining against four of them. Before him sat a *pîr*—a shaykh, a wise elder—holding a book and reading aloud to the young man. More than sixty people were gathered around the throne, engaged in prayer. Some wore white robes, others green. The *pîr* whom I saw reading was His Holiness Khezr (Khadir). Then he made a sign to me.”

We have reached the moment when we learn why the Imam summoned the shaykh. A man named Hasan Moslem has seized and desecrated this holy ground. The shaykh Hasan Jam-Karânî is to carry a message to the usurper: he must return the land, and a house of worship must be built upon it.

“At that moment the Imam called me by name and said, ‘Go to Hasan Moslem and tell him this: “For five years you have cultivated this land, and this year you have harvested its crop once again.

“But from now on you are no longer permitted to cultivate it. You must give back all the profit you have drawn from it, so that a mosque may be built on this very spot.” Say this to Hasan Moslem as well: “This is holy ground, chosen by God from among other lands.

“But you have taken possession of it as though it belonged to you. God has already taken two young sons from you, yet your conscience has not awakened. If you do not obey this command, other misfortunes will befall you until your conscience awakens.”’”

Shaykh Hasan Jam-Karânî then said to the Imam, “My lord and protector, I need a sign for this mission. Without some sign and proof, people will not listen to my words or believe what I tell them.” The Imam replied, “We shall give you a sign here, so that your words will be believed. Go now and carry our message.

“First seek out Sayyed Abû'l-Hasan Rezâ. Tell him to rise and go to Hasan Moslem. Let him demand an account of the profits that man has taken from the land over so many years, recover them from him, and use them to build the mosque. Let him summon the leading men of the region from Rahaq to Ardahâl, which is our domain, and see the building of the sanctuary through to completion.”

The Imam then sets out the conditions of the *waqf*, the charitable religious endowment, and prescribes the ritual rules pilgrims must follow when they pray at his sanctuary: the order of invocations and readings, and the number of *rak'at*, the prescribed cycles of prayer marked by bowing and prostration. These are the rules that pilgrims to Jam-Karân have observed for ten centuries. “For the pilgrim,” the Imam says, “who performs this prayer of two *rak'at* in the prescribed way, it will be as though he had performed it in the Ancient Sanctuary at Mecca”—that is, within the Kaaba itself. At a sign from the Imam, Shaykh Hasan Jam-Karânî takes his leave.

But twice, after he has walked a few steps, the Imam calls him back. The first time, the Imam tells him that in the flock of a shepherd named Ja'far Kâshânî he will find a particular male goat, with a thick black-and-white coat marked by seven distinctive signs. He must buy this animal, offer it in sacrifice, and distribute its meat among the sick and disabled, who will then be healed. This sacrifice corresponds to the sacrifice of the cow described in the second sura of the Quran (2:63–69), an act of atonement and purification.

Those Quranic verses clearly recall the Book of Numbers (19:1–10). The Imam calls the shaykh back a second time to announce that his “presence” will remain in this place for seven days: until the night in Ramadan known as the “Night of Destiny”[^EII4-335].

Clearly, the Imam's words are rich in symbols. Shaykh Hasan Jam-Karânî continues his account. He leaves the place and time of divine manifestation, where he alone had been privileged to witness what occurred, and returns to the continuous flow of ordinary time and the space of everyday perception. The fabric of daily events, interrupted by a supernatural intervention it cannot contain, resumes its course. What happens next will establish the only link in time available to us between the visionary event and an event belonging to visible history: the Imam's predictions will be fulfilled, and the mosque will be built.

“I returned home,” says the shaykh, “and spent the rest of the night in deep meditation, until daybreak.” He then goes to find a friend, and together they make their way to the place where the Imam appeared. To their amazement, they see a collection of chains and nails lying on the ground. Shaykh Hasan recognizes the promised sign. The two friends hurry to visit Sayyed Abû'l-Hasan Rezâ, as the Imam instructed. There the shaykh discovers that he is expected.

“You are from Jam-Karân, are you not?” the Sayyed asks. The shaykh tells him what happened the previous night. “Hasan,” the Sayyed replies, “last night, while I slept, someone spoke to me in a dream: ‘A man named Hasan will come to you from Jam-Karân in the morning. You must believe his words, trust what he tells you; his words will be our words. Do not reject him.’ I woke up, and I have been waiting for you ever since.”

From that moment Sayyed Abû'l-Hasan Rezâ directs the undertaking, following the Imam's instructions as delivered by Shaykh Hasan. Riding together, the three companions first make their way to the shepherd Ja'far Kâshânî beside the track. The goat described by the Imam is indeed there, and runs of its own accord toward Shaykh Hasan. They agree to buy it, but the shepherd Ja'far makes an extraordinary declaration, swearing that it is true: “Until now I had never seen this goat. It had never been part of my flock.

“I saw it for the first time this morning and tried in vain to catch it. And now it comes running to meet you.” The goat is sacrificed at the appointed place. Hasan Moslem, who had seized the holy land, is summoned and compelled to return what does not belong to him. The notables of Rahaq are called together.

In short, everything necessary is done for the Imam's mosque. Sayyed Abû'l-Hasan Rezâ takes the mysterious chains and nails to his home in Qomm. Fastened to the gateway of his house, they have extraordinary effects upon those who touch them.

But after the Sayyed's death, it seems, they disappear as mysteriously as they had appeared on the ground at Jam-Karân when dawn broke at the end of that visionary night.

Such, in brief, are the events preserved in the tradition of Jam-Karân. There, near the village, within a green enclosure, now stands the sanctuary built according to the Imam's instructions. For almost ten centuries it has been a pilgrimage destination for Shiites, particularly Iranian Shiites. It is still visited by large numbers of pilgrims today, yet remains surrounded by a remarkable discretion, like everything that concerns devotion to the Hidden Imam.

One glorious late autumn in Iran, in 1962, we had the opportunity to visit Jam-Karân with two dear Iranian companions. We had spent the day in the village of Kahak, in a high valley of the nearby mountains, where Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî had sought refuge for some ten years of solitude. One of my companions was the man whose dream I shall recount at the end of this chapter—a dream that bears witness, if any were needed, to the intensity of the Imam's presence in Shiite hearts. I retain an extraordinary memory of that pilgrimage.

Perhaps it is because, in a place of such strange geological surroundings, where the Imam's mosque stands upon the earth as a splendid challenge posed to our age by faith in the Unseen Ones, everything seems possible. In that immense, silent landscape, stories such as those we shall tell in this chapter acquire a presence and conviction wholly different from what they have when we read them in our own countries, amid the noise of cities or beside busy highways. In the desert, no track looks more like another than one desert track.

We had lost our way, and one of my companions loudly called out to a rider who happened, providentially, to pass nearby: “Which way is the sanctuary of the *Imâm al-zamân*, the Imam of this Age?” Those words, *Imâm al-zamân*, ringing out into the silence of that vast solitude, as pure as the immense sky above us, suddenly gave the One whom they had named with such hope and devotion for so many centuries the compelling force of something real. It lasted only for a flash, yet it was unmistakably real... for all three of us were seeking the road to him, and someone was showing us the way.

We said earlier that the story of the foundation of the mosque at Jam-Karân belongs to a particular kind of manifestation of the Imam during the Great Occultation. In accounts of this kind, the person granted the experience is not only brought into the Imam's presence but also knows that it is the Imam before him.

The Imam's presence suddenly enters the visionary's surroundings and envelops him “as a spiritual substance envelops a material substance.” Other accounts tell of pilgrims who are not brought into the Imam's presence, yet are nonetheless “at the Imam's home.” They must also travel through stages of a mysterious geography that will never be found on our maps, since it belongs to the “eighth clime.” The first two of the three accounts that follow are of this kind.

##### 2. *The Journey to the Green Island in the White Sea*

The first of these three accounts, the journey to the Green Island (*al-Jazîrat al-khazrâ*), was recorded by Majlisî in his great encyclopedia of Shiite *hadith* traditions[^EII4-336]. It comes from a document once kept in the library of the sanctuary at Najaf in Iraq—the sanctuary of the First Imam, 'Alî ibn Abî Tâlib. We have already mentioned this place, for it was in the treasury of the same sanctuary that our friend Osman Yahya discovered Haydar Âmolî's autograph manuscript of the *Tafsîr 'irfânî*. The document was written in the hand of an eminent shaykh from Kufa: al-Fazl ibn Yahyâ ibn 'Alî al-Tayyibî al-Kûfî.

This was the man who had heard the account directly from the person who had lived through that extraordinary experience: an Iranian shaykh from Mazandaran, the province along the southern shore of the Caspian Sea, named 'Ali ibn Fazel Mazandarani (and thus a compatriot of our Haydar Amoli; see above, Book IV, Chapter I).

The man who wrote the account down, Shaykh al-Fazl ibn Yahya, took great care to describe the circumstances. He himself was at Karbala, in Iraq, making a pilgrimage to the shrine of the Third Imam, Imam Hosayn, the Prophet's grandson, honoured as the “Prince of Martyrs” (*Sayyed al-shohada*). On the fifteenth of Sha'ban in the year 699 of the Hijra, corresponding to 19 May 1299—a significant date, since the night of the fifteenth of Sha'ban marks the birthday of the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam—he had a long conversation with two distinguished shaykhs who had also come on pilgrimage.

They were Shaykh Shamsoddin ibn Najih al-Hilli and Shaykh Jalaloddin 'Abdollah ibn al-Hawam al-Hilli, both from the mountains of Hilla in Syria, long a centre of Shiite life. They told our writer of an extraordinary story they had heard shortly before, while making a pilgrimage to Samarra—another Shiite holy place, where, as we recalled above, the Eleventh Imam, Hasan al-'Askari, died and his son entered the Occultation. At Samarra an Iranian shaykh had told them of “the strange and wonderful things he had contemplated and seen with his own eyes on the Green Island in the White Sea.”

Naturally, their listener was immediately consumed by the desire to hear the story from its hero's own lips. He set out at once for Samarra, hoping to find him still there. As it happened, he had the good fortune to meet him instead at Hilla. The meeting was made easier because the Iranian shaykh had taken up residence there with a fellow Mazandarani, Sayyed Fakhroddin Hasan Mazandarani, who had settled in Hilla. They were introduced amid all the charming courtesies of Eastern hospitality. It emerged that, in Wasit, the Iranian shaykh had known the father and brother of the man who would now record his story; they were almost family.

Other shaykhs from Hilla and the surrounding country arrived in their turn. And on the evening of 11 Shawwal 699, or 12 July 1299—almost exactly two months after he had first heard the story indirectly at Najaf—Shaykh al-Fazl ibn Yahya al-Kufi listened, spellbound, as did the rest of his learned audience, all of them Shiites, to the account of Shaykh 'Ali ibn Fazel Mazandarani. He assures us that he wrote down everything faithfully. He may have changed a word here or there, but neither the meaning nor the events were altered.

'Ali ibn Fazel's own account is equally rich in detail. It begins with a short introduction that tells us, among other things, the kind of man we are dealing with: a learned and devout man, showing no sign of a disposition toward what we today call schizophrenia. He explains that he had spent several years in Syria, specifically in Damascus, studying the disciplines that make up the traditional Islamic sciences. Among other things, he studied Qur'anic sciences under a shaykh from Andalusia, Shaykh Zaynoddin 'Ali al-Maghrebi al-Andalusi, to whom he became especially attached—not only because of the man's learning but because of his extraordinary gentleness.

For example, whenever this shaykh, who followed the Maliki school of law, had occasion to mention the Shiites, he would say, “The Imami scholars hold such-and-such an opinion on this point,” instead of using insulting names and hurling abuse, as all the other *madrasa* teachers did.

Unfortunately, after several years, the distinguished Andalusian shaykh decided to settle in Egypt. The prospect of parting was as painful to the teacher as it was to his pupil, and no less painful to a whole group of other students, expatriates (*ghoraba'*) who had grown attached to him.

Since travel formalities and expenses in those days did not present the complications familiar to us, especially for a shaykh travelling with his pupils, they made the simplest possible decision: they would all go to Egypt together. (We shall learn at the end of the story that this journey included a memorable episode of which the narrator says nothing for now.) In Cairo, Shaykh Zaynoddin al-Andalusi took up residence at the famous al-Azhar Mosque, where he gave lessons. The most eminent people in Egypt came to visit and consult him.

In short, everything went splendidly, and the students too lived in the most agreeable circumstances. Then, nine months later, misfortune arrived in the form of a company of travellers from Andalusia. “One of them,” says the narrator, “was carrying a letter from our shaykh's father. His father told him that he had been stricken by a serious illness and wished to see him before he died. He urged him to set out without delay.

“Our shaykh was deeply moved by his father's letter and wept. He resolved to leave for Andalusia at once. Some of his disciples again decided to accompany him. I was one of them, because the shaykh was very fond of me and because I greatly liked the prospect of travelling in his company.”

What route did they take? How far did they travel by caravan? Where did they board a ship? 'Ali ibn Fazel says nothing about any of this. What we do know is that, scarcely had he set foot on Andalusian soil when, at the very first stopping place, he was seized by a violent fever. His shaykh was distressed, but he was still five days' journey from his father's home and had to hurry on. He therefore entrusted the sick man to the care of the local preacher (*khatib*): once recovered, his pupil would easily be able to rejoin him.

But events took a very different course. The fever kept 'Ali in bed for three days. At the end of the third day, when it had subsided, he went out for some air in the village streets. There he noticed a group of men who had brought several consignments of goods and “had come from the mountains bordering the shore of the Western Sea (the Atlantic?).” He made inquiries. “They come,” he was told, “from a region near the land of the Berbers, in the direction of the peninsula of the *Rawafiz*”—that is, the “Dissenters,” a disparaging name used by Sunnis for Shiites.

The news filled him with joy and gave him a great longing to know that country. He asked for more precise directions. “From here to that country,” he was told, “is a journey of twenty-five days. Of those, two days are spent crossing a desert where there is not a trace of water or cultivation. Beyond it, the villages follow one after another.”

'Ali ibn Fazel hired a donkey for three dirhams, joined the group, and set off on his great adventure. He does not tell us whether or how they crossed the Strait of Gibraltar—or at least the man who recorded his account omitted it. In any case, he reached the far side of the great desert safely. There he learned that the “peninsula of the Shiites[^EII4-337]” was another three days' march away, and he continued alone. Already it is far from certain that we are following a route that could be traced on our geographical maps.

At last our traveller came to a peninsula surrounded by four walls, each defended by high, massive towers. The outermost wall ran along the seashore. He entered through a monumental gateway called the “Gate of the Berbers,” appropriately enough, since he had come from the direction of Berber country. He was shown the way to the principal mosque, an imposing building on the western side of the city, overlooking the sea. Exhausted, he found a secluded corner of the mosque and rested. Suddenly the voice of the *muezzin* rose, chanting the call to prayer.

To understand the exile's emotion, we must recall the secrecy in which Shiites, the faithful of the holy Imams, had so long been forced to live by bitter persecution across vast stretches of the Islamic world[^EII4-338]. For the first time in his life, 'Ali ibn Fazel heard, ringing out from a mosque's minaret at the end of the ritual call to prayer, the Shiite invocation asking that the “Joy” be hastened. This is the traditional name for the joy of the Imam's coming: the future appearance of the one who reigns invisibly, *incognito*, over the present age.

Could he truly have found his own people at last? Tears filled his eyes. He watched groups of worshippers perform their ritual ablutions at a spring flowing beneath a great tree, east of the mosque's outer enclosure; all followed the Shiite rite. Then a handsome man, whose whole bearing expressed dignity and gentleness, stepped away from the groups to lead the prayers. 'Ali saw that everyone performed the service, from beginning to end, according to the practices handed down by the Shiite Imams.

But he himself was too overcome by the exhaustion of his journey. He stayed in his corner, resting, and did not join in the prayer.

This was precisely what everyone reproached him for when, the prayers ended, they noticed his presence. First of all, who was he? What was he doing there? 'Ali ibn Fazel could have justified his presence simply by saying that he too was an Iranian Shiite.

But he said nothing of the kind. A Shiite, especially a Shiite travelling alone, and particularly in those days, would never be the first to speak openly. He confined himself to saying that he was an Iraqi—he had, after all, lived in Iraq—and a Muslim. He recited the twofold profession of faith, affirming the oneness of God (*tawhid*) and Muhammad's mission as Prophet.

But the others answered that these two affirmations might make him a Muslim; they were not enough to make him a *mu'min*, a true believer, faithful in the fullest sense of the word. Why did he not pronounce the third testimony, and so declare himself a true believer? Our traveller, carrying the discipline of secrecy to its very limit, pretended not to know what this third testimony was and asked them to explain.

The shaykh who had led the prayers then revealed the secret of the Imamate to him: the names of the Twelve Imams, the Twelve Friends of God (*Awliya' Allah*), the twelve Names that the divine voice had revealed to the Prophet during his Night Journey, when he was carried in ecstasy from heaven to heaven. These were the Names inscribed in blazing letters upon a mysterious emerald tablet in Fatima's possession; the very Names that Adam had contemplated, written in letters of light upon the pillars of the Throne before he left paradise; the Names that Haydar Amoli himself had seen in a vision in the night sky over Baghdad, written in gold and encircled with lapis lazuli.

In that instant, all the traveller's fear and reserve vanished, together with his fatigue. There followed a moving scene of recognition between brothers: “I am one of you; I too am a Shiite.” Now everyone vied to care for him and show him kindness, consideration and respect. As was customary, they found him a little space in an annex of the mosque, where he could live for the time being.

From this point the account begins, in a characteristic way, to become a story of initiation. That is why, as far as possible, I shall let 'Ali ibn Fazel speak for himself. The shaykh who was the imam of this Shiite community—*imam* here in the purely liturgical sense, the person who leads the prayers—became his companion on the path of initiation. They spent every day together in long conversations. During his walks, however, 'Ali ibn Fazel noticed that there were no cultivated fields anywhere nearby.

Where, then, did the inhabitants obtain their food? He asked his companion this question, and it was surely the question that had to be asked. The shaykh answered: “Their provisions come from the Green Island in the White Sea, one of the islands belonging to the sons of the Imam who is lord of this age. — And how often each year,” I asked, “do these provisions arrive? — Twice a year. The first voyage has already taken place this year. We are still waiting for the second. — And how long,” I asked again, “before the next arrival? — Four months,” he told me.

“I was dismayed by the length of that wait. I spent the first forty days among them, waiting and praying to God night and day to hasten the ships' arrival. Throughout that time everyone treated me with the greatest kindness, regard and consideration. At the end of the fortieth day, my heart grew anxious, because the waiting seemed as though it would never end. I went out and walked along the seashore, searching the open water toward the west, for the inhabitants had assured me that it was from that direction their provisions arrived.” Remembering the route followed thus far, we may be inclined to imagine ourselves on the Atlantic coast of Africa, with the island perhaps belonging to the Canary Islands.

But we would be mistaken. We have already begun to suspect this, and everything that follows will confirm it—beginning with the length of the sea voyage still before us. The topography, however precisely described, no longer belongs to the kind of geography we can recover from our maps. Elsewhere, indeed, traditions “locate” this Green Island, which here appears almost as a surviving fragment of Atlantis, in quite different places—the Caspian Sea, for example. Which is another way of saying that it has no coordinates in the geography of this world.

Our traveller stood watching on the shore, like a lookout. “Suddenly,” he says, “one day I saw something white moving far away. I questioned the local people. ‘Isn't that a white bird out there on the sea? — No,’ they said. ‘Can you see something? — Yes,’ I answered. Then they burst into joy. ‘Those,’ they told me, ‘are the ships that come to us every year from the land of the Imam's sons.’”

“Only a short time passed before the ships came into view. According to the inhabitants, they had arrived earlier than usual. A great ship entered the harbour, followed by another, then another, until the whole fleet of seven ships had arrived.

“From the great ship there descended a shaykh of noble bearing, handsome and splendidly dressed. He went straight to the mosque, performed his ablutions and the two afternoon prayers according to the rites handed down to us from the holy Imams—that is, in the Shiite manner. When he had finished, he turned to me and greeted me. I returned his greeting.

“‘What is your name?’ he asked. ‘I believe your name is 'Ali? — You are right,’ I replied. He then spoke with me as someone might who had known me very well for a long time. ‘And what is your father's name?’ he asked. ‘Fazel, I believe. Is that not so? — Yes,’ I said. After that I no longer doubted that he must have travelled with our party, in our caravan, from Damascus to Cairo.

“‘Shaykh,’ I asked him, ‘how do you know my father and me? Were you with us when we travelled from Damascus to Cairo?

“— Certainly not.

“— And you were not with us on our journey from Cairo to Andalusia either?

“— No! I swear by my lord, the Imam of this age, that I was not with you.

“— Then how do you know my name, and how do you know my father's name?

“— Know that, long before today, a description of you reached me, together with knowledge of your name, your origin, your appearance and your father's name—may God receive him in His mercy! For you must understand: I am your Companion. I have come to take you with me to the Green Island. We shall set out together for the Green Island now.’”

In this episode we unmistakably recognize the feeling known to seekers of hidden spiritual knowledge in every age and place: the feeling of exile. Such a person is cut off from his own people, from a family of good and beautiful beings whom he can barely remember, and whose way home he knows even less. Then one day a message comes from them—like the letter in the *Hymn of the Pearl*, in the *Acts of Thomas*, reminding the young Parthian prince of his origin; or like the message brought by the hoopoe to the exile imprisoned at the bottom of a well in Suhrawardi's *Tale of the Western Exile*[^EII4-339]. Here we have something more than a message.

One of those beings comes in person: one of the mysterious Companions of the Hidden Imam, appointed to accompany the man he has been sent to bring “home.” Our narrator then cries out with great feeling: “When I heard these words, I was beside myself with happiness. So they had remembered me! So they knew my name!” Was his exile, then, at an end?

The shaykh, whose name was simply Muhammad, stayed only three days—long enough to make sure that all the provisions intended for each of the Shiites on the peninsula had been distributed. Then they decided to depart. They boarded the great ship, the signal was given, and they sailed out to sea.

“On the sixteenth day of our voyage,” continues 'Ali ibn Fazel's account—and we should note this precision, since from here onward it is the only detail that gives us a sense of distance actually travelled—“I noticed that the water on the surface of the sea was completely white. Shaykh Muhammad came over to me. ‘I see,’ he said, ‘that this water has particularly caught your attention.

“— Because,” I told him, “I've noticed that it is a different colour from the rest of the sea.

“— Indeed,” he said. “This water is the White Sea, and there on the horizon is the Green Island. This white water forms a circle all around the island, like a fortified wall protecting a city. From whatever direction one approaches, one must pass through it. And by the wisdom of the Absolute Wise One, and through the spiritual power flowing from our lord and Imam who reigns over this age, whenever the ships of our enemies enter these waters, they sink, however strong and powerful they may be.”’” (This detail assures us that we have now entered the geography of another world.)

The narrator admits that he wanted to taste this water for himself. He drew up a little of it. “It tasted,” he says, “just like the water of the Euphrates[^EII4-340].”

“When we had crossed this belt of white water, we finally landed on the Green Island, whose inhabitants live in a state of perpetual youth. We disembarked from the great ship, set foot on the island, and entered the city. I saw that the city stood beside the sea and had ramparts and towers; seven walls encircled it. There were plentiful rivers and luxuriant vegetation, with every kind of fruit tree. There were shops and many public bathhouses (*hammam*). Most of the buildings were made of translucent marble. All the inhabitants wore magnificent clothing. Their faces were beautiful. My heart soared with joy at everything I beheld.”

Here begins the second part of the initiation story. We can distinguish three stages. First comes a series of conversations with the man who governs the Green Island and is none other than a grandson of the Hidden Imam. These conversations offer a first initiation into the Imam's secret. Then comes a visit to a mysterious sanctuary deep within the mountain that rises above the island. Finally, there is another series of conversations, of decisive importance.

After the travellers had rested, Shaykh Muhammad took his companion to the Great Mosque. There he saw a large assembly, “at the centre of which,” says the narrator, “sat a man whose majesty and dignity, gentleness and serenity, were beyond my power to describe.” People addressed him as Sayyed Shamsoddin Muhammad al-'Alim, meaning “the learned man,” or “the sage.” Sayyed Shamsoddin was presiding over something like what we today would call a close reading of texts. One person after another would read aloud to him a passage from the Qur'an or from the sources of Imami theology—that is, the *hadith*, the transmitted sayings of the Imams—and he would comment on their interpretations, correct them, and fill out what was missing.

'Ali ibn Fazel was introduced, and the Sayyed graciously seated him beside himself. He asked about his journey and then said these significant words: “Everything concerning you came to my knowledge long before today. It was on my instructions that your companion, Shaykh Muhammad, brought you here.” Our traveller then withdrew to a room in one of the mosque's annexes, which had been set aside for him, and rested until late afternoon.

As evening fell, “the one to whose care I had been entrusted,” as he calls Shaykh Muhammad, his companion in initiation—using almost exactly the expression we find in *The Shepherd of Hermas*—“told me that the Sayyed and his companions would come to share our evening meal.” And so they did. When the meal was finished, everyone rose and went to the mosque to recite the evening prayer, after which each returned home.

Three weeks—or eighteen days, to be exact—passed in long conversations, at the end of which our pilgrim received his first revelation. The first time he joined his new companions for the solemn Friday prayer, he noticed that the Sayyed doubled the deep bows (*rak'at*) each time, treating them as obligatory.

Yet according to the Shiite rite, this obligation applies only when the Imam is present. 'Ali ibn Fazel thought to himself, “So there are times when the Imam is here?” At the first opportunity to speak to the Sayyed alone, he asked him: “Is the Imam present here? — No,” answered the Sayyed, “but I am his personal representative (*na'ib khass*), by an order that comes directly from him. — My lord,” I said, “have you seen the Imam? — No. But my father told me that he had heard the Imam's voice without seeing him, whereas my grandfather both heard his voice and saw him in person.”

Two valuable points emerge here. First, we are certainly no longer in a place belonging to this world, where no one could claim to be the Hidden Imam's “representative,” still less to be descended from him—as will be explained later.

Second, there is something here that recalls the Shiite understanding of spiritual knowledge. To hear the voice without seeing the one who inspires is the characteristic form of the Imam's inward inspiration (*ilham*); to hear the words and at the same time see the Angel is characteristic of the divine revelation (*wahy*) received by the prophets[^EII4-341].

But another question now becomes urgent—so urgent that it will be asked again at the end of the story. “And why, my lord, is this privilege given to one person and withheld from another? Why does one man see him, while another does not?” The answer will allude to the deepest secret of Twelver Shiism, and at the same time to the secret of the Green Island.

“Brother,” the Sayyed told me, “God bestows His grace upon whichever of His faithful servants He wills, in accordance with His perfect wisdom and sovereign majesty. Among His servants God has set apart those He has chosen as prophets, messengers, and inheritors of the prophetic mission (*awsiya'*, the Imams). He has established them as Signs and symbols (*a'lam*) for humankind, as Witnesses and Guides (*Hojjat*) before His creatures, as intermediaries between them and Himself.

“Thus, only after the Sign has shone forth may ‘those who perish perish, and those who live live[^EII4-342].’ For in His tender care God never leaves the Earth without a Witness and Guarantor who answers for Him before human beings. Yet it sometimes happens that a Witness himself needs an intermediary to convey to people, in his name, what he has to tell them.”

That is precisely the situation of the last of these Witnesses, the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam. The profound conviction of Shiism, as we have already had occasion to say, is that human beings must never be able to argue against God that there was no Witness in the world to answer for Him[^EII4-343]. It is this very necessity that establishes the necessity of the Imamate after the prophetic mission has come to an end. And the Imamate continues even during the Imam's Occultation, because the ultimate reason for that concealment is to be sought entirely on the human side.

In himself, the Imam remains the Imam, whether people recognize him or whether he is wholly unknown to the mass of humankind. He remains the Pole of poles, without whose existence the human world could not continue to exist: the mystical Pole (*Qotb*), at the summit of a spiritual hierarchy governed by the same sacred law of remaining *incognito*. For God alone chooses the human beings to whom one of the Imam's Companions—or sometimes the Imam himself—will appear.

After this conversation, Sayyed Shamsoddin took 'Ali ibn Fazel by the hand—as Gurnemanz leads Parsifal toward the realm of the Grail—and they left the city together. “We walked toward the gardens. Streams of living water lay before us, and garden followed garden, with beautiful trees bearing every kind of delicious fruit ... I had never seen anything like it in either of the two Iraqs (Arab Iraq and Persian Iraq), or anywhere in Syria. As we were passing from one garden to another, we saw a handsome man coming toward us, dressed in two layers of white woollen cloth.

“As he passed, he greeted us and went on his way. His appearance struck me. I asked the Sayyed, ‘Who is that man? — Do you see that high mountain?’ the Sayyed asked me. ‘— Yes,’ I said. ‘— Well, deep within that mountain is a beautiful place where a spring of living water flows beneath a tree—a very great tree, with branches spreading in every direction. Beside the spring stands a domed place of prayer (*qobba*), built of brick. That man and a companion of his are the guardians of this little sanctuary.

“I myself go there every Friday morning to make my visit to the Imam. I perform a prayer of two cycles (*rak'at*), and there I find a sheet of paper on which are written the decisions to be made concerning the believers. Everything written there I put into practice. You too should go there and pay your visit to the Imam in that sanctuary.’”

For our part, we seem to recognize in passing, in the man dressed in white wool, the mysterious Khezr (Khadir), the counterpart of the prophet Elijah, sometimes identified with him, who has a special bond with the Twelfth Imam. (At Jam-Karan, in the preceding story, we encountered him reading aloud in the Imam's presence)[^EII4-344]. What confirms this identification for us is his presence here beside a spring that can only be the Spring of Life. It flows in the shade of a great tree, the *Tuba* tree, which spreads its shadow over paradise and is the Tree of Being. And so it is there, at the very heart of being, beneath the Tree and beside the Spring, that we find the sanctuary where one may draw nearest to the Hidden Imam.

“So I made my way toward the mountain,” our pilgrim continues. “I found the domed place of prayer exactly where the Sayyed had said it would be, and just as he had described it. I also found its two guardians. The one we had met in the gardens welcomed me, while the other gave me a cold look. The first said to him, ‘Do not be unfriendly, for I saw him in the company of Sayyed Shamsoddin al-'Alim.’ At this the second man turned to me and welcomed me too.

“Both began talking with me and then offered me bread and grapes—not the bread and wine of the mystical Last Supper, since we are in Islam, but the same symbols: bread and grapes. I drank the Water flowing beside the sanctuary, performed my ritual ablutions, and offered a prayer of two cycles. Then I ventured to ask the guardians whether it was possible to see the Imam. They said, ‘No, it is not possible to see him, and we are not permitted to tell anyone about this.’ So I asked them to pray for me. They both prayed for me, and then we parted.”

Returning from this pilgrimage, which seems to mark the high point of his stay on the Green Island, 'Ali ibn Fazel went to see his friend Shaykh Muhammad, who had come to fetch him and with whom he had sailed to the island. He told him everything about that memorable day: his ascent of the mountain, his meeting with the two guardians, and the unfriendly reception he had at first received from one of them. The shaykh explained: “If he acted that way at first, it was because he did not know you. For no one except Sayyed Shamsoddin and those who are like him is permitted to ascend to those places.”

But if the Sayyed had instructed 'Ali ibn Fazel to go up there, we must ask, did that mean that he had become one of those “like him”? There is surely a profound insight here into the meaning of Shiite devotion, one that a thinker such as Molla Sadra Shirazi was able to bring out so admirably. There is no opposition or contradiction between prophetic religion as a religion received from outside oneself and mystical religion as a religion experienced inwardly. When a spiritual seeker reaches the level at which the Imam becomes a personal, inward Guide, the seeker attains a state “like” that of the Imam. Far from abolishing the teachings concerning prophecy and the Imams, this experience fulfils them, makes them “real”[^EII4-345].

As for Sayyed Shamsoddin, the shaykh explained to his friend that he was a descendant, “one of the children of the Imam's children. Five fathers stand between him and the Imam[^EII4-346]”—that is, five generations. For anyone who insists on the material evidence of what are called historical facts, this is something extraordinary indeed. The Sayyed is a descendant of an Imam, an *Imam-zadeh*. He has a precise genealogy and a definite way of life; his teaching has real effects on human souls.

And yet, even less than his forefather the Twelfth Imam, does he appear in the ordinary world of sensory experience. He is in no sense a “myth,” yet he does not enter “history.” Even what is called “docetism”—often without any real understanding of it—is surpassed by the boldness of this faith in the world beyond the senses, and by this world of vision, which is at once sacred knowledge (*hierognosis*) and sacred history (*hierohistory*).

We now come to the final part of the story. The initiation will be completed by clarifying one of the matters closest to every faithful Shiite's heart: the condition in which the Qur'an, the sacred Book sent down from Heaven, exists today. Then a scene of triumphant manifestation will lead naturally to a question about the Imam's future appearance. Once again, with the insistence of a theme that can never be forgotten, the question will arise: is it possible to see the Imam? This last conversation prepares the way for the farewell and the journey home.

'Ali ibn Fazel, well trained in Qur'anic studies, knew the variant readings of the Qur'an perfectly and wanted the Sayyed's help in resolving the difficulties they presented. To test him, the Sayyed asked him to begin reciting the Qur'an. At every passage where variants occurred, the young Iranian listed all the readings preserved by those known in Persian as the *haft pir*, the seven masters of Qur'anic recitation.

But the Sayyed interrupted him. We do not need all those authorities. What actually happened was this: during the Prophet's last pilgrimage, known as the Farewell Pilgrimage, the Angel Gabriel descended to him once more and had him recite the entire Qur'an. Gabriel reminded him of the circumstances in which its successive passages had been revealed, explained the variant readings, and gave particular attention to the concluding sections and final verses of each sura.

Present were not only a group of well-known Companions but also the First Imam, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Commander of the Faithful, together with his two sons, Hasan and Hosayn. As the Angel spoke, 'Ali wrote down his explanations on a scroll of skin. Here, then, the Angel who interprets the text is none other than the Angel who revealed it.

But why, 'Ali ibn Fazel asks, does the text seem so disjointed? Why do certain verses appear to have no connection with what comes before or after them?

The answer given is that, immediately after the Prophet's death, the First Imam tried to present to the Quraysh the complete Qur'an as he himself had written it down.

But those who had seized the outward caliphate—for the real, hidden caliphate of the spirit was beyond their reach—rejected the Imam's offer with contempt. These were the first two caliphs recognized by the Sunnis, Abu Bakr and 'Omar, who thus set Islam on the course it subsequently followed. Instead they chose to gather, fragment by fragment, whatever portions of the text were in the possession of the Muslims. Naturally, they removed everything that clearly concerned the Imamate and might have testified against them. This, the account explains, is why the text has gaps and seems disjointed. In spite of them, however, the Book is indeed the Word of God.

But the only authentic copy of its heavenly archetype—the copy written by the First Imam's own hand—is held by the one who is now the Hidden Imam[^EII4-347].

We can imagine that, once the conversation had taken this direction, it hardly remained confined to harmless questions of religious law. It must have touched on Shiite spiritual knowledge, but the rule of secrecy will prevent us from ever knowing what was said. 'Ali ibn Fazel himself warns us: “From the Sayyed's teaching I have written down the answers to a great many questions, about ninety in all. I possess the text. I have gathered them in a book that I have called *The Teachings of Shams* (*al-fawa'id al-shamsiya*).

“But I can make it known only to a select few among the faithful. You will see this book, God willing.” Alas, no one has yet reported finding a manuscript of it.

Meanwhile, on the very next Friday, which fell on the middle day of the month—we have already encountered the symbolism of this date—the Sayyed had, as usual, led the prayers and begun presiding over his gathering of students when 'Ali ibn Fazel suddenly heard a great commotion outside the mosque. He asked what was happening. The Sayyed told him: “Whenever the middle day of the month falls on a Friday[^EII4-348], the commanders of our army assemble to await the Joy”—the traditional expression, as we already know, for the Imam's manifestation.

'Ali ibn Fazel asked permission to see them and went outside. There he found an assembly of horsemen, singing a triumphant hymn that called upon God to hasten the joy of the Appearance of the Imam who will bring the divine Cause to triumph, Muhammad al-Mahdi, who reigns invisibly over this age. How many knights make up this supernatural company? Three hundred and thirteen, the Sayyed later explained. This is indeed one of the numbers given by traditions concerning the hidden spiritual hierarchy, always present *incognito* in this world in the Imam's service[^EII4-349].

But here, as the account specifies, the number refers only to the commanders of this esoteric army.

This moving scene naturally led 'Ali ibn Fazel to ask the question every Shiite carries deep in the heart: “When will the Joy—the future appearance of the Imam—take place? — Brother,” the Sayyed answered, “that knowledge belongs to God alone, and the matter rests with His will, so completely that even the Imam himself does not know.

“But there will be Signs and indications announcing his appearance.” Here the image of the Sword enters the story: the Sword will speak, asking the Imam to wield it.

But this is a sword that has descended from Heaven, not a blade forged from the metals of this world[^EII4-350]. These two details suggest that the Imam's battles and victories will not be quite what some enthusiastic literal-minded believers perhaps expect. We also know that his manifestation cannot even be conceived until human beings have changed their hearts and become capable of seeing him.

“To see the Imam.” This burning desire runs through the story from beginning to end. 'Ali ibn Fazel knew perfectly well the terms of the Imam's last letter, in which he had declared in advance that anyone claiming to have seen him would be an impostor. “How is it, then,” he asks, “that there are people among you who see him? — What you say is true,” replies the Sayyed. “The Imam did indeed make that declaration at the time, because his enemies were so numerous—alas, even among his own family, as well as elsewhere, among the pharaoh-like brood of the Abbasids. The need for secrecy was then so great that Shiites forbade themselves even to speak of the matter among themselves.

“But much time has passed since then. Our enemies have abandoned all hope of reaching the Imam. This land of ours lies beyond their reach, beyond their power to do us violence. Through the spiritual influence of the Imam, none of our enemies is able to come as far as this place[^EII4-351].”

The inviolable Green Island is therefore truly like the realm of the Grail, the land “on distant shores that no mortal can approach,” except those summoned by a mysterious message. Only they may be admitted for a time, and even they do not find the road through any initiative of their own. We already know that the Imam may appear to any human being in distress, but that the person will almost always understand who appeared only afterward. This very truth will be disclosed, through a kind of argument addressed to the traveller's own experience, in a farewell scene that must be translated in full: it cannot be summarized.

“‘My lord,’ I said, ‘I would so love to stay among you until[^EII4-352] God permits the Joy’—that is, the Coming of the Imam.

“‘Alas, my brother, even before today the order came to me that you must return to your own country, and neither you nor I can oppose that order. You have people dependent on you, and you have already been kept away from them for a very long time. You cannot delay any longer.’

“When I heard these words, I was overcome and wept. Then I said, ‘My lord, is there absolutely no possibility of changing the order that concerns me?’

“‘No. It is impossible.’

“‘Will you at least allow me to tell everything I have seen and heard here?’

“‘Nothing prevents you from telling the faithful believers, so that their hearts may be at peace. But you must tell it in a particular way.’”

“And he told me what, in any event, I must not say (here again the ‘discipline of secrecy’ comes into play).

“‘My lord,’ I finally asked, ‘is it not possible to behold the beauty and radiance of the Imam?’

“‘No. But know this, my brother: a believer whose heart is wholly sincere may indeed see the Imam without knowing that it is the Imam he sees—without realizing it, without recognizing him.’

“‘But my lord, I am among those whose hearts are wholly sincere, and yet I have never seen the Imam!’

“‘On the contrary! You have seen him twice. The first time was when you were approaching Samarra, where you had never been before. Your companions had gone ahead, and you had fallen behind alone, having lost their trail. You came to a hollow in a dry riverbed. Just then you saw a young horseman riding toward you on a white horse, carrying a long lance tipped with Damascus steel. At first you were afraid he would take your clothes.

“But when he drew near, he said: “Do not be afraid. Go and rejoin your companions. They are waiting for you beneath that tree you can see in the distance.”’

“‘Yes, my lord, I call God to witness! It happened exactly as you have said.’

“‘The second time was when you had left Damascus for Cairo in the company of your Andalusian shaykh. You fell behind and became separated from the caravan, and you were terribly afraid. Then a horseman appeared before you. His horse had a white mark on its forehead, and its feet were white as well. This rider, too, carried a long lance. He said: “Do not be afraid. Turn to your right. You will soon reach a village. Spend the night with its people. You may speak openly of your religion to them, for they are all devoted followers of the Immaculate Imams.” Did it not happen just so, Ibn Fâzel?’

“‘Indeed, everything happened exactly so [...][^EII4-353]. But tell me, my lord, is it true that the Imam makes the pilgrimage, season after season?’

“‘O Ibn Fâzel! This whole earthly world is no more than a single step beneath the feet of a true believer. How, then, could crossing it be difficult for one of whom we say that the world endures only through his existence and that of those who came before him?’” (That is, each Imam is the mystical Pole of the world.)

Nothing could suggest more powerfully than these last words of the Sayyed what Nâ-kojâ-Âbâd really is: the “place” that is not contained in any place in this world, yet can itself contain and encompass them all.

The story now hastens to its close. “Do not prolong your stay in the land of the West[^EII4-354],” the Sayyed advises. The traveler is generously supplied with provisions for the journey. As money for the road, the Sayyed gives him gold coins whose inscriptions proclaim four things: the oneness of God (*tawhîd*), Mohammad’s prophetic mission, the Imamate of the First Imam, and that of the Twelfth[^EII4-355].

The ships are waiting—the very ships on which the traveler came to the Green Island, and which will now carry him away. He lands on the “Shiite peninsula,” where he had originally embarked with Shaykh Mohammad. From that point onward, however, our Iranian traveler covers his tracks. In accordance with Sayyed Shamsoddîn’s advice, he does not return to Andalusia.

We shall never know whether he was reunited with his beloved shaykh, who had been obliged to go and attend his aged father’s deathbed. The first identifiable city he mentions now is Tripoli, and only to tell us: “I joined the western pilgrimage caravan bound for Mecca. I performed the pilgrimage and then set out for Iraq, intending to settle in holy Najaf for the rest of my life.”

The Story of the Green Island invites a wealth of commentary. I have been able to draw attention to only a few of its recurring themes along the way; but even a brief survey shows how extraordinarily rich this story is.

Let us single out those themes whose symbolic power gives the imaginative vision—this knowledge of sacred realities, or *hierognosis*—its remarkable coherence. **1)** The Green Island is one of the islands belonging to the sons of the Twelfth Imam.

We shall meet this theme again in another, shorter story. **2)** Rather than depending on other lands for its sustenance, as an island of our world would be expected to do, the Green Island sustains other lands. It is a living symbol of the Source from which Shiite faith draws its nourishment. **3)** It lies in the west. Here, therefore, the west does not particularly stand, as it does in Suhrawardi’s *Tale of the Western Exile* and throughout a whole realm of Gnostic thought, for the world of exile, the world of dark matter.

The Green Island seems instead to correspond to what elsewhere is symbolized by Jâbarsâ, the city situated in the western region of the *mundus imaginalis*, the imaginal world. As a kind of “western paradise,” it bears a strange resemblance to Amitabha’s paradise in Pure Land Buddhism, or to Tir-nan-Og, “one of the otherworlds of the Celts,” the land of those who remain forever young[^EII4-356].

Moreover, since the Twelfth Imam himself invites comparison with Maitreya, the Buddha yet to come, we might also recall the mystical city of Shambhala. **4)** Like the realm of the Grail, the Green Island is an intermediary world, directly connected with the higher worlds and complete in itself. **5)** It is protected against every attempt to penetrate it from outside.

Besides a stretch of sea that no enemy can cross, seven walls surround it and guard its approaches. (We are not told whether each wall is a different color, like those of ancient Ecbatana, present-day Hamadan, where Tobias and the Angel once came. An eleventh-century Ismaili author, Hamîdoddîn Kermânî, even organized one of his books, *Râhat al-Aql*, around the architecture of seven walls.) **6)** No one can find the way there unless summoned. The person who is called receives a message, or a messenger, from the Invisible Ones, who know that person by name—or to whose family the person belongs. This is a characteristic feature of other Gnostic tales.

**7)** A mountain rises above the Green Island. Deep within it, or at its summit, the Source of Life springs forth beneath the great symbolic Tree. There stands the small Temple where communication with the Hidden Imam is possible, tended by the mysterious prophet Khezr. **8)** Like Montsalvat, the destination of the Grail quest, the inviolable Green Island is the place where believers draw near to the mystical Pole of the world: the Hidden Imam, who reigns invisibly over the present age and is the jewel of Shiite faith.

##### 3. The Islands of the Five Cities

The account of the pilgrimage to the Green Island is not unique, though it may be the most characteristic example of this literature. At any rate, it is one document among many that testify to the intimate bond in which Shiite consciousness has lived with its Imam for more than ten centuries.

One of the most striking features—also one of the most surprising when judged by the standards of rational consciousness—is the Hidden Imam’s family or descendants. (Here again we would have something like a dynasty of the Grail.) Yet none of his children or grandchildren succeeds him as Imam, since he himself remains the Imam throughout the period known as the Greater Occultation. The Green Island, as we have just seen, is one of the islands of the Imam’s sons.

Another story, equally rich in detail, gives us a more precise account of their geography—though this, of course, is no geography we can transfer onto our maps. This story is more than a century and a half older than the Story of the Green Island, and we possess it only at second hand. Its compiler, a certain Mohammad ibn ‘Alî al-‘Alawî al-Hosaynî, based his text on the account of someone who heard the story directly, Kamâloddîn Ahmad ibn Mohammad al-Anbârî. Since this man reports the very words of the person who lived through the adventure, we again have a first-person narrative, a testimony.

On the evening of 10 Ramadan, in the year 543 of the Hijra (22 January 1149)[^EII4-357], a certain vizier—or, more properly, *wazîr*, following the usual Arabic and Persian pronunciation—named ‘Awnoddîn Yahyâ ibn Hobayra was giving a large dinner in Medina, Arabia, to mark the breaking of the fast. Just as the guests were preparing to leave, someone announced that it had begun to rain. The vizier invited them to stay, and the conversation resumed with renewed energy. Eventually the talk turned to religion.

The vizier, a Sunni whose religious convictions were rather simplistic, launched into a violent attack on the Shiites. After all, he said, they were only a minority; and how could a minority possibly be right? May God wipe them from the face of the earth! Now, among the guests was a man to whom the vizier had shown particular respect all evening. This man, whose name we shall never learn and who is to become the hero of our story, listened silently to the vizier’s outburst.

Clearly he was not someone who regarded being in the minority as certain proof of being wrong. At last he spoke. “I should like to contribute to your discussion,” he said, “but only by telling you something I know from my own experience. Otherwise I would rather remain silent.” After a moment’s thought, the vizier replied, “Please, then, tell us what happened to you.”

The events took place about twenty years before that Ramadan evening, in the year 522/1128, to be exact. The man—who, as the narrative will reveal, was a Christian merchant—begins by describing his homeland, where Muslims form only a small minority. Unfortunately, the geographical clues are very vague. We learn that it is a vast country, requiring two months to cross. There are references to islands and continents, a great city called al-Bahîya (the Beautiful, the Splendid), a common frontier with the Abyssinians and Nubians, and another with the Franks and Byzantines. None of this is enough to locate the country on a map, even if it belongs to the actual geography of our world.

But that is not, in the end, what matters. What matters is the account of the extraordinary voyage the narrator undertook with his father some twenty years earlier.

As usual, they had chartered a ship together with other merchants and put out to sea. What exactly happened next? No one will ever explain it to us. At any rate, they sailed far beyond the time when they should normally have reached their familiar, intended destinations.

Yet the hope of profitable trade kept them from becoming too anxious, and they continued farther and farther into the open sea. At last they approached an immense island, lush with vegetation and enclosed by magnificent walls. The travelers asked their captain, “What island is this?”

But the unfortunate man could only answer, “God is my witness! I have never landed here. I know no more about this country than you do—nothing at all.”

They cast anchor, make their way up to the city, and begin asking questions. “What is this city called?” “Al-Mobâraka—the Blessed City,” the inhabitants tell them. “Who is its king?” “His name is al-Tâher—the Pure.” “Where does he live?” “In the city of al-Zâhera—the Radiant City, bright as flowers.” “Where is that?” “Ten nights’ journey by sea, or fifteen nights by land. All its inhabitants are Muslims.”

For the moment, however, our travelers would like to pay the legally required tithe on their cargo so that they can get on with their business. “That is very simple,” they are told. “Just present yourselves to the king’s representative (*nâ’ib*).” “Where are his offices, his officials?” they ask. “But he has no offices and no officials! Anyone with a rightful claim need only appear before him, and it will be granted.”

Delighted by the simplicity of administration in this beautiful country, the travelers have themselves taken to the governor. They find a handsome young man of distinguished bearing, with one *‘abâ* (cloak) over his shoulders and another spread beneath his feet as a rug. He is busy copying a book. Greetings are exchanged. Where have they come from? They explain. Are they all Muslims? No; some are Muslims, but others are Jews and Christians. “That is very simple,” says the young governor.

“Those of you who are *Ahl al-Kitâb*—People of the Book, believers who possess a scripture revealed through a prophet, in other words Christians and Jews—need only pay the prescribed poll tax. Then you may attend to your affairs in peace, as you please.” And so, the narrator says, “my father paid the share for five Christians: for himself, for me, and for three others who were with us. Then nine more of our companions, who were Jews, paid theirs.”

Everything seems to be going splendidly until the Muslims’ turn comes. They are asked to state their profession of faith.
