[^EII4-347]: We give here the translation of this passage (Majlisî, pp. 146–147): “I said: ‘My lord, I find that some of the verses have no connection either with what comes before or with what follows them. My limited understanding cannot penetrate the reason.’ ‘Indeed,’ the Sayyed replied, ‘things are as you observe. The reason is this. When the prince of humankind (the Prophet), Mohammad ibn 'Abdillah, passed from this perishable dwelling to the everlasting Dwelling, and the two men of the Quraysh (the first two Sunni caliphs, Abû Bakr and 'Omar) did what they did, seizing the outward and public caliphate by force, the Commander of the Faithful (the First Imam) gathered the whole Quran into a leather covering and brought it to them while the Quraysh were assembled in the mosque. He said: “This is the Book of God which the Messenger of God commanded me to present to you, so that, on the Day of Resurrection, a witness may rise before God to testify against you.” But the Pharaoh and Nimrod of this community (that is, Caliph 'Omar ibn al-Khattâb) answered: “We have no need of your Quran.” The Imam replied: “The Messenger of God, my dearest friend, foretold that you would give me this answer. Yet I wished, by doing this, to bring forth testimony against you.” And the Commander of the Faithful returned to his home, saying: “There is no God but You, You alone. You have no partner. No one can overturn what has always been within Your knowledge, or oppose what Your wisdom requires. So be Yourself the Witness who will testify on my behalf against them on the Day of Resurrection.” Then Ibn Abî Qahâfa summoned the Muslims and said to them: “Whoever has in his possession a verse or a sura of the Quran, let him bring it here.” Then came Abû 'Obaydallah, 'Othmân, Mo'awiya, and others [...]. Each brought a verse or a sura, and from these they assembled the Quran we now have. But they left out everything that would have proved the wrongs they had committed since the Prophet's death. This is why the verses are not connected with one another. As for the Quran which the Commander of the Faithful compiled in his own handwriting, that is preserved with the *Sâhib al-Amr* (the Hidden Imam). It contains everything, absolutely everything. Nevertheless, concerning the Quran in our hands, there must be no doubt of its validity, nor of its being truly the Word of God. What I have just said I transmit exactly as it came from the Imam.’”


[^EII4-348]: The symbolism of this rite speaks for itself. In the Shiite liturgical calendar, Friday is the day of the week especially dedicated to the Twelfth Imam (*Mafâtîh al-Jinân*, 1331 solar Hijri, p. 56). In the lunar calendar, moreover, the middle of the month marks the division of the lunar cycle, and the middle of Sha'bân is the anniversary of the Twelfth Imam's birth.


[^EII4-349]: This mystical hierarchy is also known in forms of Sufism that are not Shiite, but there is too strong a tendency to forget that its underlying principle and structure presuppose the Shiite idea. See 'Alî Asghar Borûjardî, op. cit., Chapter X, pp. 178 ff.; and earlier in the present work, Book I, Chapter III, § 4; vol. III, Book III, Chapter III; vol. IV, Book VI, Chapter III, § 3.


[^EII4-350]: See Quran 57:25: “We sent down the Book and the Balance ... We sent down Iron; in it is formidable strength, but also benefit for humankind.” Shiite gnosis has meditated at length on this verse, seeing in it a reference to the Imam's sword and his place in *fotowwat*, or spiritual chivalry. It notes that the verse says *anzalnâ* (“We sent it down”), not *kholiqa* (“it was created”). The reference, therefore, is not to iron as a metal of this world, but to a source—or symbol—of invincible strength that does not belong to earthly creation and descends from Heaven through the ministry of the angels. As an attribute of the Imamate, this sword illuminates its nature. See the introduction to Haydar Âmolî's commentary on Ibn 'Arabî's *Fosûs*, Jarullah 1470, fol. 42b (edition in preparation).


[^EII4-351]: In short, the Sayyed's reply addressed only the literal meaning of the prohibition against mentioning the Imam in the presence of people whose trustworthiness is uncertain. See Hâjj Zaynol-'Âbidîn Khân Kermânî's treatise referred to in n. 98 of Book I (*Risâla-ye haftâd mas'ala*, Kerman, 1379/1960, question 62, pp. 442–454). At this point in the dialogue, 'Alî ibn Fâzel asks the Sayyed two questions of religious law. We saw no reason to include them here, since they have only a superficial connection with the context. Indeed, 'Alî ibn Fâzel himself says he did not include them among the ninety questions he asked the Sayyed to resolve.


[^EII4-352]: The pilgrim in Suhrawardi's *Tale of the Western Exile* expresses a similar wish. He, however, is told that he may return whenever he wishes, but must now depart (see Book II, Chapter VI, here). No such reassuring answer is given to the pilgrim to the Green Island, because the initiative does not lie with him. Compare the anecdote referred to above at p. 338, n. 24.


[^EII4-353]: Here are the details of the episode. The mysterious horseman says to 'Alî ibn Fâzel: “Spend the night with the people who live there. Tell them what religion you were born into. You need not observe *taqîyeh* (the ‘discipline of secrecy’) with them, for they are all, like the inhabitants of several villages south of Damascus, believers of utterly sincere heart, serving God according to the religion of 'Alî ibn Abî-Tâleb and the Immaculate Imams of his line. Did not everything happen exactly so, O Ibn Fâzel?” “I said: ‘Indeed it did! I went to the people of that village. I spent the night with them, and they showed me every courtesy. I asked them about their religion. They answered, without the slightest *taqîyeh* toward me: “We follow the religion of the Commander of the Faithful, heir of the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds, and of the Immaculate Imams descended from him.” I asked them: “How did this religion reach you? Who brought it to you?” They replied: “Abû Dharr al-Ghaffârî (one of the Prophet's companions), when 'Othmân (the third Sunni caliph) exiled him from Medina to Syria, and then Mo'awiya exiled him from Damascus to this country of ours. His spiritual influence extends to us all.” When morning came, I asked them to help me rejoin my caravan, and I in turn told them my religion. They provided two men who guided me back to my caravan.’”

The hadith begins: “I heard our shaykh, a specialist in hadith named Ahmad ibn Fâris al-Adîb, tell the following: ‘In Hamadan I heard a story, which I recount just as I heard it, for one of my brothers who had asked me to write it down for him, and whose request I had no reason not to fulfill. So I transcribed it, relying on the authority of the man who told it to me.’” The chain of transmission is therefore: (1) the shaykh of the Banî Râshid; (2) the man from Hamadan to whom that shaykh told the story; (3) Shaykh Ahmad ibn Fâris al-Adîb, who wrote it down; (4) the shaykh's disciple, who transmitted it.

Their Persian texts, with French summaries, are now available in *Opera metaphysica et mystica* III. A complete French translation of Suhrawardi's cycle of tales is in preparation (scheduled for publication in 1972). See also Book II, Chapter V onward, above.


[^EII4-364]: Let us recall the essential point about this word, used frequently throughout the present work. *Imaginal* (Latin *imaginalis*) derives from *imago*, like other words formed in the same way (compare derivatives of *origo*: *originarius*, *originalis*, etc.). Latin distinguishes *imaginare*, to present an image as a mirror presents it (the function expressed by Arabic *mazharîya*, and above all the nature of the *'âlam al-Mithâl*, *mundus imaginalis*), from the deponent verb *imaginari*, to imagine or picture something to oneself.


[^EII4-365]: See our *Avicenne et le Récit visionnaire*, vol. I, pp. 18, 27, 31. We must distinguish the fact of *exitus* (departure) from spiritual death. If *exitus* is to be a real “departure” from this world, spiritual resurrection must have preceded it. Otherwise, those who are spiritually dead—that is, dead in the true sense—will never “leave” this world. Their *exitus* is only entry into the “second death,” for only those who are truly “alive” depart from this world. This teaching appears both in the *Gospel of Philip* and in an Ismaili treatise by Nasîroddîn Tûsî. Indeed, the entire spiritual education of Ismaili gnosis is founded on the “resurrection of the dead” (see *Kitâb al-'âlim wa'l-gholâm*, *Annuaire*, 1970–1971, pp. 226 ff.). Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î also teaches extensively on the subject in his commentary on the *Ziyârat al-Jâmi'a*.

[^EII4-382]: A member of the Order of St John added a notice to the notebook containing this autobiography, certifying that it was indeed “the very book, in his own handwriting, of Rulman Merswin, our founder—the book of the first four years of his spiritual life, as he wrote it and was bound to write it himself in obedience to God and to his secret companion, the dear Friend of God in the Highlands; just as the brothers of the *Ordo Sancti Johannis* found it, after Rulman Merswin's death, in a locked chest with his own silver seal affixed to the lid, on the feast of St Mary Magdalene [22 July], in the year of our Lord 1382” (ibid., p. 50).


[^EII4-383]: See the letter sent by the Friend of God to the commander of the house on the Green Island. In it he reminds the commander of the extraordinary bond between himself and Rulman: they had the same inward visions at the same time and experienced the same bodily pains at the same hour. He explains that this house, placed under the care of the Knights of St John four years after its foundation, was genuinely the work of the Spirit, not an arbitrary human initiative. “Now you must know, dear friend, that Rulman and I both had, on the same night of St Denis, the same vision in a dream. We dreamt that we should help one another and should plan to build a cloister (*Kloster*) in Strasbourg. After this dream, I came down to Rulman within ten days and immediately asked him whether he had recently dreamt anything strange. He answered yes, and told me that down here in Strasbourg he had had the very same dream that I had had up above (in the Highlands).” The Friend of God then explains how both men came to conclude that “the time for building new cloisters had passed,” before continuing: “Then, the following Christmas night, at midnight on that holy night of Christ, we both—he below and I above—felt at the same time, in our nature (that is, in our bodies), such pain and suffering that we each imagined ourselves at the point of death. And in this suffering we received a revelation, so clear that it could only be believed, that we must found a cloister in Strasbourg. Thus the Green Island came into being” (ibid., p. 53).


[^EII4-384]: Ibid., pp. 53–55. Hélyot's *Dictionnaire des Ordres religieux ou Histoire des Ordres monastiques, religieux et militaires*, vol. II (Migne, *Encyclopédie théologique*, vol. XXI), Paris, 1848, cols. 855 ff., gives an entirely outward, historical account of the Green Island. He knows Rulman Merswin's role well but does not mention the Friend of God. After completely restoring the Green Island, Rulman Merswin “gave it to the Order of St John of Jerusalem on condition that the chaplain brothers of that Order would celebrate the divine office there in perpetuity. This donation was accepted by Conrad de Brunsberg, Grand Prior of Germany, and later confirmed by Grand Master Raymond Bérenger and the general chapter.” Raymond Bérenger, from the Dauphiné, was the Order's thirty-second Grand Master (d. 1373).


[^EII4-385]: Ibid., p. 55. Letters and short works written respectively by the Friend of God and Rulman Merswin were carefully collected and copied by the brothers of St John into magnificent manuscripts. Treasured within the Order as sacred relics, these are the source of what we know about the Friend of God. In brief, the collection comprises (1) the “Great German Memorial” (*Das grosse deutsche Memorial*), of which a Latin translation was made but has not survived; (2) the “Master's Book” (*Das Meisterbuch*), a collection of illustrated documents owned by Grand Prior Conrad von Brunsberg but now lost; and (3) the “Book of Letters” (*Das Briefbuch*). See W. Rath's description of the surviving Strasbourg manuscripts, op. cit., pp. 119–127. Nearly all this material has been published and, to some extent, translated, but unfortunately it is scattered through unrelated books that are now unobtainable. There is an urgent need to bring it together in one corpus, with the original texts and full translations. Several scholars have attempted to pierce the Friend of God's “anonymity,” identifying him, for example, with Nicholas of Basel. We believe these attempts to identify the historical individual have taken the wrong path; in any case, they fall outside our present concern.

See our *L'homme de lumière dans le soufisme iranien*, p. 132.

Nor do we need to consider here the later history of the Sovereign Order of St John of Jerusalem: the failure, if not betrayal, of Grand Master Ferdinand von Hompesch, who handed Malta over to Bonaparte; the knights' election of Tsar Paul I as Grand Master, by which the Order became *ipso facto* an “ecumenical religion”; or the papal order known as the “Order of Malta,” which was in fact newly created by a *motu proprio* of Pope Pius VII in 1803.

(Montserrat with its twelve hermitages!). The connection between Montserrat and classical Weimar began when Wilhelm von Humboldt described his ascent of that mountain as a completion of the *Stimmung*, the mood or emotional atmosphere to which Goethe had given form in his poem *Die Geheimnisse*. Goethe later forgot that he had learned of Montserrat only some twenty years after composing the unfinished poem, and then through Humboldt's description. Hence his reply to the Göttingen students who questioned him about the poem in 1816: Goethe retrospectively felt that he had already seen the description of Montserrat at the time. That impression was doubtless mistaken chronologically, but it had a deeper truth—the same truth that allows us to recognize the same mystical mountain in Montserrat, Montsalvat, and Montségur. For the *ubi* (the “where”) of Mount Qâf is an *ubique* (“everywhere”), and that “everywhere” is the place where the Hidden Imam manifests himself. (We intentionally retain the etymological two-word spelling in our text.)

As long as *walâyat* and *wilâyat* (a Sufi concept too readily translated as “sainthood”) are simply confused with one another, there is little hope of clarifying what is actually at stake.

While Adam's other sons devote themselves to crafts that will enable them to gain the world, Seth dedicates himself wholly to divine service. The angel Gabriel brings from paradise a green (*sabz*) woolen (*sûf*) robe and clothes Seth in it. The angels visit him, then return to heaven and announce to the others: there is someone “clothed in wool” (*sâfî*) who devotes himself to divine service on earth! Thus, from the time of the prophet Seth, the name “those clothed in wool” is given to the group called “Sufis.” This tale illustrates the most common explanation of the word *Sufi*. Bîrûnî proposed another, connecting Arabic *sufi* with Greek *sophos*.
